Table d'hôte—A common table for guests. Fr.
Tableau vivant—A group in which statues or pictures are represented by living persons. Fr.
Tabula rasa—A smooth or blank tablet; a blank surface.
Tacent, satis laudant—Their silence is praise 50 enough. Ter.
Tâche sans tache—A task, or work, without a blemish. M.
Tacitæ magis et occultæ inimicitiæ sunt, quam indictæ et opertæ—Enmities unavowed and concealed are more to be feared than when open and declared. Cic.
Tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus—The secret wound still lives in her heart. Virg.

p.hi: Tact is one of the first of mental virtues, the absence of which is often fatal to the best talents. It supplies the place of many talents.

div.p: Tadeln kann ein jeder Bauer; besser machen wird ihm sauer—Every boor can find fault; it would baffle him to do better. Ger. Pr.
Tadeln können zwar die Thoren, / Aber klüger handeln nicht—Fools can find fault indeed, but they cannot act more wisely. Langbein.
Tædium vitæ—Weariness of life; disgust with existence. Gell.
Tages Arbeit, Abends Gäste, / Saure Wochen, 5 frohe Feste, / Sei dein künftig Zauberwort—Be work by day, guests at eve, weeks of toil, festive days of joy, the magic spell for thy future. Goethe.

p.hi: Take a bird from a clean nest.
Take a farthing from a thousand pounds, it will be a thousand pounds no longer.
Take a hair of the same dog that bit you, and it will heal the wound.
Take a stick to a Highland laddie, and it's no him you hurt, but his ancestors.

div.p: Take all that is given, whether wealth, / Or 10 love, or language; nothing comes amiss; / A good digestion turneth all to health. George Herbert.

p.hi: Take any subject of sorrowful regret, and see with how much pleasure it is associated.
Take away desire from the heart, and you take away the air from the earth.
Take care of the pence; the pounds will take care of themselves.
Take care to be an economist in prosperity; there is no fear of your not being one in adversity.

div.p: Take each man's censure, but reserve thy 15 judgment. Ham., i. 3.
Take everything easy (leicht); leave off dreaming and brooding (Grübeln), and you will be ever well guarded from a thousand evils. Uhland.

p.hi: Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her, for she is thy life.
Take from the philosopher the pleasure of being heard, and his desire for knowledge ceases.
Take heed, and beware of covetousness; for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.

div.p: Take heed of the vinegar of sweet wine. Pr. 20

p.hi: Take heed you find not that you do not seek.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart; and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
Take no thought for the morrow; for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.

div.p: Take no thought for your life, what ye shall 25 eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Jesus.

p.hi: Take not His name who made thy mouth in vain: / It gets thee nothing, and has no excuse.

div.p: Take note, take note, O world, / To be direct and honest is not safe. Othello, iii. 3.
Take physic, pomp; / Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel; / That thou mayst shake the superflux to them, / And show the heavens more just. Lear, iii. 4.

p.hi: Take the Muses' servants by the hand; / ... And where ye justly can commend, commend them; / And aiblins when they winna stand the test, / Wink hard, and say the folks hae done their best.

div.p: Take the showers as they fall, / ... Enough 30 if at the end of all / A little garden blossom. Tennyson.

p.hi: Take this rule, ... The best-bred child hath the best portion.
Take thou the beam out of thine own eye; then shalt thou see clearly to take the mote out of thy brother's.
Take thought for thy body with steadfast fidelity. The soul must see through these eyes alone; and if they are dim, the whole world is beclouded.

div.p: Take time in time, ere time be tint (lost). Sc. Pr. 35

p.hi: Take time in turning a corner.
Take up the torch and wave it wide, / The torch that lights Time's thickest gloom.
Take your thirst to the stream, as the dog does.

Taking, therefore, my opinion of the English from the virtues and vices practised among the vulgar, they at once present to a stranger all their faults, and keep their virtues up only for the inquiring of a philosopher.

div.p: Tale tuum carmen nobis, divine poeta, / Quale 40 sopor fessis—Thy song is to us, O heavenly bard, as sleep to wearied men. Virg.

p.hi: Talent alone cannot make a writer. There must be a man behind the book.
Talent for literature, thou hast such a talent? Believe it not, be slow to believe it! To speak or to write, Nature did not peremptorily order thee; but to work she did.
Talent forms itself in secret; character, in the great current of the world.

div.p: Talent has almost always this advantage (Vorsprung) over genius—that the former endures, the latter often explodes, or runs to waste (verpufft). Gutzkow.
Talent is a cistern; genius, a fountain. Whipple. 45

p.hi: Talent is a gift which God has imparted in secret, and which we reveal without knowing it.
Talent is some one faculty unusually developed; genius commands all the faculties.

Talent is something, but tact is everything. It is not a seventh sense, but is the life of all the five. It is the open eye, the quick ear, the judging taste, the keen smell, and the lively touch; it is the interpreter of all riddles, the surmounter of all difficulties, the remover of all obstacles.
Talent is that which is in a man's power; genius is that in whose power a man is.

div.p: Talent ist Form, Genie Stoff—Talent is form, 50 genius is substance. Gutzkow.

p.hi: Talent, lying in the understanding, is often inherited; genius, being the action of reason and imagination, rarely or never.
Talents angel-bright, if wanting worth, are shining instruments in false ambition's hand, to finish faults illustrious, and give infamy renown.
Talents give a man a superiority far more agreeable than that which proceeds from riches, birth, or employments, which are all external. Talents constitute our very essence.

div.p: Taliter qualiter—Such as it is.

Talk, except as the preparation for work, is 5 worth almost nothing; sometimes it is worth infinitely less than nothing; and becomes, little conscious of playing such a fatal part, the general summary of pretentious nothingnesses, and the chief of all the curses the posterity of Adam are liable to in this sublunary world. Carlyle.

p.hi: Talk of the devil and he'll appear.
Talk that does not end in action is better suppressed altogether.
Talk to him of Jacob's ladder, and he would ask the number of the steps.

div.p: Talkers are no good doers. Rich. III., i. 3.
Talking is one of the fine arts. Holmes. 10

p.hi: Talking is the disease of age.
Talking of love is making it.
Talking with a host is next best to talking with one's self.... He is wiser than to contradict his guest in any case; he lets him go on, he lets him travel.

div.p: Tam deest avaro quod habet, quam quod non habet—The miser is as much in want of that which he has as of that which he has not. Pub. Syr.

Tam diu discendum est, quum diu nescias, et, 15 si proverbio credimus, quam diu vivas—You must continue learning as long as you do not know, and, if the proverb is to be believed, as long as you live. Sen.
Tam Marte quam Minerva—As much by Mars as by Minerva; as much by courage as by wisdom. Pr.
Tam Marti quam Mercurio—As much for Mars as for Mercury; as well qualified for war as for business.
Tam felix utinam, quam pectore candidus, essem—Oh, that I were as happy as I am clear in conscience. Ovid.

p.hi: Tam lo'ed him like a vera brither; / They had been fou for weeks thegither.

div.p: Tamen me / Cum magnis vixisse invita fatebitur 20 usque / Invidia—Nevertheless, even envy, however unwilling, will have to admit that I have lived among great men. Hor.
Tandem fit surculus arbor—A twig in time becomes a tree. M.
Tandem poculum mœroris exhausit—He has exhausted at last the cup of grief. Cic.
[Greek: ta neura tou polemou]—The sinews of war. Pr.
Tangere ulcus—To touch a sore; to renew one's grief. Ter.
Tanquam in speculo—As in a mirror. 25
Tanquam nobilis—Noble by courtesy.
Tanquam ungues digitosque suos—As well as his nails and fingers; at his fingers' ends. Pr.
Tant de fiel entre-t-il dans l'âme des dévots?—Can so much gall find access in devout souls? Boileau.
Tant mieux—So much the better. Fr.
Tant pis—So much the worse. Fr. 30
Tant va la cruche à l'eau qu'à la fin elle se brise—The pitcher goes so often to the well that it is broken at last. Fr.
Tantæ molis erat Romanam condere gentem—Such a task it was to found the Roman race. Virg.
Tantæne animis cœlestibus iræ?—Can heavenly minds cherish such dire resentment? Virg.
Tanti eris aliis, quanti tibi fueris—You will be of as much value to others as you have been to yourself. Cic.
Tanto brevius omne tempus, quanto felicius—The 35 happier the moments the shorter. Pliny.
Tanto buon, che val niente—So good as to be good for nothing. It. Pr.
Tanto fortior, tanto felicior!—The more pluck, the better luck!

Tanto più di pregio reca all' opera l'umiltà dell' artista, quanto più aggiunge di valori al numero la nullità del zero—The modesty of the artist adds as much to the merit of his work as does a cipher (of no value in itself) to the number to which it is joined. Bernini.
Tanto vale la Messa detta quanto la cantata—A mass is as good said as sung. It. Pr.
Tantum quantum—Just as much as. 40
Tantum religio potuit suadere malorum—Could such cruelties have been perpetrated in the name of religion? Lucret. in reference to the sacrifice of Iphigenia.
Tantum series juncturaque / Tantum de medio sumptis accedit honoris—Such is the power of order and arrangement: so much grace may be imparted to subjects from common life. Hor.
Tantum vertice in auras / Aetherias quantum radice in Tartara tendit—Its summit stretches as far into the upper ether as its root into the nether deep.
Tantus amor laudum, tantæ est victoria curæ—Such is the love of praise, so great the anxiety for victory. Virg.

Tapfer ist der Löwesieger, / Tapfer ist der 45 Weltbezwinger, / Tapfer wer sich selbst bezwang—Brave is the lion-vanquisher, brave is the world-subduer, but braver he who has subdued himself. J. G. Herder.
Tarda sit illa dies, et nostro serior ævo—Slow may that day approach, and long after our time. Ovid.
Tarda solet magnis rebus inesse fides—Men are slow to repose confidence in undertakings of magnitude. Ovid.
Tarde, quæ credita lædunt, credimus—We are slow to believe that which, if believed, would work us harm. Ovid.
Tarde sed tute—Slow but sure. M.
Tarde venientibus ossa—To those who come late 50 the bones. Pr.
Tardiora sunt remedia quam mala—Remedies are slower in their operation than diseases. Tac.

p.hi: Tasks in hours of insight willed, / In hours of gloom must be fulfilled.
Taste can only be educated by contemplation, not of the tolerably good, but of the truly
Taste depends upon those finer emotions which make the organisation of the soul.

Taste, if it mean anything but a paltry connoisseurship, must mean a general susceptibility to truth and nobleness; a sense to discern and a heart to love and reverence all beauty, order, goodness, wheresoever found and in whatsoever form and accompaniment.
Taste is the very maker of judgment.
Taste may change, but inclination never.

div.p: [Greek: ta syka syka, tên skaphên de skaphên onomazôn]—Calling 5 a fig a fig, and a spade a spade. Plut.
Taurum tollet qui vitulum sustulerit—He who has carried the calf will be able by and by to carry the ox. Pr.
Te Deum laudamus—We praise Thee, O God.
Te digna sequere—Follow what is worthy of thee. M.

Te, Fortuna, sequor: procul hinc jam fœdera sunto: / Credidimus fatis, utendum est judice bello—Thee, Fortune, I follow; hence far all treaties past; to fate I commit myself, and the arbitrament of war. Lucan on the crossing of the Rubicon by Cæsar.
Te hominem esse memento—Remember thou 10 art a man.
Te sine nil altum mens inchoat—Without thee my mind originates nothing lofty. Virg. to Mæcenas.

p.hi: Teach me to feel another's woe, / To hide the fault I see; / That mercy I to others show, / That mercy show to me.
Teach self-denial, and make its practice pleasurable, and you create for the world a destiny more sublime than ever issued from the brain of the wildest dreamer.
Teach your children poetry; it opens the mind, lends grace to wisdom, and makes the heroic virtues hereditary.

div.p: Teaching has not a tithe of the efficacy of 15 training. Horace Mann.

p.hi: Teaching is of more importance than exhortation.
Tears are due to human misery.

div.p: Tears are often to be found where there is 20 little sorrow, and the deepest sorrow without tears. Johnson.

p.hi: Tears are the deluge of sin and the world's sacrifice.
Tears are the symbol of the inability of the soul to restrain its emotion and retain its self-command.

Tears, idle tears, I know not what they mean, / Tears from the depth of some divine despair / Rise in the heart and gather in the eyes, / In looking on the happy autumn fields, / And thinking of the days that are no more.
Tears of joy are the dew in which the sun of righteousness is mirrored.

div.p: Tears of joy, like summer rain-drops, are 25 pierced by sunbeams. H. Ballou.
Tecum habita—Live with yourself; keep within your means.

p.hi: Teeth, hair, nails, and the human species, prosper not when separated from their place. A wise man, being informed of this, should not totally forsake his native home.

div.p: Tel brille au second rang, qui s'éclipse au premier—Some who are eclipsed in the first rank may shine in the second. Voltaire.
Tel coup de langue est pire qu'un coup de 30 lance—Such a stroke with the tongue is worse than one with a lance. Fr. Pr.

Tel, en vous lisant, admire chaque trait, / Qui dans le fond de l'âme vous craint et vous hait—Such a one, in reading your work, admires every line, but, at the bottom of his soul, he fears and hates you. Boileau.
Tel excelle à rimer qui juge sottement—Some excel in rhyme who reason foolishly. Boileau.
Tel maître, tel valet—Like master, like man. Fr. Pr.
Tel père, tel fils—Like father, like son. Fr. Pr.

Tel vous semble applaudir, qui vous raille et 35 vous joue; / Aimez qu'on vous conseille, et non pas qu'on vous loue—Such a one seems to applaud, while he is really ridiculing you; attach yourself to those who advise you rather than to those who praise. Boileau.

p.hi: Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon.
"Tell me how you bear so blandly the assuming ways of wild young people?" Truly they would be unbearable if I had not also been unbearable myself as well.
Tell me not, in mournful numbers, / "Life is but an empty dream," / For the soul is dead that slumbers, / And things are not what they seem.
Tell me what you like, and I will tell you what you are.

div.p: Tell me where is fancy bred, / Or in the heart, 40 or in the head? / How begot, how nourishéd? / It is engender'd in the eyes, / With gazing fed. Mer. of Venice, iii. 2.

p.hi: Tell me with whom you associate, and I will tell you who you are; if I know what it is with which you occupy yourself, I know what you may become.

div.p: Tell the truth and shame the devil. 1 Henry IV., iii. 1.
Telum imbelle sine ictu—A feeble dart thrown without effect. Virg.
Temeritas est florentis ætatis, prudentia senescentis—Rashness belongs to youth, prudence to old age. Cic.
Temper—a weapon that we hold by the blade. 45 J. M. Barrie.
Temper is so good a thing that we should never lose it. (?)

p.hi: Temperament lies behind mood; back of the caprice of will lies the fate of character; back of both is the bias of family; back of that, the tyranny of race; still deeper, the power of climate, of soil, of geology, the whole physical and moral environment. Still we are free men only so far as we rise above these.
Temperance and labour are the two best physicians of man.
Temperance is a bridle of gold.
Temperance is a tree which has for its root very little contentment, and for its fruit calm and peace.
Temperance is the nurse of chastity.

div.p: Tempi passati!—Bygone times! Joseph II. at sight of a picture representing a predecessor doing penance to the Pope.
Templa quam dilecta!—How lovely are thy temples! M. of the Duke of Buckingham, whose family name is Temple.

Tempora labuntur, tacitisque senescimus annis; 5 / Et fugiunt fræno non remorante dies—Time glides away, and we grow older through the noiseless years; the days flee away, and are restrained by no rein. Ovid.
Tempora mutantur, nos et mutamur in illis—Times change, and we change with them. Kaiser Lothar I.
Tempore ducetur longo fortasse cicatrix; / Horrent admotas vulnera cruda manus—A wound may, perhaps, through time be closed, but, when fresh, it shrinks from the touch. Ovid.

p.hi: Tempted Fate will leave the loftiest star.

div.p: Tempus anima rei—Time is the soul of business.
Tempus edax rerum—Time, the devourer of all 10 things. Ovid.
Tempus erit quo vos speculum vidisse pigebit—The time will come when it will disgust you to look in a mirror. Ovid.
Tempus est quædam pars æternitatis—Time is a certain fraction of eternity. Cic.
Tempus ferax, tempus edax rerum—Time the producer, time the devourer of things.
Tempus fugit—Time flies.
Tempus in agrorum cultu consumere dulce 15 est—It is delightful to spend one's time in the tillage of the fields. Ovid.
Tempus omnia revelat—Time reveals all things.
Tempus rerum imperator—Time is sovereign over all things. M.

p.hi: Ten censure wrong for one who writes amiss.

div.p: [Greek: tên de malista gamein, hêtis sethen engythi naiei]—Be sure you take for wife a woman of your own neighbourhood. Hesiod.
Tenax et fidelis—Steadfast and faithful. M. 20
Tenax propositi—Tenacious of his purpose. M.

p.hi: Tendency to sentimental whining or fierce intolerance may be ranked among the surest symptoms of little souls and inferior intellects.
Tenderness is the repose of passion.

div.p: Tenebo—I will hold. M. 25
Teneros animos aliena opprobria sæpe / Absterrent vitiis—The disgrace of others often deters tender minds from vice. Hor.
Tenet insanabile multos / Scribendi cacoëthes—An incurable itch for writing possesses many. Juv.
Tenez la bride haute à votre fils—Keep a tight hand over your son (lit. hold the bridle high). Fr. Pr.
Tenir le haut du pavé—To keep the best place (lit. the highest side of the pavement). Fr. Pr.

Tentanda via est qua me quoque possim / 30 Tollere humo, victorque virûm volitare per ora—I too must attempt a way by which I may raise myself above the ground, and soar triumphant through the lips of men. Virg.

p.hi: Tenterden steeple was the cause of Goodwin Sands.

div.p: Ter conatus ibi collo dare brachia circum, / Ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago—Thrice I attempted to throw my arms round her neck there, and her ghost, thrice clutched in vain, eluded my grasp. Virg.
Teres atque rotundum—Smooth-polished and rounded. Hor.
Terminus a quo—The point from which anything starts.
Terminus ad quem—The point of destination. 35
Terra antiqua, potens armis atque ubere glebæ—An ancient land, powerful in arms and in the fertility of its soil. Virg., of Italy.
Terra firma—Dry land, in contradistinction to sea.
Terra incognita—An unknown land or domain of things.
Terra innanzi, e terra poi—Earth originally, and earth finally. It. Pr.
Terra malos homines nunc educat, atque 40 pusillos—The earth now supports many bad and weak men. Juv.
Terræ filius—A son of the earth; a man of obscure or low origin. Pers.
Terram cœlo miscent—They mingle heaven and earth.

p.hi: Terrible penalty, with the ass-ears or without them, inevitable as death, written for ever in heaven, against all who, like Midas, misjudge the inner and the upper melodies, and prefer gold to goodness, desire to duty, falsehood to fact, wild nature to God, and a sensual piping Pan to a high-souled, wise-hearted, and spirit-breathing Apollo.
Ed., apropos to the fable of Midas.

div.p: Tertium quid—A third something, produced by the union or interaction of two opposites.
Tertium sal—A third salt; a neutral salt; the 45 union of an acid and an alkali.
Tertius e cœlo cecidit Cato—A third Cato has come down from heaven. Juv., in mockery.
[Greek: tês aretês hidrôta theoi proparoithen ethêkan]—The gods have placed sweat in front of virtue. Hesiod.

p.hi: Testimony is like an arrow shot from a long bow; the force of it depends upon the strength of the hand that draws it. Argument is like an arrow from a cross-bow, which has equal force though shot by a child.

div.p: Tête-à-tête—Face to face; a private conversation. Fr.
Tête d'armée!—Head of the army! Last words 50 of Napoleon.
Tête de fou ne blanchit jamais—A fool's head never grows grey. Pr.

Teuer ist mir der Freund, doch auch den Feind kann ich nützen; / Zeigt mir der Freund, was ich kann, lehrt mich der Feind, was ich soll—Dear is to me the friend, yet can I make even my very foe do me a friend's part. My friend shows me what I can do; my foe teaches me what I should do. Schiller.

p.hi: That action is not warrantable which either blushes to beg a blessing, or, having succeeded, dares not present a thanksgiving.

div.p: That but this blow / Might be the be-all and the end-all here, / But here, upon this bank and shoal of time, / We'd jump the life to come. Macb., i. 7.
That carries anger as the flint bears fire; / Who, much enforcèd, shows a hasty spark, / And straight is cold again. Jul. Cæs., iv. 3.

p.hi: That cause is strong which has not a multitude, but one strong man behind it.
That circle of beings, which dependence gathers round us, is almost ever unfriendly.

div.p: That civility is best which excludes all superfluous formality. (?)
That cutting up, and parcelling, and labelling, 5 of the indivisible human soul into what are called "faculties," I have from of old eschewed, and even hated. Carlyle.
That death's unnatural that kills for loving. Othello, v. 2.

p.hi: That elevation of mind which we see in moments of peril, if it is uncontrolled by justice, and strives only for its own advantage, becomes a crime.
That friendship only is, indeed, genuine when two friends, without speaking a word to each other, can, nevertheless, find happiness in being together.
That friendship, which is exerted in too wide a sphere, becomes totally useless.

div.p: That gentleman who sells an acre of land, 10 sells an ounce of credit. Lord Burleigh.

p.hi: That golden key that opes the palace of eternity.
That government is the best which makes government unnecessary.

That great mystery of time, were there no other; the illimitable, silent never-resting thing called "time," rolling, rushing on, swift, silent like an all-embracing oceantide, on which we and all the universe swim like exhalations, like apparitions which are and then are not—this is for ever very literally a miracle, a thing to strike us dumb; for we have no word to speak about it.
That grief is light which is capable of counsel.

div.p: That he is mad 'tis true; 'tis true, 'tis pity; / 15 And pity 'tis 'tis true. Ham., ii. 2.
That in the captain's but a choleric word, / Which in the soldier is flat blasphemy. Meas. for Meas., ii. 2.

p.hi: That intention which fixes upon God as its only end will keep men steady in their purposes, and deliver them from being the jest and scorn of fortune.
That is a most wretched fortune which is without an enemy.
That is a treacherous friend against whom you must always be on your guard. Such a friend is wine.

div.p: That is always best which gives me to myself. 20 Emerson.

p.hi: That is but an empty purse that is full of other men's money.
That is friendship which is not feigned.
That is gold that is worth gold.

That is indeed a twofold knowledge which profits alike by the folly of the foolish and the wisdom of the wise. It is both a shield and a sword; it borrows its security from the darkness, and its confidence from the light.

div.p: That is not a council wherein there are no 25 sages. Hitopadesa.

p.hi: That is not a duty in which there is not virtue.
That is not possible which is impossible.
That is not virtue from which fear approacheth us.
That is the best part of beauty which a picture cannot express.

div.p: That is the best part of each writer which has 30 nothing private in it. Emerson.

p.hi: That is the briefest and sagest of maxims which bids us "meddle not."
That is the true light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
That is the true season of love, when we believe that we alone can love, that no one could ever have loved so before us, and that no one will love in the same way after us.
That is true love which is always the same, whether you give everything or deny everything to it.

div.p: That is well spoken that is well taken. Pr. 35

p.hi: That last infirmity of noble minds.
That learning which thou gettest by thy own observation and experience is far beyond that which thou gettest by precept; as the knowledge of a traveller exceeds that which is got by reading.
That life is long which answers life's great end.

div.p: That man has advanced far in the study of 40 morals who has mastered the difference between pride and vanity. Chamfort.

p.hi: That man is always happy who is in the presence of something which he cannot know to the full, which he is always going on to know.
That man is an ill husband of his honour that entereth into any action, the failing wherein may disgrace him more than the carrying of it through can honour him.
That man is learned who reduceth his learning to practice.
That man is little to be envied whose patriotism would not gain force upon the plain of Marathon, or whose piety would not grow warmer among the ruins of Iona.

div.p: That man lives twice that lives the first life 45 well. Herrick.

p.hi: That man may last, but never lives, / Who much receives but nothing gives; / Whom none can love, whom none can thank—/ Creation's blot, creation's blank.

div.p: That man that hath a tongue, I say, is no man, / If with his tongue he cannot win a woman. Two Gent. of Verona, ii. 1.

p.hi: That man will never be a perfect gentleman who lives only with gentlemen. To be a man of the world we must view that world in every grade and in every perspective.
That Mirabeau understood how to act with others, and by others—this was his genius, this was his originality, this was his greatness.

div.p: That must be true which all men say. Pr. 50

p.hi: That nation is in the enjoyment of liberty which stands by its own strength, and does not depend on the will of another.
That net that holds no great, takes little fish.
That one man should die ignorant who had capacity for knowledge, this I call tragedy.
That one will not, another will.

div.p: That philanthropy has surely a flaw in it which 5 cannot sympathise with the oppressor equally as with the oppressed. Lowell.

p.hi: That rich man is great who thinketh not himself great because he is rich; the proud man (who is the poor man) braggeth outwardly but beggeth inwardly; he is blown up, but not full.
That single effort by which we stop short in the down-hill path to perdition is of itself a greater exertion of virtue than a hundred acts of justice.
That souls which are created for one another so seldom find each other and are generally divided, that in the moments of happiest union least recognise each other—that is a sad riddle!

div.p: That State must sooner or later perish where the majority triumphs and unintelligence (Unverstand) decides. Schiller.
That state of life is alone suitable to a man in 10 which and for which he was born, and he who is not led abroad by great objects is far happier at home. Goethe.
That strain again! It had a dying fall: / Oh, it came o'er my ear like the sweet sound / That breathes upon a bank of violets, / Giving and stealing odour! Twelfth Night, i. 1.

p.hi: That suit is best that best fits me.
That that comes of a hen will scrape.

div.p: That that is, is. As You Like It, iv. 2.

That the voice of the common people is the voice 15 of God, is as full of falsehood as commonness. For who sees not that those black-mouthed hounds, upon the mere scent of opinion, as freely spend their mouths in hunting counter, or, like Actæon's dogs, in chasing an innocent man to death, as if they followed the chase of truth itself, in a fresh scent? A. Warwick.

p.hi: That thee is sent receive in buxomness: / The wrestling of this world asketh a fall. / Here is no home, here is but wilderness. / Forth, pilgrim, forth—on, best out of thy stall. / Look up on high, and thank the God of all.

That thought I regard as true which is fruitful to myself, which is connected with the rest of my thoughts, and at the same time helps me on. Now it is not only possible, but natural, that such a thought should not connect itself with the mind of another, nor help him on ... consequently he will regard it as false. Once we are thoroughly convinced of this, we shall never enter upon controversies.

div.p: That ugly treason of mistrust. Mer. of Ven., iii. 2.

p.hi: That unity which has not its origin in the multitude is tyranny.

div.p: That very law which moulds a tear, / And bids 20 it trickle from its source; / That law preserves the earth a sphere, / And guides the planets in their course. Rogers.

p.hi: That vice has often proved an emancipator of the mind is one of the most humiliating, but also one of the most unquestionable, facts in history.
That virtue which requires to be ever guarded is scarcely worth the sentinel.

That voluntary debility, which modern language is content to term indolence, will, if it is not counteracted by resolution, render in time the strongest faculties lifeless, and turn the flame to the smoke of virtue.

That warrior on his strong war-horse, fire flashes through his eyes; force dwells in his arm and heart; but warrior and war-horse are a vision; a revealed force, nothing more. Stately they tread the earth, as if it were firm substance. Fool! the earth is but a film; it cracks in twain, and warrior and war-horse sink beyond plummet's sounding.

div.p: That we devote ourselves to God is seen / In 25 living just as though no God there were. Browning.
That we shall die, we know; 'tis but the time / And drawing days out, that men stand upon. Julius Cæsar, iii. 1.

p.hi: That we should find our national existence depend on selling manufactured cotton at a farthing an ell cheaper than any other people, is a most narrow stand for a great nation to base itself on.

div.p: That we would do, / We should do when we would; for this "would" changes, / And hath abatements and delays as many / As there are tongues, are hands, are accidents; / And then this "should" is like a spendthrift's sigh, / That hurts by easing. Ham., iv. 7.

p.hi: That were but a sorry art which could be comprehended all at once; the last point of which could be seen by one just entering its precincts.

div.p: That which builds is better than that which is 30 built. Emerson.

p.hi: That which can be done with perfect convenience and without loss, is not always the thing that most needs to be done, or which we are most imperatively required to do.
That which each man can do best, not but his Maker can teach him.
That which God writes on thy forehead thou wilt come to.
That which hath been is now; and that which is to be hath already been.

div.p: That which I crave may everywhere be had, / 35 With me I bring the one thing needful—love. Goethe.
That which in mean men we entitle patience, / Is pale cold cowardice in noble breasts. Rich. II., i. 2.

p.hi: That which, intellectually considered, we call Reason, considered in relation to nature we call Spirit.
That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
That which is good to take is good to keep.

div.p: That which is in the midst of fools is made 40 known. Bible.

p.hi: That which is not allotted the hand cannot reach, and what is allotted will find you wherever you may be.
That which is past is gone and irrevocable, and wise men have enough to do with things present and to come; therefore they do but trifle with themselves that labour in past matters.
That which is possible is ever possible.
That which is truly and indeed characteristic of the man is known only to God.

div.p: That which makes men happy is activity (die Thätigkeit), which, first producing what is good, soon changes evil itself into good by power working in a god-like manner. Goethe.
That which one least anticipates soonest 5 comes to pass. Pr.

p.hi: That which produces and maintains cheerfulness is nothing but activity.
That which proves too much proves nothing.
That which seems to be wealth may in verity be only the gilded index of far-reaching ruin; a wrecker's handful of coin gleaned from the beach to which he has beguiled an argosy.
That which the droning world, chained to appearances, will not allow the realist to say in his own words, it will suffer him to say in proverbs without contradiction.

div.p: That which the sun doth not now see will be 10 visible when the sun is out, and the stars are fallen from heaven. Sir Thomas Browne.

p.hi: That which two will takes effect.

div.p: That which upholdeth him, that thee upholds—His honour. King John, iii. 1.

p.hi: That which was bitter to endure may be sweet to remember.
That which we do not believe we cannot adequately say, though we may repeat the words never so often.

div.p: That which we have we prize not to the 15 worth; / But being lacked and lost, why then we rake its value. Much Ado, iv. 1.

p.hi: That which we may live without we need not much covet.
That which will not be butter must be made into cheese.
That which will not be spun, let it not come between the spindle and the distaff.
That woman is despicable who, having children, ever feels ennui.

div.p: That wretchedness which fate has rendered 20 voiceless and tuneless is not the least wretched, but the most. Carlyle.

p.hi: That's a lee wi' a lid on, / And a brass handle to tak ho'd on.
That's my good that does me good.
That's the best gown that goes up and down the house.

div.p: That's the humour of it. Henry V., ii. 1.

That's what a man wants in a wife, mostly: 25 he wants to make sure o' one fool as'll tell him he's wise. But there's some men can do wi'out that—they think so much o' themselves a'ready—an' that's how it is there's old bachelors. George Eliot.

p.hi: The abandoning of some lower end in obedience to a higher aim is often made the very condition of securing the lower one.
The abiding city and post at which we can live and die is still ahead of us, it would appear.

The absent one is an ideal person; those who are present seem to one another to be quite commonplace. It is a silly thing that the ideal is, as it were, ousted by the real; that may be the reason why to the moderns their ideal only manifests itself in longing.
The absent party is still faulty.

div.p: The accepted and betrothed lover has lost the 30 wildest charms of his maiden in her acceptance of him. She was heaven whilst he pursued her as a star—she cannot be heaven if she stoops to such a one as he. Emerson.

p.hi: The accusing spirit, which flew up to heaven's chancery with the oath, blushed as he gave it in; and the recording angel, as he wrote it down, dropped a tear upon the word and blotted it out for ever.
The acknowledgment of our weakness is the first step towards repairing our loss.
The actual well seen is the ideal.
The advice that is wanted is commonly unwelcome; that which is not wanted is evidently impertinent.

div.p: The affection of young ladies is of as rapid 35 growth as Jack's beanstalk, and reaches up to the sky in a night. Thackeray.

p.hi: The afflictions of earth exalt the spirit and lift the soul to God.
The age made no sign when Shakespeare, its noblest son, passed away.
The age of chivalry is gone. That of sophisters, economists, and calculators has succeeded; and the glory of Europe is extinguished for ever.
The age of curiosity, like that of chivalry, is ended, properly speaking, gone. Yet perhaps only gone to sleep.

div.p: The age of great men is going; the epoch of 40 the anthill, of life in multiplicity, is beginning. Amiel.

p.hi: The age of miracles past! The age of miracles is for ever here.
The ages of greatest public spirit are not always eminent for private virtue.
The agnosticism of doubt is as far from the agnosticism of devotion as blindness for want of vision from blindness through excess of light.

The aim of all morality, truly conceived, is to furnish men with a standard of action and a motive to work by, which shall not intensify each man's selfishness, but raise him ever more and more above it.

div.p: The aim of education should be to teach us 45 rather how to think than what to think. Beattie.

p.hi: The aim of life is work, or there is no aim at all.
The aim of the legislator should be, not truth, but expediency.
The air seems nimble with the glad, / Quaint fancies of our childhood dear.
The alchemists in their search for gold discovered other things of greater value.

div.p: The all in all of faith is that we believe; of 50 knowledge, what we know, as well as how much and how well. Goethe.

p.hi: The alpha and omega of Socialism is the transmutation of private competing capital into united collective capital.

The amateur, however weak may be his efforts at imitation, need not be discouraged, ... for one advances to an idea the more surely and steadily the more accurately and precisely he considers individual objects. Only it will not do to measure one's self with artists; every one must go on in his own style.
The ambitious are ever followed by adulation, for such alone receive most pleasure from flattery.

div.p: The amount of intellect necessary to please us 5 is a most accurate measure of the amount of intellect we have ourselves. Helvetius.

p.hi: The ancient Spartan custom of killing weak-bodied children is not much crueller than that of propagating weak-minded ones.
The ancients tell us what is best; but we must learn of the moderns what is fittest.
The anger of a strong man can always bide its time.
The animal is capable of enjoyment, only man is capable of serenity of mind and gladness of heart.

div.p: The animals look for man's intentions right 10 into his eyes. Even a rat, when you hunt him and bring him to bay, looks you in the eye. H. Powers.
The apparel oft proclaims the man. Ham., i. 3.

p.hi: The apprehension and representation of what is individual is the very life of art.

div.p: The apprehension of the good / Gives but the greater feeling to the worse. Rich. II., i. 3.
The archer who overshoots the mark misses, 15 as well as he that falls short of it. Pr.

p.hi: The argument all bare is of more worth / Than when it hath my added praise beside.
The army is a good book to open to study human life.
The army is a school in which the niggardly become generous and the generous prodigal.
The arrows of sarcasm are barbed with contempt.... It is the sneer in the satire or the ridicule that galls or wounds.

div.p: The art of exalting lowliness and giving greatness 20 to little things is one of the noblest functions of genius. Palgrave.

p.hi: The art of living is like every other art; only the capacity is born with us; it must be learned and practised with incessant care.
The art of pleasing is the art of deceiving.
The art was his to break vexations with a ready jest.
The art which is produced hastily will also perish hastily.

div.p: The artist belongs to his work, not the work 25 to the artist. Novalis.

p.hi: The artist is the son of his age; but pity for him if he is its pupil, or even its favourite.

div.p: The artist must conceive with warmth (mit Feuer) and execute with coolness. Winkelmann.

p.hi: The artist stands higher than the art, higher than the object: he uses art for his own purposes, and deals with the object after his own fashion.
The artist's vocation is to send light into the depths of the human heart.

div.p: The arts of deceit and cunning do continually 30 grow weaker, and less effectual and serviceable to them that use them. Tillotson.

p.hi: The astonishing intellect that occupies itself in splitting hairs, and not in twisting some kind of cordage and effectual draught tackle to take the road with, is not to me the most astonishing of intellects. I want twisted cordage, steady pulling, and a peaceable bass tone of voice; not split hairs, hysterical spasmodics, and treble.
The Atlantic Ocean beat Mrs. Partington. She was excellent at a slop or a puddle, but she should not have meddled with a tempest.
The atmosphere of moral sentiment is a region of grandeur which reduces all material magnificence to toys, yet opens to every wretch that has reason the doors of the universe.
The attainment of a truer and truer aristocracy, or government again by the Best,—all that democracy ever meant lies there.

div.p: The attempt, and not the deed, / Confounds us. 35 Macb., ii. 2.

p.hi: The attraction of love is in an inverse proportion to the attraction of the Newtonian philosophy.
The author is often obscure to readers because, as has been said, he proceeds from the thought to the expression, whereas they proceed from the expression to the thought.
The awful shadow of some unseen Power / Floats, though unseen, among us.
The axe of intemperance has lopped off his green boughs and left him a withered trunk.

div.p: The axis of the earth sticks out visibly through 40 the centre of each and every town or city. Holmes.

p.hi: The back of one door is the face of another.
The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways.
The bad fortune of the good turns their faces up to heaven; and the good fortune of the bad bows their heads down to the earth.

div.p: The bad (böse) man has not only the good, but 45 also the bad against him. Bischer.

p.hi: The barrenest of mortals is the sentimentalist.
The basest thought about man is that he has no spiritual nature; and the foolishest, that he has, or should have, no animal nature.
The basis of good manners is self-reliance.
The battle of belief against unbelief is the never-ending battle.
The beams of joy are made hotter by reflection.

div.p: The bearers of the thyrsus (the symbol of the Bacchus inspiration) are many, but the Bacchants (the truly inspired) are few. Gr. Pr.
The bearing and the training of a child is 5 woman's wisdom. Tennyson.

p.hi: The beaten road is the safest.
The beautiful is a manifestation of secret laws of nature, which, but for its appearance, had been for ever concealed from us.
The beautiful is higher than the good; the beautiful includes in it the good.
The beautiful is like sunshine to the world; the beautiful lives for ever.

div.p: The beautiful rests on the foundation of the 10 necessary. Emerson.

p.hi: The beggar is never out of the fashion, or limpeth awkwardly behind it.
The beggar is not expected to become bail or surety for any one.
The beggar is not required to put on court mourning.
The beggar is the only free man in the universe.

div.p: The beggar is the only man in the universe 15 who is not obliged to study appearances. Lamb.

p.hi: The beggar weareth all colours, fearing none.
The beggar's costume hath undergone less change than the Quaker's.

The beginning, and very nearly the end, of bodily education for a girl, is to make sure that she can stand and sit upright; the ankle vertical, and firm as a marble shaft; the waist elastic as a reed, and as unfatiguable.
The beginning of all good law, and nearly the end of it, is that every man shall do good work for his bread, and that every man shall have good bread for his work.

div.p: The beginning of all temptations and wickedness 20 is the fickleness of our own minds and want of trust in God. Thomas à Kempis.
The beginning of creation (in man's soul as in Nature) is light. Till the eye have vision, the whole members are in bonds. Carlyle.

p.hi: The beginning of inquiry is disease.
The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention before it be meddled with.

div.p: The beginning of wisdom is to look fixedly on clothes (i.e. symbols), till they become transparent. Carlyle.
The being whose strength exceeds its necessities 25 is strong; the being whose necessities exceed its strength is feeble. Rousseau.

p.hi: The bell strikes one. We take no note of time / But for its loss.
The belly is chains to the hands and fetters to the feet. He who is a slave to his belly seldom worships God.
The beloved of the Almighty are the rich who have the humility of the poor, and the poor who have the magnanimity of the rich.
The benefactors of mankind are those who grumble to the best purpose. Grumbling has raised man from the condition of the gorilla to that of the judge on the bench of justice.

div.p: The benevolent heart will not solicit, but command 30 our reverence and applause. Arliss.

p.hi: The benevolent person is always by preference busy on the essentially bad.
The best advice is, Follow good advice and hold old age in highest honour.
The best architecture is the expression of the mind of manhood by the hands of childhood.
The best courages are but beams of the Almighty.

div.p: The best effect of any book is that it excites 35 the reader to self-activity. Carlyle.

p.hi: The best fish swim near the bottom.
The best friends in the world may differ sometimes.
The best gifts find the fewest admirers, and most men mistake the bad for the good.
The best government is that which teaches us to govern ourselves.

div.p: The best independence is to have something to 40 do, and something that can be done, and done most perfectly in solitude. P. G. Hamerton.

p.hi: The best is but in season best.
The best is not to be explained by words.
The best laid schemes o' mice an' men / Gang aft a-gley, / And lea'e us naught but grief and pain / For promised joy.

div.p: The best loneliness is when no human eye has 45 rested on our face for a whole day. Auerbach.

p.hi: The best may slip, and the most cautious fall;/ He's more than mortal that ne'er err'd at all.
The best mirror is an old friend.
The best of angels do not live in community, but by themselves.
The best of lessons, for a good many people, would be to listen at a keyhole. It is a pity for such that the practice is dishonourable.

div.p: The best of men/ That e'er wore earth about 50 him was a sufferer; / A soft, meek, patient, humble, tranquil spirit; / The first true gentleman that ever breathed. Decker.

p.hi: The best of the sport is to do the deed and say nothing.
The best part of our knowledge is that which teaches us where knowledge leaves off and ignorance begins.
The best path through life is the highway.
The best portraits are those in which there is a slight mixture of caricature.

div.p: The best preservative to keep the mind in 55 health is the faithful admonition of a friend. Bacon.

p.hi: The best remedy against an ill man is much ground between both.
The best rules to form a young man are, to talk little, to hear much, to reflect alone upon what has passed in company, to distrust one's own opinions, and value others' that deserve it.
The best self-forgetfulness is to look at the things of the world with attention and love.
The best son is not enough a son.
The best, the only correct actions are those which demand no explanation and no apology.
The best thing I know between France and England is the sea.

div.p: The best thing which we derive from history 5 is the enthusiasm which it raises in us. Goethe.

p.hi: The best things are worst to come by.
The best use of money is to pay debts.
The best way to come to truth is to examine things as they really are, and not to conclude they are, as we have been taught by others to imagine.
The best way to make the audience laugh is by first laughing yourself.

div.p: The best way to please one half of the world is 10 not to mind what the other half says. Goldsmith.

p.hi: The best work in the world is done on the quiet.
The best work never was, nor ever will be, done for money at all.
The best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from unmarried or childless men, which, both in affection and means, have married and endowed the public.

div.p: The better a man is morally, the less conscious 15 he is of his virtues. The greater the artist, the more aware he must be of his shortcomings. Froude.

p.hi: The better day the better deed.

div.p: The better I know men the more I admire dogs. (?)
The better part of valour is discretion. 1 Hen. IV., v. 4.

p.hi: The better you understand yourself, the less cause you will find to love yourself.

div.p: The Bible contains many truths as yet undiscovered. 20 Butler.

p.hi: The Bible contains more true sublimity, more exquisite beauty, more pure morality, more important history, and finer strains of poetry and eloquence than can be collected from all other books, in whatever age or language they have been written.

(The Bible) contains plain teaching for men of every rank of soul and state of life, which so far as they honestly and implicitly obey, they will be happy and innocent to the utmost powers of their nature, and capable of victory over all adversities, whether of temptation or pain.
The Bible is the great family chronicle of the Jews.

The Bible of a nation, the practically credited God's message to a nation, is, beyond all else, the authentic biography of its heroic souls. This is the real record of the appearances of God in the history of a nation; this, which all men to the marrow of their bones can believe, and which teaches all men what the nature of this universe, when you go to work in it, really is.

div.p: The Bible tells us what Christian graces are; 25 but it is in the struggle of life that we are to find them. Beecher.

p.hi: The biography of a nation embraces all its works. No trifle is to be neglected. A mouldering medal is a letter of twenty centuries.
The bird of wisdom flies low, and seeks her food under hedges; the eagle himself would be starved if he always soared aloft and against the sun.
The birds without barn or storehouse are fed: / From them let us learn to trust for our bread.
The birth of a child is the imprisonment of a soul.

div.p: The birth of a golden deer is impossible. Hitopadesa. 30

The bishop has set his foot in it, i.e., the broth is singed. Pr. (The explanation of which, according to Grose, is: Whenever a bishop passed through a town or a village, all the inhabitants ran out to receive his blessing; this frequently caused the milk on the fire to be left till burnt.)

p.hi: The blanks as well as the prizes must be drawn in the cheating lottery of life.
The blast that blows loudest is soon overblown.

div.p: The blaze of reputation cannot be blown out, 35 but it often dies in the socket. Johnson.

p.hi: The blessed work of helping the world forward does not wait to be done by perfect men.
The blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
The blind man bears the lame, and onward hies, / Made right by lending feet and borrowing eyes.
The block of granite, which was an obstacle in the pathway of the weak, becomes a stepping-stone in the pathway of the strong.

div.p: The blood more stirs / To rouse a lion than to 40 start a hare. Hen. IV., i. 3.

p.hi: The blood of man should never be shed but to redeem the blood of man. It is well shed for our family, for our friends, for our God, for our country, for our kind. The rest is vanity, the rest is crime.
The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.
The blue-bird carries the sky on his back.
The blue of heaven is larger than the cloud.

div.p: The blush is Nature's alarm at the approach of 45 sin, and her testimony to the dignity of virtue. Fuller.

p.hi: The body of a sensualist is the coffin of a dead soul.
The body of Christ is wherever human bodies are, and he who has any bitterness against his brother is always committing sacrilege.
The book of Nature is the book of Fate.
The bookful blockhead, ignorantly read, / With loads of learned lumber in his head.
The books which help you most are those which make you think the most.
The borrower runs in his own debt.
The bough that is dead shall be cut away for the sake of the tree itself. Let the Conservatism that would preserve the tree, cut it away.
The bounds of a man's knowledge are easily concealed if he has but prudence.

div.p: The boy stands astonished; his impressions 5 guide him; he learns sportfully; seriousness steals on him by surprise. Goethe.

p.hi: The boy's story is the best that is ever told.
The boy's will is the wind's will, / And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts.

div.p: The brain may devise laws for the blood; but a hot temper leaps o'er a cold decree. Mer. of Ven., i. 2.

p.hi: The brain-women never interest us like the heart-women; white roses please less than red.

div.p: The brave man thinks of himself last of all. 10 Schiller.

p.hi: The bravest are the tenderest, / The loving are the daring.

div.p: The breach of custom / Is breach of all. Cymbeline, iv. 2.

p.hi: The breeding of a man makes him courageous by instinct, true by instinct, loving by instinct, as a dog is; and therefore, felicitously above, or below (whichever you like to call it), all questions of philosophy and divinity.
The British nation—and I include in it the Scottish nation—has produced a finer set of men than you will find it possible to get anywhere else in this world.

div.p: The bud may have a bitter taste, / But sweet 15 will be the flower. Cowper.

p.hi: The buke o' May-bees is very braid.
The burden one likes is cheerfully borne.
The burning of a little straw may hide the stars of the sky; but the stars are there, and will reappear.
The burst of new light, by its suddenness, always appears inimical to the unprepared heart.

div.p: The busiest of living agents are certain dead 20 men's thoughts. Bovee.

p.hi: The calling of a man's self to a strict account is a medicine sometimes too piercing and corrosive; reading good books of morality is a little flat and dead ... but the best receipt (best to work, and best to take) is the admonition of a friend.

div.p: The camomile, the more it is trodden on, the faster it grows; yet youth, the more it is wasted, the sooner it wears. 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.

p.hi: The canary-bird sings the sweeter the longer it has been trained in a darkened cage.
The cancer of jealousy on the breast can never wholly be cut out, if I am to believe great masters of the healing art.

div.p: The canker galls the infants of the spring / 25 Too oft before their buttons are disclosed, / And in the morn and liquid dew of youth / Contagious blastments are most imminent. Ham., i. 3.

p.hi: The capacity of apprehending what is high is very rare; and therefore, in common life a man does well to keep such things for himself, and only to give out so much as is needful to have some advantage against others.
The captive bands may chain the hands, / But love enslaves the man.

The Carlyles were men who lavished their heart and conscience upon their work; they builded themselves, their days, their thoughts and sorrows, into their houses; they leavened the soil with the sweat of their rugged brows.
The casting away things profitable for the maintenance of man's life is an unthankful abuse of the fruits of God's good providence towards mankind.

div.p: The castle which Conservatism is set to defend 30 is the actual state of things, good and bad. Emerson.

p.hi: The cat shuts its eyes when stealing the cream.

div.p: The cause which pleased the gods has in the end to please Cato also. (?)

p.hi: The centuries are all lineal children of one another; and often, in the portrait of early grandfathers, this and the other enigmatic feature of the newest grandson will disclose itself, to mutual elucidation.
The centuries are conspirators against the sanity and authority of the soul.

div.p: The certain way to be cheated is to fancy one's 35 self more cunning than others. Charron.

p.hi: The chains of habit are generally too small to be felt till they are too strong to be broken.
The champion true / Loves victory more when, dim in view, / He sees her glories gild afar / The dusky edge of stubborn war, / Than if th' untrodden bloodless field / The harvest of her laurels yield.
The change of a man's self is a very laborious undertaking.
The character of a nation is not to be learned from its fine folks.

div.p: The character of the person that commends 40 you is to be considered before you set a value on his esteem. The wise man applauds him whom he thinks most virtuous; the rest of the world, him who is most wealthy. (?)

p.hi: The character of the true philosopher is to hope all things not unreasonable.

div.p: The characteristic mark of minds (Geister) of the first order is the directness (Unmittelbarkeit) of all their judgments. All that they bring forth (vorbringen) is the result of their own thinking. Schopenhauer.

p.hi: The characteristic of a philosopher is that he looks to himself for all help or harm.
The characteristic of Chaucer is intensity; of Spencer, remoteness; of Milton, elevation: of Shakespeare, everything.

div.p: The chariest maid is prodigal enough / If she 45 unmask her beauty to the moon. Ham., i. 1.

p.hi: The charitable give out at the door, and God puts in at the window.
The charity that thinketh no evil trusts in God and trusts in man.
The chaste mind, like a polished plane, may admit foul thoughts, without receiving their tincture.
The cheap swearer through his open sluice / Lets his soul run for nought.
The cheapness of man is every day's tragedy.

div.p: The chief glory of every people arises from its 5 authors. Johnson.

p.hi: The chief of all the curses of this unhappy age is the universal gabble of its fools, and of the flocks that follow them, rendering the quiet voices of the wise of all past time inaudible.
The chief requisites for a courtier are a flexible conscience and an inflexible politeness.
The chief value and virtue of money consists in its having power over human beings; a power which is attainable by other means than by money.
The child is father of the man.

div.p: The child is not to be educated for the present, 10 but for the remote future, and often in opposition to the immediate future. Jean Paul.

p.hi: The child who desires education will be bettered by it; the child who dislikes it, only disgraced.

The child's murmuring is more and is less than words; there are no notes, and yet it is a song; there are no syllables, and yet it is language.... This poor stammering is a compound of what the child said when it was an angel, and of what it will say when it becomes a man.
The childhood shows the man / As morning shows the day.
The children of others we never love so much as our own; error, our own child, is so near our heart.

div.p: The choicest thing this world has for a man is 15 affection. J. G. Holland.

p.hi: The Christian doctrine, that doctrine of Humility, in all senses godlike, and the parent of all godlike virtue, is not superior, or inferior, or equal to any doctrine of Socrates or Thales, being of a totally different nature; differing from these as a perfect ideal poem does from a correct computation in arithmetic.
The Christian religion having once appeared, cannot again vanish; having once assumed its divine shape, can be subject to no dissolution.
The Christian religion is an inspiration and life—God's life breathed into a man and breathed through a man.

The Christian religion is especially remarkable, as it so decidedly lays claim to mere goodwill in man, to his essential temper, and values this independently of all culture and manifestation. It stands in opposition to science and art, and properly to enjoyment.

div.p: The Christian religion, often enough dismembered 20 and scattered abroad, will ever in the end again gather itself together at the foot of the cross. Goethe.

p.hi: The Christian religion, once here, cannot again pass away; in one or the other form, it will endure through all time. As in Scripture, so also in the heart of man, it is written, "The gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
The Christianity that cannot get on without a minimum of four thousand five hundred, will give place to something better that can.
The Church is a mere organisation to help a man to fulfil his duties; it is not the source from whence those duties sprung.
The Church is the working recognised union of those who by wise teaching guide the souls of men.

div.p: The Church! Touching the earth with one 25 small point (the event, viz., at Bethlehem of the year one); springing out of one small seed-grain, rising out therefrom, ever higher, ever broader, high as the heaven itself, broad till it overshadow the whole visible heaven and earth, and no star can be seen but through it. From such a seed-grain so has it grown; planted in the reverences and sacred opulences of the soul of mankind; fed continually by all the noblenesses of forty generations of man. The world-tree of the nations for so long! Carlyle.

p.hi: The Churchmen fain would kill their Church, / As the Churches have killed their Christ.
The circle of noble-minded people is the most precious of all that I have won.
The city does not take away, neither does the country give, solitude: solitude is within us.
The city is recruited from the country.

div.p: The civil guest / Will no more talk all, than 30 eat all the feast. George Herbert.

p.hi: The civilised man lives not in wheeled houses. He builds stone castles, plants lands, makes life-long marriage contracts; has long-dated, hundred-fold possessions, not to be valued in the money-market; has pedigrees, libraries, law-codes; has memories and hopes, even for this earth, that reach over thousands of years.

The civilised nation consists broadly of mob, money-collecting machine, and capitalist; and when the mob wishes to spend money for any purpose, it sets its money-collecting machine to borrow the money it needs from the capitalist, who lends it on condition of taxing the mob generation after generation.

div.p: The civilised savage (Wilde) is the worst of all savages. C. J. Weber.

p.hi: The Classical is healthy, the Romantic sickly.

div.p: The clergy are at present divided into three 35 sections: an immense body who are ignorant; a small proportion who know and are silent; and a minute minority who know and speak according to their knowledge. Huxley.

The cloud-capp'd towers, the gorgeous palaces, / The solemn temples, the great globe itself, / Yea, all that it inherit, shall dissolve; / And, like this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. Tempest, iv. 1.

p.hi: The cloud incense of the altar hides / The true form of the God who there abides.
The clouds never pass against the wind.
The clouds that gather round the setting sun / Do take a sober colouring from an eye / That hath kept watch o'er man's mortality.

The clouds that wrap the setting sun / ... Why, as we watch their floating wreath, / Seem they the breath of life to breathe? / To Fancy's eye their motions prove / They mantle round the sun for love.

div.p: The clouds treat the sea as if it were a mill-pond 5 or a spring-run, too insignificant to make any exceptions to. John Burroughs.
The cock, that is the trumpet of the morn, / Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding throat / Awake the god of day. Ham., i. 1.
The coin that is most current among mankind is flattery; the only benefit of which is that by hearing what we are not we may be instructed what we ought to be. (?)

p.hi: The combined arts appear to me like a family of sisters, of whom the greater part were inclined to good company, but one was light-headed, and desirous to appropriate and squander the whole goods and chattels of the household—the theatre is this wasteful sister.
The comic and the tragic lie close together, inseparable, like light and shadow.

div.p: The command "thou shalt" is in all circumstances 10 a hard one, unless it is softened down by the adjunct "for that which 'thou shalt' is just the same as that which rationally thou also willest." Lindner.

p.hi: The commencement of atonement is / The sense of its necessity.
The common crowd but see the gloom / Of wayward deeds and fitting doom; / The close observer can espy / A noble soul and lineage high.
The common fluency of speech in many men and most women is owing to a scarcity of matter and a scarcity of words.
The common "keeping up appearances" of society is a mere selfish struggle of the vain with the vain.

div.p: The company of fools may at first make us 15 smile, but at last never fails of rendering us melancholy. Goldsmith.

p.hi: The complete poet must have a heart in his brain or a brain in his heart.
The complete spiritualisation of the animal element in nature is the task of our species.
The conceived is never food save to the mind that conceives.
The concessions of the weak are the concessions of fear.

div.p: The condition of the great body of the people in 20 a country is the condition of the country itself. Carlyle.
The condition of the most fascinated (bezaubertsten) enthusiast is to be preferred to him who, from sheer fear of error, dares in the end no longer to affirm or deny. Wieland.

p.hi: The conditions necessary for the arts of men are the best for their souls and bodies.
The confidant of my vices is my master, though he were my valet.

The conflict of the old, the existent, and the persistent, with development, improvement, and transfigurment is always the same. Out of every arrangement arises at last pedantry; to get rid of this latter the former is destroyed, and some time must elapse before we become aware that order must be re-established.

div.p: The conscience is the inviolable asylum of the 25 liberty of man. Napoleon.

p.hi: The conscience is the most elastic material in the world. To-day you cannot stretch it over a mole-hill, to-morrow it hides a mountain.
The conscience of the man who is given over to his passions is like the voice of the shipwrecked mariner overwhelmed by the tempest.
The conscious utterance of thought by speech or action, to any end, is art.
The conscious water saw its god and blushed.
Dryden, on the water into wine at Cana.

div.p: The consolation which is derived from truth, 30 if any there be, is solid and durable; that which may be derived from error must be, like its original, fallacious and fugitive. Johnson.

p.hi: The contagion of crime is like that of the plague.
The contingent facts of history can never become the proof of the truths of reason.
The conversation of a friend is a powerful alleviator of the fatigue of walking.
The core will come to the surface.

div.p: The cormorant Oblivion swallows up / The 35 carcases that Time has made his prey. Crowe.

p.hi: The corpse is not the whole animal; there is still something that appertains to it, still a corner-stone, and in this case, as in every other, a very chief corner-stone—life, the spirit that makes everything beautiful.
The counsel thou wouldst have another keep, first keep thyself.
The country where the entire people is, or even once has been, laid hold of, filled to the heart with an infinite religious idea, has "made a step from which it cannot retrograde."

div.p: The courage (Muth) of truth is the first condition of philosophic study. Hegel.
The courage that dares only die is on the 40 whole no sublime affair.... The courage we desire and prize is not the courage to die decently, but to live manfully. Carlyle.

p.hi: The course of nature is the art of God.

div.p: The course of Nature's phases, on this our little fraction of a planet, is partially known to us; but who knows what deeper courses these depend on; what infinitely larger cycle (of causes) our little epicycle revolves on? Carlyle.

p.hi: The course of prayer who knows?
The course of scoundrelism, any more than that of true love, never did run smooth.

div.p: The course of true love never did run smooth. Mid. N.'s Dream, i. 1.

p.hi: The court does not render a man contented, but it prevents his being so elsewhere.
The court is like a palace of marble; it is composed of people very hard and very polished.
The court, nor cart, I like, nor loathe; / Extremes are counted worst of all: / The golden mean betwixt them both / Doth surest sit, and fears no fall.

div.p: The court of the past differs from all living 5 aristocracy in this; it is open to labour and to merit, but to nothing else. Ruskin.

p.hi: The covetous man heaps up riches, not to enjoy them, but to have them.
The covetous man never has money, and the prodigal will have none shortly.
The coxcomb is a fool of parts, a flatterer, a knave of parts.
The craftiest wiles are too short and ragged a cloak to cover a bad heart.

div.p: The crafty man is always in danger; and 10 when he thinks he walks in the dark, all his pretences are so transparent, that he that runs may read them. Tillotson.

p.hi: The creation of a thousand forests is in one acorn; and Egypt, Greece, Rome, Gaul, Britain, America, lie folded already in the first man.
The credit of advancing science has always been due to individuals, never to the age.
The creed of the true saint is to make the best of life, and make the most of it.

div.p: The crickets sing, and man's o'er-laboured sense / Repairs itself by rest. Cymbeline, ii. 2.
The cross is the invincible sanctuary of the 15 humble. Cass.

p.hi: The cross of Christ is the key of Paradise; the weak man's staff; the convert's convoy; the upright man's perfection; the soul and body's health; the prevention of all evil, and the procurer of all good.
The cross was the fitting close of a life of rejection, scorn, and defeat.

div.p: The crow doth sing as sweetly as the lark / When neither is attended, and I think / The nightingale, if she should sing by day, / when every goose is cackling, would be thought / No better a musician than the wren. Mer. of Venice, v. 1.

p.hi: The crowd ... if they find / Some stain or blemish in a name of note, / Not grieving that their greatest are so small, / Inflate themselves with some insane delight, / And judge all Nature from her feet of clay, / Without the will to lift their eyes, and see / Her godlike head crown'd with spiritual fire / And touching other worlds.

div.p: The cruelty of the affectionate is more dreadful 20 than that of the hardy. Lavater.

p.hi: The cry of the God-forsaken is from the heart of God himself.
The cuffs and thumps with which fate, our lady-loves, our friends and foes, put us to the proof, in the mind of a good and resolute man, vanish into air.
The cunning workman never doth refuse / The meanest tool that he may chance to use.
The cup of life which God offers to our lips is not always sweet; ... but, sweet or bitter, it is ours to drink it without murmur or demur.

div.p: The cups that cheer, but not inebriate. Cowper. 25

p.hi: The cure for false theology is mother wit.
The curfew tolls the knell of parting day, / The lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea, / The ploughman homeward plods his weary way, / And leaves the world to darkness and to me.
The curiosity of knowing things has been given to man for a scourge.
The curious unthrift makes his clothes too wide, / And spares himself, but would his tailor chide.

div.p: The current that with gentle murmur glides, / 30 Thou know'st, being stopp'd, impatiently doth rage. Two Gent. of Ver., ii. 7.

p.hi: The curtains of yesterday drop down, the curtains of to-morrow roll up; but yesterday and to-morrow both are. Pierce into the Time-element, glance into the Eternal.

div.p: The cut (of the vesture) betokens intellect and talent, so does the colour betoken temper and heart. Carlyle.

p.hi: The cynic is one who never sees a good quality in a man, and never fails to see a bad one.
The danger of dangers is illusion.

div.p: The danger past and God forgotten. Pr. 35

p.hi: The dark in soul see in the universe their own shadow; the shattered spirit can only reflect external beauty, in form as untrue and broken as itself.
The darkest day, live till to-morrow, will have passed away.
The darkest hour is nearest the dawn.
The day is longer than the brae; we'll be at the top yet.

div.p: The day of days ... is the day on which the 40 inward eye opens to the unity of things, to the omnipresence of law—sees that what is must be, and ought to be, or is the best. Emerson.

p.hi: The day wasted on others is not wasted on one's self.
The days are too short even for love, how can there ever be time for quarrelling?
The dead do not need us; but for ever and for evermore we need them.

The dead letter of religion must own itself dead, and drop piecemeal into dust, if the living spirit of religion, freed from its charnel-house, is to arise on us, new born of Heaven, and with new healing under its wings.

div.p: The decline of literature indicates the decline 45 of the nation. The two keep pace in their downward tendency. Goethe.

p.hi: The deeper the sorrow, the less tongue hath it.
The deity works in the living, not in the dead; in the becoming and the changing, not in the become and the fixed.
The delight of the destroyer and denier is no pure delight, and must soon pass away.
The democrat is a young conservative; the conservative is an old democrat.
The demonic in music stands so high that no understanding can reach it, and an influence flows from it which masters all, and for which none can account.
The demonic is that which cannot be explained by reason or understanding, which is not in one's nature, yet to which it is subject.

div.p: The dependant is timid. Gael. Pr. 5

p.hi: The depth of our despair measures what capability and height of claim we have to hope.
The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul.
The desire of a man is his kindness: and a poor man is better than a liar.
The desire of perfection is the worst disease that ever afflicted the human mind.

div.p: The desire of power in excess caused the 10 angels to fall; the desire of knowledge in excess caused man to fall; but in charity there is no excess, neither can man or angel come in danger by it. Bacon.

p.hi: The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow, / The devotion to something afar / From the sphere of our sorrow.
The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour.
The destiny of any nation at any given time depends on the opinions of its young men under five-and-twenty.
The destruction of the poor is their poverty.

div.p: The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose! / 15 An evil soul producing holy witness / Is like a villain with a smiling cheek, / A goodly apple rotten at the heart. Mer. of Ven., i. 3.

p.hi: The devil has a great advantage against us, inasmuch as he has a strong bastion and bulwark against us in our own flesh and blood.

div.p: The devil hath power / To assume a pleasing shape. Ham., ii. 2.

p.hi: The devil helps his servants for a season; but when they come once to a pinch, he leaves 'em in the lurch.

div.p: The devil is a busy bishop in his own diocese. 20 Bishop Latimer.

p.hi: The devil is an unfortunate who knows not what it is to love.

div.p: The devil knew not what he did when he made man politic; he crossed himself by it. Tim. of Athens, iii. 3.
The devil lurks behind the cross. Pr. 25

p.hi: The devil may get in by the keyhole, but the door won't let him out.
The devil taketh not lightly unto his working such as he findeth occupied in good works.
The devil tempts all other men, but idle men tempt the devil.
The devil tempts us not—'tis we tempt him, / Beckoning his skill with opportunity.

div.p: The devil was sick, the devil a monk would 30 be; / The devil was well, the devil a monk was he. Rabelais.

p.hi: The dewdrop and the star shine sisterly, / Globing together in the common work.

The dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution is one of those pleasant falsehoods ... which all experience refutes. History teems with instances of truth put down by persecution. If not suppressed for ever, it may be thrown back for centuries.
The difference between Socrates and Jesus? The great Conscious; the immeasurably great Unconscious.
The difference between the great celebrities and the unknown nobodies is this, the former failed and went at it again, the latter gave up in despair.

div.p: The difficulty is not so great to die for a friend as 35 to find a friend worth dying for. Henry Home.

p.hi: The difficulty is to teach the multitude that something can be both true and untrue at the same time.
The dignity of truth is lost with much protesting.
The dilettante takes the obscure for the profound, violence for vigour, the indefinite for the infinite, and the senseless for the supersensuous.
The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord.

div.p: The discovery of what is true, and the practice 40 of that which is good, are the two most important objects of philosophy. Voltaire.

p.hi: The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.

The disease of the mind leading to fatalist ruin is the concentration of man upon himself, whether his heavenly interests or his worldly interests, matters not; it is their being his own interests which makes the regard of them mortal.
The disease which afflicts bureaucratic governments, and which they usually die of, is routine.
The disease with which the human mind now labours is want of faith.

div.p: The dispute about religion and the practice of 45 it seldom go together. Young.

p.hi: The disputes of two of equal strength and fortune are worthy of attention; but not of two, the one great, the other humble.
The dissection of a sentence is as bad a way to the understanding of it, as the dissection of a beast to the biography of it.
The distances of nations are measured, not by seas, but by ignorances; and their divisions determined, not by dialects, but by enmities.
The distant landscape draws not nigh / For all our gazing.

div.p: The distant sounds of music, that catch new 50 sweetness as they vibrate through the long-drawn valley, are not more pleasing to the ear than the tidings of a far-distant friend. Goldsmith.

p.hi: The distinction between man and nature is, that man is a being becoming, and nature a being become.
The distinctive character of a child is to live always in the tangible present.
The distinguishing sign of slavery is to have a price and be bought for it.
The distinguishing trait of people accustomed to good society is a calm, imperturbable quiet, which pervades all their actions and habits.

div.p: The Divine mind is as visible in its full energy 5 of operation on every lowly bank and mouldering stone, as in the lifting of the pillars of heaven, and setting the foundations of the earth. Ruskin.

p.hi: The divine power of the love, of which we cease not to sing and speak, is this, that it reproduces every moment the grand qualities of the beloved object, perfect in the smallest parts, embraced in the whole; it rests not either by day or by night, is ravished with its own work, wonders at its own stirring activity, finds the well-known always new, because it is every moment begotten anew in the sweetest of all occupations. In fact the image of the beloved one cannot become old, for every moment is the hour of its birth.
The divine state, "par excellence," is silence and repose.
The doctor sees all the weakness of mankind, the lawyer all the wickedness, the theologian all the stupidity.
The dog that fetches will carry.

div.p: The dog that starts the hare is as good as the 10 one that catches it. Ger. Pr.

p.hi: The dog, to gain his private ends, / Went mad, and bit the man.
