div.p: The stoical exemption which philosophy affects 15 to give us over the pains and vexations of human life is as imaginary as the state of mystical quietism and perfection aimed at by some crazy enthusiast. Scott.

p.hi: The stoical scheme of supplying our wants by lopping off our desires is like cutting off our feet when we want shoes.
The stone that lieth not in your way need not offend you.
The stone which the builders refused has become the head of the corner.

div.p: The storm of sad mischance will turn into 20 something that is good, if we list to make it so. Taylor.

p.hi: The stranger who turneth away from a house with disappointed hopes leaveth there his own offences, and departeth, taking with him all the good actions of the owner.
The stranger's greeting thou shouldst aye return!

div.p: The strawberry grows under the nettle, / And wholesome berries thrive and ripen best / Neighbour'd by fruit of baser quality. Hen. V., i. 1.

p.hi: The stream can never rise above the spring-head.

div.p: The street is full of humiliations to the proud. 25 Emerson.

p.hi: The strength and power of a country depends absolutely on the quantity of good men and women in it.
The strength of aquatic animals is the waters; of those who dwell in towns, a castle; of footsoldiers, their own ground; of princes, an obedient army.
The string o'erstretched breaks, and the music flies; / The string o'erslack is dumb, and music dies; / Tune us the sitar neither low nor high.
The string that jars / When rudely touch'd, ungrateful to the sense, / With pleasure feels the master's flying fingers, / Swells into harmony and charms the hearers.

div.p: The stroke that comes transmitted through 30 a whole galaxy of elastic balls, is it less a stroke than if the last ball only had been struck and sent flying? Carlyle.

p.hi: The strokes of the pen need deliberation as much as those of the sword need swiftness.
The strong man is the wise man; the man with the gift of method, of faithfulness, of valour; who has insight into what is what, into what will follow out of what, the eye to see and the hand to do.
The strong mind is nowise the mind acquainted with its strength.
The strong must build stout cabins for the weak; / Must plan and stint; must sow and reap and store; / For grain takes root though all seems bare and bleak.

div.p: The strong thing is the just thing: this thou 35 wilt find throughout in our world;—as indeed was God and Truth the maker of it, or was Satan and Falsehood? Carlyle.

p.hi: The strong torrents, which in their own gladness fill the hills with hollow thunder and the vales with winding light, have yet their bounden charge of field to feed and barge to bear.
The strongest arm is impotent to impart momentum to a feather.
The strongest castle, tower, and town, / The golden bullet beats it down.

div.p: The strongest oaths are straw / To the fire i' the blood. Tempest, iv. 1.

The student is to read history actively and 40 not passively; to esteem his own life the text, and books the commentary. Thus compelled, the muse of history will utter oracles as never to those who do not respect themselves. Emerson.

p.hi: The study of books is a languishing and feeble motion that hearts not, whereas conversation teaches and exercises at once.
The stumbler stumbles least in rugged way.

The style of an author is a faithful copy of his mind. If you would write a lucid style, let there first be light in your own mind; and if you would write a grand style, you ought to have a grand character.
The style of letters should not be too highly polished. It ought to be neat and correct, but no more.

The style of writing required in the great world is distinguished by a free and daring grace, a careless security, a fine and sharp polish, a delicate and perfect taste; while that fitted for the people is characterised by a vigorous natural fulness, a profound depth of feeling, and an engaging naïveté.
The sublime is in a grain of dust.

div.p: The sublime is the temple-step of religion, as 5 the stars are of immeasurable space. When what is mighty appears in nature—a storm, thunder, the starry firmament, death—then utter the word "God" before the child. A great misfortune, a great blessing, a great crime, a noble action, are building-sites for a child's church. Jean Paul.

p.hi: The sublime produces a beautiful calmness in the soul which, entirely possessed by it, feels as great as it ever can feel. When we compare such a feeling with that we are sensible of when we laboriously harass ourselves with some trifle, and strain every nerve to gain as much as possible for it, as it were, to patch it out, striving to furnish joy and aliment to the mind from its own creation, we then feel sensibly what a poor expedient, after all, the latter is.
The sublime, when it is introduced at a seasonable moment, has often carried all before it with the rapidity of lightning, and shown at a glance the mighty power of genius.
The sublimest canticle to be heard on earth is the stammering of the human soul on the lips of infancy.
The sublimity of wisdom is to do those things living which are to be desired when dying.

div.p: The substance of a diligent man is precious. 10 Bible.

p.hi: The substance of a man is full good when sin is not in a man's conscience.
The substantial wealth of a man consists in the earth he cultivates with its plants and animals, and in the rightly produced works of his own hands.
The success of many works is found in the relation between the mediocrity of the author's ideas and that of the ideas of the public.
The suffering man ought really "to consume his own smoke;" there is no good in emitting smoke till you have made it into fire.

div.p: The sufficiency of my merit is to know that my 15 merit is not sufficient. St. Augustine.

p.hi: The sun can be seen by nothing but its own light.
The sun flings out impurities, gets balefully incrusted with spots; but it does not quench itself, and become no sun at all, but a mass of darkness.
The sun! God's crest upon his azure shield, the heavens.

div.p: The sun may do its duty, though your grapes 20 are not ripe. Pr.

p.hi: The sun passeth through pollutions, and itself remains as pure as before.

The sun-steeds of time, as if goaded by invisible spirits, bear onward the light car of our destiny, and nothing remains for us but, with calm self-possession, to grasp the reins, and now right, now left, to steer the wheels, here from the precipice, and there from the rock. Whither he is hasting, who knows? Does any one consider whence he came?
The sun's power cannot draw a wandering star from its path. How then could a human being fall out of God's love!
The sunshine of life is made up of very little beams, that are bright all the time.

div.p: The superstition in which we have grown up 25 does not lose its hold over us even when we recognise it for such. Those who scoff at their fetters are not all free men. Lessing.

p.hi: The sure way to miss success is to miss the opportunity.
The surest sign of age is loneliness.
The surest test of a man's critical power is his judgment of contemporaries.
The surest way not to fail is to determine to succeed.

div.p: The surest way to have redress is to be earnest 30 in pursuit of it. Goldsmith.

p.hi: The surgeon practises on the orphan's head.
The sweetest music is not in the oratorio, but in the human voice when it speaks from its instant life tones of tenderness, truth, or courage.
The sweetest wine makes the sharpest vinegar.
The sweetness of the lips increaseth learning.

div.p: The sweets of love are washed with tears. 35 George Herbert.

p.hi: The sword is but a hideous flash in the darkness; right is an eternal ray.
The sympathy of sorrow is stronger than the sympathy of prosperity.
The system of the world is entirely one; small things and great are alike part of one mighty whole.
The tabernacle of the upright shall flourish.

div.p: The tallest trees are most in the power of the 40 winds, and ambitious men of the blasts of fortune. Wm. Penn.

p.hi: The tanager flies through the green foliage as if he would ignite the leaves.
The teaching of art is the teaching of all things.
The teachings of Heaven are given—by sad law—in so obscure, nay, often in so ironical a manner, that a blockhead necessarily reads them wrong.
The tear of joy is a pearl of the first water; the mourning tear, only of the second.

div.p: The tears of penitents are the wine of angels. 45 St. Bernard.

p.hi: The tell-tale out of school is of all wits the greatest fool.
The temper of the pedagogue suits not with the age; and the world, however it may be taught, will not be tutored.

div.p: The temperate man's pleasures are durable, because they are regular; and all his life is calm and serene, because it is innocent. (?)

p.hi: The tempest never rooteth up the grass, which is feeble, humble, and shooteth not up on high; but exerteth its power even to distress the lofty trees; for the great use not their might but upon the great.

div.p: The temple of our purest thoughts is—silence! 5 Mrs. Hale.

p.hi: The tendency of laws should be rather to diminish the amount of evil than to produce an amount of happiness.
The tendency of party-spirit has ever been to disguise and propagate and support error.
The tender flower that lifts its head, elate, / Helpless must fall before the blasts of fate, / Sunk on the earth, defaced its lovely form, / Unless your shelter ward th' impending storm.
The tender heart o' leesome luve / The gowd and siller canna buy.

div.p: The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel. 10 Bible.

p.hi: The term of man's life is half wasted before he has done with his mistakes and begins to profit by his lessons.
The test of civilisation is the estimate of woman.
The test or measure of poetic genius is to read the poetry of affairs, to fuse the circumstance of to-day.

The theatre has often been at variance with the pulpit; they ought not to quarrel. How much is it to be wished that in both the celebration of nature and of God were intrusted to none but men of noble minds!

div.p: The There is never Here. Schiller. 15

p.hi: The thin edge of the wedge is to be feared.
The thing a lie wants, and solicits from all men, is not a correct natural history of it, but the swiftest possible extinction of it, followed by entire silence about it.
The thing done avails, and not what is said about it.
The thing men get to believe is the thing they will infallibly do.

div.p: The thing that hath been, it is that which 20 shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done. Bible.

p.hi: The thing that is, what can be so wonderful? what, especially to us that are, can have such significance?
The thing that matters most, both for happiness and for duty, is that we should strive habitually to live with wise thoughts and right feelings.
The thing to be anxious about is not to be right with man, but with mankind.

The thing visible, nay, the thing imagined, the thing in any way conceived of as visible, what is it but a garment, a clothing of the higher, celestial invisible, "unimaginable, formless, dark with excess of bright"?

div.p: The thing which is deepest rooted in Nature, 25 what we call truest, that, and not the other, will be found growing at last. Carlyle.

p.hi: The things that destroy us are injustice, insolence, and foolish thoughts; and the things which save us are justice, self-command, and true thought, which things dwell in the loving powers of the gods.

div.p: The things that threatened me, / Ne'er look'd but on my back; when they shall see / The face of Cæsar, they are vanished. Jul. Cæsar, ii. 2.

p.hi: The thinker requires exactly the same light as the painter, clear, without direct sunshine, or blinding reflection, and, where possible, from above.
The thinking minds of all nations call for change. There is a deep-lying struggle in the whole fabric of society; a boundless, grinding collision of the new with the old.

div.p: The third pays for all. Twelfth Night, v. 1. 30

p.hi: The thirst for truth still remains with us, even when we have wilfully left the fountains of it.

div.p: The thorny point / Of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show / Of smooth civility. As You Like It, ii. 7.

p.hi: The thought is always prior to the fact; all the facts of history pre-exist in the mind as laws.
The thought is parent of the deed.

div.p: The thought of foolishness is sin. Bible. 35

p.hi: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord.
The thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts.

The thoughts we have had, the pictures we have seen, can be again called back before the mind's eye and before the imagination; but the heart is not so obliging; it does not reproduce its pleasing emotions.

div.p: The thrall in person may be free in soul. 40 Tennyson.

p.hi: The throne is established by righteousness.
The time for words has passed, and deeds alone suffice.

div.p: The time has been / That when the brains were out the man should die, / And there an end. Macb., iii. 4.
The time is out of joint; O cursèd spite, / That ever I was born to set it right. Ham., i. 5.
The time of breeding is the time of doing 45 children good; and not as many who think they have done fairly if they leave them a good portion after their decease. George Herbert.

p.hi: The time that bears no fruit deserves no name.
The Times are the masquerade of the Eternities; trivial to the dull, tokens of noble and majestic agents to the wise.
The timid are in fear before danger, the cowardly in danger, and the courageous after danger.
The timing of things is a main point in the dispatch of all affairs.
The tired ocean crawls along the beach sobbing a wordless sorrow to the moon.
The toil of life alone teaches us to value the blessings of life.
The tomb is the pedestal of greatness.

div.p: The tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly 5 evil, full of deadly poison. St. James.

p.hi: The tongue ever turns to the aching tooth.
The tongue is not of steel, but it cuts.
The tongue is the worst part of a bad servant.
The tongue of the just is as choice silver.

div.p: The tongue tells the thought of one man only, 10 whereas the face expresses a thought of nature itself; so that every one is worth attentive observation, even though every one may not be worth talking to. Schopenhauer.

p.hi: The tongue's aye quick at saying "Na," / Though a' the while the heart be dumb.

div.p: The tongues of dying men / Enforce attention like deep harmony. Rich. II., ii. 1.

p.hi: The too good opinion man has of himself is the nursing-mother of all false opinions, both public and private.
The torments of martyrdoms are probably most keenly felt by the bystanders.

div.p: The total loss of reason is less deplorable than 15 the total depravation of it. Cowley.
The training (Bildung) of the thinking, of the dispositions and the morals, is the only education that deserves the name. Herder.

p.hi: The trappings of a monarchy would set up an ordinary commonwealth.
The traveller who goes round the world prepares himself to pass through all latitudes and to meet all changes.
The traveller without observation is a bird without wings.

div.p: The treasures of heaven are not negations of 20 passion but realities of intellect, from which all passions emanate, uncurbed in their eternal glory. Wm. Blake.

p.hi: The tree doth not withdraw its shade, even from the woodcutter.
The tree Igdrasil, which reaches up to heaven, goes down to the kingdom of hell; and God, the Everlasting Good and Just, is in it all.
The tree is no sooner down than every one runs for his hatchet.
The tree of knowledge is grafted upon the tree of life; and that fruit which brought the fear of death into the world, budding on an immortal stock, becomes the fruit of the promise of immortality.

div.p: The tree of knowledge is not that of life. 25 Byron.

p.hi: The tree of liberty only grows when watered by the blood of tyrants.
The tree of silence bears the fruit of peace.
The tree which yieldeth both fruit and shade is highly to be esteemed: but if Providence, perchance, may have denied it fruit, by whom is its shade refused?
The trenchant blade, Toledo trusty, / For want of fighting was grown rusty, / And ate into itself, for lack / Of somebody to hew and hack.

div.p: The trident of Neptune is the sceptre of the 30 planet. Lemierre.

p.hi: The triumphs of delusion are but for a day.
The trivial round, the common task, / Will furnish all we ought to ask. / Room to deny ourselves, a road / To bring us daily nearer God.
The true and the good will be reconciled when the two are wedded to each other in the beautiful.
The true art of being agreeable is to appear well pleased with all the company, and rather to seem well entertained with them than to bring entertainment to them.

div.p: The true beginning is oftenest unnoticed and 35 unnoticeable. Carlyle.

p.hi: The true "compulsory education" now needed is not catechism, but drill.
The true cross of the Redeemer is the sin and sorrow of the world.
The true end of tragedy is to purify the passions.
The true epic of our times is, not arms and the man, but tools and the man—an infinitely wider kind of epic.

div.p: The true eye for talent presupposes the true 40 reverence for it. Carlyle.

p.hi: The true fire of heaven always comes from heaven direct.
The true function of intellect is not that of talking, but of understanding and discerning with a view to performing.
The true God's voice, voice of the Eternal, is in the heart of every man.

div.p: The true good (all of it) and glory even of this world, not to speak of any that is to come, must be bought still, as it always has been, with our toil and with our tears. That is the final doctrine, the inevitable one, not of Christianity only, but of all heroic faith and heroic being. Ruskin.

The true harvest of my daily life is somewhat 45 as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning or evening. It is a little stardust caught, a segment of the rainbow which I have clutched. Thoreau.

p.hi: The true historical genius, to our thinking, is that which can see the nobler meaning of the events that are near him.
The true labourer is worthy of his hire, but, in the beginning and first choice of industry, his heart must not be the heart of an hireling.
The true ladder of heaven has no steps.
The true liberty of a man consists in his finding out, or being forced to find out, the right path, and to walk therein.

div.p: The true life of man is in society. Simms. 50

p.hi: The true life of man, like God's, lies in the ungrudging imparting of himself to alike the worthy and unworthy without fear of forfeiture or claim of reward.
The true literary man is the light of the world; the world's priest guiding it, like a sacred pillar of fire, in its dark pilgrimage through the waste of time.
The true mind of a nation, at any period, is always best ascertainable by examining that of its greatest men.
The true original ground of all disquiet is within.
The true philosophical act is annihilation of self; this is the real beginning of all philosophy; all requisites for being a disciple of philosophy point hither.
The true poet is even more than a finder or troubadour; he is a seer, a prophet, and an interpreter between the divine and the human.

div.p: The true poet, who is but the inspired thinker, 5 is still an Orpheus whose lyre tames the savage beasts, and evokes the dead rocks to fashion themselves into palaces and stately inhabited cities. Carlyle.

p.hi: The true poetic soul needs but to be struck, and the sounds it yields will be music.
The true preacher can be known by this, that he deals out to the people his life—life passed through the fire of thought.
The true scholar learns from the known to unfold the unknown, and approaches more and more to being a master.

div.p: The true strength of every human soul is to 10 be dependent on as many nobler as it can discern, and to be depended upon by as many inferior as it can reach. Ruskin.

p.hi: The true, strong, and sound mind is the mind that can embrace equally great things and small.

div.p: The True that is identical with the Divine can never be directly known by us; we behold it only in reflexion (Abglanz), in example, in symbol, in individual and related phenomena; we perceive it as incomprehensible life, which yet we cannot renounce the wish to comprehend. This is true of all the phenomena of the conceivable world. Goethe.

p.hi: The true university of these days is a collection of books.
The true value of a man's book is determined by what he does not write.

div.p: The true veins of wealth are purple—not in 15 rock, but in flesh—(and) the final outcome and consummation of all wealth is in producing as many as possible full-breathed, bright-eyed, and happy-hearted human creatures. Ruskin.

p.hi: The true way of softening one's troubles is to solace those of others.
The truly strong mind, view it as intellect or morality, or under any other aspect, is nowise the mind acquainted with its strength.
The truly sublime is always easy, and always natural.
The truly wise man should have no keeper of his secrets but himself.

div.p: The truth shall make you free. Jesus. 20

p.hi: The truth we need is only lightly veiled, not deeply buried by the wise hand which has designed it for us.
The truth works sometimes from without as from within.
The truths of Nature are one eternal change, one infinite variety.
The two best rules for a system of rhetoric are: first, have something to say; and next, say it.

div.p: The two foes of human happiness are pain and 25 ennui. Schopenhauer.

p.hi: The two great movers of the human mind are the desire of good and the fear of evil.
The two most beautiful things in the universe are the starry heavens above us and the feeling of duty within us.
The two most engaging powers of an author are to make new things familiar and familiar things new.
The two sources of all quack-talent are cunning and impudence.

div.p: The ultimate rule (in writing) is: Learn so far 30 as possible to be intelligible and transparent—no notice taken of your style, but solely of what you express by it. Carlyle.

p.hi: The ultimate tendency of civilisation is towards barbarism.
The unconscious is the alone complete.
The Understanding is indeed thy window, too clear thou canst not make it; but Fantasy is thy eye, with its colour-giving retina, healthy or diseased.

div.p: The undiscovered country, from whose bourn / No traveller returns. Ham., iii. 1.
The unfortunate are loud and loquacious 35 in their complaints, but real happiness is content with its own silent enjoyment. Gibbon.
The unhappy (malheureux) are always wrong: wrong in being so, wrong in saying so, wrong in needing help of others, wrong in not being able to help them. Mirabeau.

p.hi: The unimaginative person can neither be reverent nor kind.

The universe has three children, born at one time ... called cause, operation, and effect, or, theologically, the Father, the Spirit, and the Son. These three are equal ... and each has the power of the others latent in him.
The universe is a thought of God.

div.p: The universe is an infinite sphere, the centre 40 of which is everywhere, and the circumference nowhere. Pascal after St. Augustus.

p.hi: The universe is but one vast symbol of God; nay, if thou wilt have it, what is man himself but a symbol of God; is not all that he does symbolical; a revelation to sense of the mystic god-given force that is in him; a "gospel of freedom," which he, the "Messias of Nature," preaches, as he can, by act and word?
The universe is full of love, but also of inexorable sternness and severity.
The universe is not dead and demoniacal, a charnel-house with spectres, but godlike, and my Father's.
The universe is one great city, full of beloved ones, human and divine, by nature endeared to each other.

div.p: The universe is that great egoist that decoys 45 us by the grossest bird-calls. Renan.

p.hi: The universe is the realised thought of God.
The universe stands by him who stands by himself.
The universe would not be rich enough to buy the vote of an honest man.
The unlearned man knoweth not what it is to descend into himself and call himself to account; nor the pleasure of that most pleasant life which consists in our daily feeling ourselves become better.

The unlettered peasant, whose views are only directed to the narrow sphere around him, beholds Nature with a finer relish, and tastes her blessings with a keener appetite, than the philosopher whose mind attempts to grasp a universal system.

div.p: The unpastured sea hungering for calm. 5 Shelley.

p.hi: The unworn spirit is strong; life is so healthful that it even finds nourishment in death.
The upper classes and people of wealth suffer most from ennui.

div.p: The Upper Crust, i.e., the Upper Ten. Amer.
The Upper Ten, i.e., the aristocracy; the upper circles (contracted from Upper Ten Thousand). Amer.
The upper current of society presents no certain 10 criterion by which we can judge of the direction in which the under-current flows. Macaulay.

p.hi: The upright shall dwell in the land, and the perfect shall remain in it.
The ups and downs of the world concern the beggar no longer.

The use of knowledge in our sex, besides the amusement of solitude, is to moderate the passions, and learn to be contented with a small expense, which are the certain effects of a studious life; and it may be preferable to that fame which men have engrossed to themselves, and will not suffer us to share.
The use of travelling is to regulate imagination by reality, and instead of thinking how things may be, to see them as they are.

div.p: The useful encourages itself, for the multitude 15 produce it, and no one can dispense with it; but the beautiful must be encouraged, for few can set it forth, and many need it. Goethe.

p.hi: The useless men are those who never change with the years.
The usurer is the greatest Sabbath-breaker, because his plough goeth every Sunday.
The utmost point and acme of honour is not merely in doing no evil, but in thinking none.
The uttered part of a man's life bears to the unuttered, unconscious part of it a small unknown proportion; he himself never knows it, much less do others.

div.p: The valiant in himself, what can he suffer? / 20 Or what need he regard his single woes? Thomson.

p.hi: The valour of a just man is to conquer the flesh, to contradict his own will, ... to contemn the flatteries of prosperity, and inwardly to overcome the fears of adversity.
The valour that struggles is better than the weakness that endures.
The value of a man, as of a horse, consists in your being able to bridle him, or, what is better, in his being able to bridle himself.
The value of a thing is its life-giving power.

div.p: The vanity of loving fine clothes and new 25 fashions, and valuing ourselves by them, is one of the most childish pieces of folly that can be. Sir Matthew Hale.

p.hi: The veneration we have for many things entirely proceeds from their being carefully concealed.

div.p: The very head and front of my offending / Hath this extent, no more. Othello, i. 3.

p.hi: The very joy of a true man's heart is to admire, when he can; nothing so lifts him from all his mean imprisonments, were it but for moments, as true admiration.
The very meanest things are made supreme / With innate ecstasy.

div.p: The very nature of the dilettanti is that they 30 have no idea of the difficulties which lie in a subject, and always wish to undertake something for which they have no capacity. Goethe.

p.hi: The very pain of loving is all other joys before.
The very society of joy redoubles it, so that, whilst it lights upon my friend, it rebounds upon myself, and the brighter his candle burns the more easily will it light mine.
The vessel that will not obey her helm will have to obey the rocks.
The vice of our housekeeping is that it does not hold man sacred.

div.p: The vices we scoff at in others laugh at us 35 within ourselves. Sir Thomas Browne.

p.hi: The victories of character are instant, and victories for all.
"The victory of Miltiades does not suffer me to sleep."
Themistocles, in reference to the battle of Marathon.

The violets and the mayflowers are as the inscriptions or vignettes of spring. It always makes a pleasant impression on us when we open again at these pages of the book of life, its most charming chapter.

div.p: The virtue of great souls is justice (Gerechtigkeit). Platen.
The virtue of justice consists in moderation, 40 as regulated by wisdom. Arist.

p.hi: The virtue of man is, in a word, the great proof of God.
The virtue of prosperity is temperance; the virtue of adversity is fortitude; which in morals is the more heroical virtue.
The virtue of sex is the occasion of mutual teaching; the woman preaching love in the ears of justice, and the man justice in the ears of love.
The virtue of the man who lives according to the precepts of reason shows itself equally great in avoiding as in overcoming dangers.

The virtuous delight in the virtuous; but he who is destitute of the practice of virtue delighteth not in the virtuous. The bee retireth from the forest to the lotus, whilst the frog is destitute of shelter.
The virtuous man, from his justice and the affection he hath for mankind, is the dispeller of sorrow and pain.

The virtuous soul is pure and unmixed light, springing from the body as a flash of lightning darts from the cloud; the soul that is carnal and immersed in sense, like a heavy and dank vapour, can with difficulty be kindled, and caused to raise its eyes heavenward.
The visible creation is the terminus or the circumference of the invisible world.

div.p: The vitality of man is great. Carlyle. 5

p.hi: The voice of conscience is so delicate that it is easy to stifle it; but it is also so clear that it is impossible to mistake it.
The voice of prophecies is like that of whispering-places; they who are near hear nothing, those at the first extremity will know all.
The voice of the majority is no proof of justice.
The voice of the people ought always to meet with attention, though it does not always claim obedience.

div.p: The vulgar estimate themselves by what they 10 do; the noble by what they are. Schiller.

p.hi: The vulgar great are comprehended and adored, because they are in reality on the same moral plane with those who admire; but he who deserves the higher reverence must himself convert the worshipper.
The vulgar keep no account of your hits, but of your misses.
The wail of grief is more sympathetic than the shout of triumph.
The walking of man and all animals is a falling forward.

div.p: The want of belief is a defect which ought to 15 be concealed when it cannot be overcome. Swift.

p.hi: The want of occupation is no less the plague of society than of solitude.
The want of perception is a defect which all the virtues of the heart cannot supply.
The warl'ly race may riches chase, / And riches still may flee them; / And though at last they catch them fast, / Their hearts can ne'er enjoy them.
The watchful mother tarries nigh, / Though sleep has clos'd her infant's eye.

div.p: The way in which we form our ideas gives 20 character to our minds. Rousseau.

p.hi: The way of the superior man is threefold—virtuous, he is free from anxieties; wise, he is free from perplexities; bold, he is free from fear.
The way of the wicked is an abomination unto the Lord.
The way of the world is to make laws, but follow customs.
The way of this world is to praise dead saints and persecute living ones.

div.p: The way to avoid evil is not by maiming our 25 passions, but by compelling them to yield their vigour to our moral nature. Ward Beecher.

p.hi: The way to avoid the imputation of impudence is not to be ashamed of what we do, but never to do what we ought to be ashamed of.
The way to be original is to be healthy.

The way to get rid of wretchedness is to despise it; to conquer the devil is to defy him; to gain heaven is to turn your back upon it, and be as unflinching as the gods themselves. Satan may be roasted in his own flames; Tophet may be exploded with its own sulphur.
The way to heaven is set with briars and thorns; and they who arrive at the kingdom travel over craggy rocks and comfortless deserts.

div.p: The way to make thy son rich is to fill / His 30 mind with rest, before his trunk with riches. George Herbert.

p.hi: The way to mend the bad world is to create the right world.
The way to wealth is as plain as the way to market; it depends chiefly on two words—industry and frugality.
The way to write quickly is to write well.
The way, truth, and life have been found in Christianity, and will not now be found outside of it.

div.p: The way's not easy where the prize is great. 35 Quarles.

p.hi: The ways in which most men get their living, that is, live, are mere makeshifts, and a shirking of the real business of life; chiefly because they do not know, but partly because they do not mean better.

div.p: The weakest goes to the wall. Rom. and Jul., i. 1.

p.hi: The weakest spot in every man is where he thinks himself to be the wisest.
The wealth of a country is in its good men and women, and in nothing else.

div.p: The wealth of a man is the number of things 40 which he loves and blesses, which he is loved and blessed by. Carlyle.

p.hi: The wealth of both Indies seems in great part but an accessory to the command of the seas.
The wealth of both the Indies cannot redeem one single opportunity which you have once let slip.
The wealth of the land / Comes from the forge and the smithy and mine, / From hammer and chisel, and wheel and band, / And the thinking brain and the skilful hand.
The wealth we cannot wisely administer is an encumbrance.

div.p: The weariest and most loathéd worldly life, / 45 That age, ache, penury, and imprisonment / Can lay on nature, is a paradise / To what we fear of death. Meas. for Meas., iii. 1.

p.hi: The wearisome is in permanence here.
The weary night o' care and grief / May hae

div.p: The web of this world is woven of necessity and contingency; the reason of man places itself between them, and knows how to rule them both. It treats the necessary as the ground of its existence; the contingent it knows how to direct, lead, and utilise; and it is only while reason stands firm and steadfast that man deserves to be called the god of the earth. Woe to him who has accustomed himself from his youth to incline to find something arbitrary in what is necessary, who would fain ascribe a kind of reason to the contingent, which it were even a religion to follow; what is that but to disown one's own understanding, and to give loose reins to one's inclinations? We imagine it piety to saunter along (hinschlendern) without consideration, and to allow ourselves to be determined by agreeable accidents, and finally give to the results of such a vacillating life the name of Divine guidance. Goethe.

The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and ill together; our virtues would be proud if our faults whipped them not, and our crimes would despair if they were not cherished by our virtues. All's Well, iv. 3.

p.hi: The wedge will rend rocks; but its edge must be sharp and single; if it is double, the wedge is bruised in pieces, and will rend nothing.
The wheel is always in motion, and the spoke which is uppermost will soon be under; therefore mix trembling with all your joy.

div.p: The whole art of war consists in getting at 5 what is on the other side of the hill, or, in other words, in learning what we do not know from what we do. Duke of Wellington.

p.hi: The whole course of things goes to teach us faith.

The whole difference between a man of genius and other men ... is that the former remains in great part a child, seeing with the large eyes of children, in perpetual wonder, not conscious of much knowledge—conscious rather of infinite ignorance, and yet infinite power.
The whole economy of nature is bent on expression.
The whole interest of history lies in the fortunes of the poor.

div.p: The whole function of the artist in the world is 10 to be a seeing and a feeling creature; to be an instrument of such tenderness and sensitiveness that no shadow, no hue, no line, no instantaneous and evanescent expression of the visible things around him, nor any of the emotions which they are capable of conveying to the spirit which has been given him, shall either be left unrecorded, or fade from the book of record. Ruskin.

p.hi: The whole man to one thing at a time.
The whole of chivalry and of heraldry is in courtesy.
The whole past is the possession of the present.

The whole spiritual universe exists only in process—what Hegel calls "Der Process des Geistes"—the process of the spirit, that is to say, not as become, but as becoming; and if it once ceases to become, it ceases as such to be.

div.p: The whole universe is at all moments saying 15 "Nay" to the Spirit of God, and God's Spirit is at all moments saying "Yea" to the stolid "Nay" of the universe, which would fain be let alone; but stubborn as the material looks and is, it has to obey, and does obey, the voice of God. Ed.
The whole world is, properly speaking, a tragic embarras. Rahel.

p.hi: The whole world of truth and conscience is nothing without I.
The wide pasture is but separate spears of grass; the sheeted bloom of the prairies but isolated flowers.
The wife can carry more out of the house in her apron than the man can bring in on a harvest-waggon.

div.p: The wife is the key of the house. Pr. 20

p.hi: The wife that expects to have a good name / Is always at home as if she were lame; / And the mind that is honest, her chiefest delight, / Is still to be doing from morning till night.
The will appears without its mask only in the affections and the passions.
The willow which bends to the tempest often escapes better than the oak which resists it.
The wind that has its nest in trees.

div.p: The winds and the waves are always on the 25 side of the ablest navigators. Gibbon.
The winter of our discontent. Rich. III., i. 1.

p.hi: The wisdom of life is in preventing all the evil we can, and using what is inevitable to the best purpose.

The wisdom of nations lies in their proverbs, which are brief and pithy. Collect and learn them; they are notable measures and directions for human life; you have much in little; they save time in speaking; and upon occasion may be the fullest and safest answers.
The wisdom of the wise and the experience of ages may be preserved by quotation.

div.p: The wise are instructed by reason, ordinary 30 minds by experience, the stupid by necessity, and brutes by instinct. Cic.

p.hi: The wise are polite all the world over, but fools are only polite at home.
The wise are those who travel through error to truth; the foolish are those who persist in their error.
The wise grumbler ... is a public benefactor.
The wise have all ever said the same thing, and the fools, who are always in the majority, have always done just the opposite.

div.p: The wise in heart shall be called the prudent. 35 Bible.

p.hi: The wise man always looks to the degree of his indulgences.
The wise man can dispense with the favour of the mighty, but the mighty cannot dispense with the teaching of the wise.
The wise man does not grasp at what is far off in order to find what is near, and his hand does not grasp at the stars in order to kindle
The wise man, even destitute of riches, enjoyeth elevated and very honourable stations; whilst the wretch, endowed with wealth, acquireth the post of disgrace.
The wise man expects everything from himself; the fool looks to others.
The wise man had rather be envied for providence than pitied for prodigality.
The wise man has long ears and a short tongue.

div.p: The wise man knows his master; always some 5 creature larger than himself, some law holier than himself. Ruskin.

p.hi: The wise man knows that he does not know; the ignoramus thinks he knows.
The wise man may strive to conquer, but he should never fight; because victory, it is observed, cannot be constant to both combatants.
The wise man moveth with one foot, and standeth fast with the other. A man should not quit one place until he hath fixed upon another.
The wise man must go to the foolish, else would his wisdom go for nought, since the foolish never come to the wise.

div.p: The wise man often shuns society for fear of 10 being bored. La Bruyère.

p.hi: The wise man ought to despise glory, but not honour. Honour is but seldom where glory is, and glory almost more rarely still where honour is.
The wise man should study the acquisition of science and riches as if he were not subject to sickness and death; but to the duties of religion he should attend as if death had seized him by the hair.
The wise man will commit no business of importance to a proxy when he may do it himself.
The wise men of old have sent most of their morality down the stream of time in the light skiff of apothegm or epigram.

div.p: The wise through excess of wisdom is made a 15 fool. Emerson.

p.hi: The wise weigh their words in a balance for gold.
The wise will determine from the gravity of the case; the irritable, from sensibility to oppression; the high-minded, from disdain and indignation at abusive power in unworthy hands.
The wiser mind / Mourns less for what age takes away / Than what it leaves behind.
The wisest at most observe only how fate leads them, and are content.

div.p: The wisest doctor is gravelled by the inquisitiveness 20 of a child. Emerson.

p.hi: The wisest, happiest of our kind are they / That ever walk content with Nature's way.

The wisest is omnipresent, and reveals His secrets universally to the seeing eye and the hearing ear. The revelation in all its fullness is nowhere wanting, only the sense to discern it, and the courage to be true to it.
The wisest man the warl' e'er saw, / He dearly lo'ed the lasses O.
The wisest men are wise to the full in death.

div.p: The wisest, most melodious voice cannot in 25 these days pass for a divine one; the word "inspiration" still lingers, but only in the shape of a poetic figure, from which the once earnest, awful, and soul-subduing sense has vanished without return. Carlyle.

p.hi: The wisest of us must, for by far the most part, judge like the simplest; estimate importance by mere magnitude, and expect that which strongly affects our own generation, will strongly affect those that are to follow.
The wisest truly is, in these times, the greatest.
The wisest woman you talk with is ignorant of something that you know, but an elegant woman never forgets her elegance.

div.p: The wish was father to the thought. 2 Hen. IV., iv. 4.
The wished-for comes too late. Pr. 30

p.hi: The wit of language is so miserably inferior to the wit of ideas that it is deservedly driven out of good company.
The wit of one man, and the wisdom of many.
Lord John Russell's definition of a proverb.
The wit one wants spoils what one has.

div.p: The woman and the soldier who do not defend 35 the first pass will never defend the last. Fielding.

p.hi: The woman that deliberates is lost.
The woman's cause is man's: they rise or sink / Together.
The women are quick enough—they're quick enough. They know the rights of a story before they hear it, and can tell a man what his thoughts are before he knows 'em himself.

div.p: The word is always bolder than the deed. 40 Schiller.

p.hi: The Word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.
The word of a gentleman is as good as his bond—sometimes better.
The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the well-spring of wisdom as a flowing brook.
The words of a tale-bearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly.

div.p: The words of men are like the leaves of trees; 45 when they are too many they hinder the growth of the fruit. Steiger.

p.hi: The words of the wise are as goads.
The words that a father speaks to his children in the privacy of home are not heard by the world, but, as in whispering-galleries, they are clearly heard at the end and by posterity.

The work an unknown good man has done is like a vein of water flowing hidden under ground, secretly making the ground green; it flows and flows, it joins itself with other veins and veinlets; one day it will start forth as a visible perennial well.
The work of righteousness shall be peace.
The work of science is to substitute facts for appearances, and demonstrations for impressions.
The works of the great poets have only been read for most part as the multitude read the stars, at most, astrologically, not astronomically.
The world can never give / The bliss for which we sigh; / 'Tis not the whole of life to live, / Nor all of death to die.

div.p: The world cannot be governed without juggling. 5 Selden.

p.hi: The world cannot do without great men, but great men are very troublesome to the world.
The world considers eccentricity in great things genius: in small things, folly.
The world does not progress so quickly as a man grows old.
The world exists by change, and but for that / All matter would to chaos back / To form a pillar for a sleeping god.

div.p: The world exists for the education of each 10 man. Emerson.

p.hi: The world exists only by the strength of its silent virtue.
The world goes up, and the world goes down, / And the sunshine follows the rain; / And yesterday's sneer, and yesterday's frown, / Can never come over again.
The world grows more majestic, but man grows less.
The world has no business with my life; the world will never know my life, if it should write and read a hundred biographies of me.

div.p: The world has to obey him who thinks and 15 sees in the world. Carlyle.

p.hi: The world is a carcase, and they who gather round it are dogs.
The world is a comedy to those who think, a tragedy to those who feel.
The world is a grand book from which to become wiser.

The world is a looking-glass, and gives back to every man the reflection of his own face. Frown at it, and it will in turn look sourly upon you; laugh at it and with it, and it is a jolly kind companion.

div.p: The world is a prison. Goethe. 20

p.hi: The world is a thing that man must learn to despise, and even to neglect, before he can learn to reverence it, and work in it and for it.
The world is a wheel, and it will all come round right.
The world is all barren to him who will not cultivate the fruit it offers.

The world is always ready to receive talent with open arms. Very often it does not know what to do with genius. Talent is a docile creature. It bows its head meekly while the world slips the collar over it. It backs into the shafts like a lamb.

div.p: The world is an excellent judge in general, 25 but a very bad one in particular. Lord Greville.

p.hi: The world is an old woman, that mistakes any gilt farthing for a gold coin; whereby, being often cheated, she will henceforth trust nothing but the common copper.
The world is as you take it.
The world is but an allegory; the idea is more real than the fact.
The world is content with words; few think of searching into the nature of things.

div.p: The world is everywhere perfect except where 30 man comes with his pain. Schiller.

p.hi: The world is fain to sully what is resplendent, and to drag down to the dust what is exalted.
The world is for him who has patience.
The world is glorious to look at, but dreadful in reality; it is one thing as a drama to a spectator, quite another thing to the actors in the plot, for in it the will is thwarted at every turn.
The world is governed much more by opinion than by laws.

div.p: The world is governed too much. (?) 35

p.hi: The world is not our peers, so we challenge the jury.

div.p: The world is not thy friend, nor the world's law. Rom. and Jul., v. 1.

p.hi: The world is not to be despised but as it is compared with something better. Company is in itself better than solitude, and pleasure better than indolence.
The world is nothing but a wheel; in its whole periphery it is everywhere similar, but, nevertheless, it appears to us so strange, because we ourselves are carried round with it.

div.p: The world is nothing; the man is all. Emerson. 40

p.hi: The world is only governed by self-interest.

The world is so busied with selfish pursuits, ambition, vanity, interest, or pleasure, that very few think it worth their while to make any observation on what passes around them, except where that observation is a sucker, or branch of the darling plant they are rearing in their fancy.

div.p: The world is still deceived with ornament. / In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt, / But, being seasoned with a gracious voice, / Obscures the show of evil? In religion, / What damnéd error but some sober brow / Will bless it and approve it with a text, / Hiding the grossness with fair ornament? Mer. of Ven., iii. 2.

p.hi: The world is too much with us; late and soon, / Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers; / Little we see in Nature that is ours.

div.p: The world is undone by looking at things at a 45 distance. Sir Thomas More.

p.hi: The world is upheld by the veracity of good men; they make the earth wholesome.

The world is wide enough for all to live and let live, and every one has an enemy in his own talent, who gives him quite enough to do. But no! one gifted man and one talented persecutes another ... and each seeks to make the other hateful.
The world is wider than any of us think.
The world knows nothing of its greatest men.
The world looks at ministers out of the pulpit to know what they mean when in it.
The world ... may overlook most of us; but "reverence thyself."

div.p: The world never let a man bless it but it first 5 fought him. Ward Beecher.

p.hi: The world of Nature for every man is the fantasy of himself; this world is the multiplex "image of his own dream."

The world of reality has its limits; the world of imagination is boundless. Not being able to enlarge the one, let us contract the other; for it is from their difference alone that all the evils arise which render us really unhappy.

The world of thought must remain apart from the world of action, for if they once coincided the problem of life would be solved, and the hope which we call heaven would be realised on earth. And therefore men "Are cradled into poetry by wrong; / They learn in suffering what they teach in song."
The world owes all its onward impulses to men ill at ease.

div.p: The world owes infinitely more to those who 10 have no history than to those who have; and the silent noble ones, who have enriched and exalted it by their mere presence, form a much grander and greater host than those do whose names stand emblazoned in written story, and are the loud boast of all. Ed.

p.hi: The world remains ever the same.
The world seldom offers us any choice between solitude on the one hand and vulgarity on the other.
The world-spirit is a good swimmer, and storms and waves cannot drown him.

The world still wants its poet-priest, who shall not trifle with Shakespeare, the player, nor shall grope in graves with Swedenborg, the mourner; but who shall see, speak, and act with equal inspiration.

div.p: The world that surrounds you is the magic 15 glass of the world within you. To know yourself you have only to set down a true statement of those that ever loved or hated you. Lavater.

p.hi: The world throws its life into a hero or a shepherd, and puts him where he is wanted. Dante and Columbus were Italians in their time; they would be Russians or Americans to-day.
The world truly exists only in the presence of man, acts only in the passion of man. The essence of light is in his eyes—the centre of force in his soul—the pertinence of action in his deeds.
The world, which took but six days to make, is like to take six thousand to make out.
The world's a bubble, and the life of man less than a span.

div.p: The world's a room of sickness, where each 20 heart / Knows its own anguish and unrest! / The truest wisdom there, and noblest art, / Is his who skills of comfort best. Keble.

p.hi: The world's a wood, in which all lose their way, / Though by a different path each goes astray.

The world's battle-fields have been in the heart chiefly. More heroism has there been displayed in the household and in the closet, I think, than on the most memorable military battle-fields of history.
The world's great men have not commonly been great scholars, nor its great scholars great men.

div.p: The world's wealth is its original men; by 25 these and their works it is a world and not a waste; the memory and record of what Men it loves—this is the sum of its strength, its sacred "property for ever," whereby it upholds itself and steers forward, better or worse, through the yet undiscovered deep of Time. Carlyle.

p.hi: The worse the man, the better the soldier; if soldiers be not corrupt, they ought to be made so.
The worse things are, the better they are.
The worship of beauty apart from the soul becomes an idolatry enkindling desire instead of a reverence awakening devotion.
The worst deluded are the self-deluded.

div.p: The worst education which teaches self-denial 30 is better than the best which teaches everything else, and not that. John Sterling.

p.hi: The worst of madmen is a saint run mad.
The worst of many is that their goodness is distributed rather than concentrated. They are like a sheet of water instead of being like a running stream, which can be used to turn a wheel.
The worst superstition is to consider our own the most tolerable.
The worst wheel in the waggon creaks the loudest.

div.p: The worst wild beast is called "Tyrant," and 35 the "Flatterer" the worst tame one. Lessing.

p.hi: The worth of a state, in the long-run, is the worth of the individuals composing it.
The wrath of brothers is fierce and devilish.
The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.

div.p: The wretchedness which fate has rendered 40 voiceless and tuneless is not the least wretched, but the most. Carlyle.

p.hi: The wrinkles of the heart are more indelible than those of the brow.
The writer of a book, is not he a preacher preaching not to this parish or that, on this day or that, but to all men in all times and places?
The wronged side is always the safest.
The young disease, that must subdue at length, / Grows with his growth, and strengthens with his strength.

div.p: The young mind is naturally pliable and imitative, 45 but in a more advanced state it grows rigid, and must be warmed and softened before it will receive a deep impression. Joshua Reynolds.

p.hi: The young talk generously of relieving the old of their burdens, but the anxious heart is to the old when they see a load on the back of the young.
The youth gets together his materials to build a bridge to the moon, or perchance a palace on the earth; at length middle-aged, he concludes to build a woodshed with them.
The youth of the soul is everlasting, and eternity is youth.
Their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.

div.p: Their chief pleasure is being displeased. 5 Whipple.

p.hi: Their only labour was to kill the time, / And labour dire it is, and weary woe.
Their own will to all men, all their will to women.
Their strength is to sit still.
Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do or die.

div.p: Them as ha' never had a cushion don't miss it. 10 George Eliot.

p.hi: Then draw we nearer day by day, / Each to his brethren, all to God; / Let the world take us as she may, / We must not change our road.

div.p: Then fare-ye-weel, auld Nickle Ben, / Oh wad ye tak' a thought and men', / Ye aiblins (perhaps) might—I dinna ken, / Still hae a stake;/ I'm wae to think upon yon den / E'en for your sake. Burns.

p.hi: Then gently scan your brother man, / Still gentler sister woman; / Though they may gang a kennin' wrang, / To step aside is human.
Then in the strife the youth puts forth his powers, / Knows what he is, and feels himself a man.

div.p: Then let us pray that come it may, / As come 15 it will for a' that, / That sense an' worth, o'er a' the earth, / May bear the gree and a' that. Burns.

Then was I as a tree / Whose boughs did bend with fruit; but, in one night, / A storm, or robbery, call it what you will, / Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves, / And left me bare to weather. Cymbeline, iii. 3.

p.hi: Theoretical principles must sometimes be suffered to give way for the sake of practical advantages.
Theories of genius are the peculiar constructions of our philosophical times; ages of genius have passed away, and they left no other record than their works.

div.p: Theories are very thin and unsubstantial; experience 20 only is tangible. H. Ballou.

p.hi: Theories which do not connect measures with men are not theories for this world.
Theory and practice always act upon one another. It is possible to construe from what we do what we think, and from what we think what we will do.

div.p: Theory in and by itself is of no use except in so far as it proves to us the connection (Zusammenhang) that subsists among the phenomena. Goethe.
[Greek: theos hê anaideia]—Impudence is a god.
There are a thousand occasions for sorrow, 25 and a hundred for fear that day by day assail the fool; not so the wise man. Hitopadesa.

p.hi: There are always more tricks in a town than are talked of.

There are at bottom but two possible religions—that which rises in the moral nature of man, and which takes shape in moral commandments, and that which grows out of the observance of the material energies which operate in the external universe.
There are attractions in modest diffidence above the force of words. A silent address is the genuine eloquence of sincerity.
There are but three classes of men—the retrograde, the stationary, and the progressive.

div.p: There are but two ways of paying debt—increase 30 of industry in raising income; increase of thrift in laying it out. Carlyle.

p.hi: There are cases where little can be said and much must be done.
There are certain things in which mediocrity is not to be endured, such as poetry, music, painting, public speaking.

There are certain times in our life when we find ourselves in circumstances, that not only press upon us, but seem to weigh us down altogether. They give us, however, not only the opportunity, but they impose on us the duty of elevating ourselves, and thereby fulfilling the purpose of the Divine Being in our creation.
There are charms made only for distant admiration. No spectacle is nobler than a blaze.

div.p: There are cloudy days for the mind as well as 35 for the world, and the man who has the most genius is twenty times a day in the clouds. Beaumelle.

p.hi: There are depths in the soul which are deeper than hell.
There are enough unhappy on this earth.
There are faces so fluid with expression that we can hardly find what the mere features are.

There are falsehoods which are not lies ... which is the case in parables, fables, &c.... In such instances no confidence is destroyed, because none was reposed; no promise to speak the truth is violated, because none was given.

div.p: There are few circumstances in which it is not 40 best either to hide all or to tell all. La Bruyère.

p.hi: There are few faces that can afford to smile. A smile is sometimes bewitching; in general vapid; often a contortion.
There are few men so obstinate in their atheism whom a pressing danger will not reduce to an acknowledgment of the Divine power.
There are few persons to whom truth is not a sort of insult.
There are few things that are worthy of anger, and still fewer that can justify malignity.

There are few thoughts likely to come across ordinary men which have not already been expressed by greater men in the best possible way; and it is a wiser, more generous, more noble thing to remember and point out the perfect words than to invent poorer ones, wherewith to encumber temporarily the world.
There are few who, either by extraordinary endowment or favour of fortune, have enjoyed the opportunity of deciding what mode of life in especial they would wish to embrace.
There are few wild beasts more to be dreaded than a communicative man having nothing to communicate.
There are fewer students of man than of geometry.

div.p: There are forty men of wit for one of sense; 5 and he that will carry nothing about him but gold, will be every day at a loss for want of ready change. (?)

p.hi: There are heads sometimes so little that there is no room for wit, sometimes so long that there is no wit for so much room.
There are in man, in the beginning / And at the end, two blank book-binder's leaves—childhood and age.
There are in the history of a man only three epochs, his birth, his life, and his death; he is not conscious of being born; he submits to die; and he forgets to live.

There are in this day, as in all days, around and in every man, voices from the gods, imperative to all, if obeyed by even none, which say audibly: Arise, thou son of Adam, son of Time, make this thing more divine, and that thing, and thyself of all things, and work, and sleep not; for the Night cometh wherein no man can work.

div.p: There are in this loud stunning tide / Of 10 human care and crime, / With whom the melodies abide / Of th' everlasting chime; / Who carry music in their heart, / Through dusty lane and wrangling mart, / Plying their daily task with busier feet, / Because their secret souls a holy strain repeat. Keble.

p.hi: There are interests by the sacrifice of which peace is too dearly purchased. One should never be at peace to the shame of his own soul, to the violation of his integrity or of his allegiance to God.
There are many men who do not believe in evaporation. They get all they can, and keep all they get, and so are not fertilisers, but only stagnant, miasmatic pools.
There are many religions, but there is only one morality.
There are many troubles which you cannot cure by the Bible and the hymn-book, but which you can cure by a good perspiration and a breath of fresh air.

div.p: There are many truths of which the full 15 meaning cannot be realised until personal experience has brought it home. J. S. Mill.
There are men who, by long consulting their own inclination, have forgotten that others have a claim to the same deference. (?)

p.hi: There are men who dwell on the defects of their enemies. I always have regard to the merits of mine, and derive profit therefrom.
There are men whose tongues are more eloquent than those of women, but no man possesses the eloquence of a woman's eye.

There are moments in life when the heart is so full of emotion, / That if by chance it be shaken, or into its depths like a pebble / Drops some careless word, it overflows; and its secret, / Spilt on the ground like water, can never be gathered together.

div.p: There are more fools than wise men, and even 20 in the wise men more folly than wisdom. Chamfort.

p.hi: There are more men ennobled by study than by nature.

div.p: There are more offences at my beck than I have thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape, or time to act them in. Ham., iii. 1.
There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, / Than are dreamt of in your philosophy. Ham., i. 5.

p.hi: There are more ways to the wood than one.

div.p: There are nae fules like auld fules. Sc. Pr. 25

p.hi: There are natures that are great by what they attain, and others by what they disdain.
There are no better masters than poverty and want.
There are no chagrins so venomous as the chagrins of the idle; no pangs so sickening as the satieties of pleasure.
There are no English lives worth reading except those of players, who by the nature of the case have bidden Respectability good-day.

div.p: There are no fixtures in Nature. The universe 30 is fluid and volatile. Emerson.

p.hi: There are no grotesques in Nature.
There are no laws by which we can write Iliads.
There are no obstructions more fatal to fortune than pride and resentment.
There are no persons more solicitous about the preservation of rank than those who have no rank at all.

div.p: There are no proverbial sayings which are not 35 true. Cervantes.

p.hi: There are no real pleasures without real needs.

div.p: There are no tricks in plain and simple faith. Jul. Cæs., iv. 2.

p.hi: There are no troubles which have such a wasting and disastrous effect upon the mind as those which must not be told, but which cause the mind to be continually rolling and turning over upon itself in ceaseless convolutions and unrest.
There are no twin souls in God's universe.

div.p: There are none but men of strong passions 40 capable of going to greatness; none but such capable of meriting the public gratitude. Mirabeau.

p.hi: There are none of the charges brought against Socialism which might not have been brought against Christianity itself.
There are omens in the air, / And voices whispering Beware!—/ But never victor in the fight / Heeded the portents of fear and care.

There are only three classes of people—those who have found God and serve him; those who have not found God and seek him; and those who live without either seeking or finding him—the first, rational and happy; the second, unhappy and rational; the third, foolish and unhappy.
There are only two ways of rising in the world, either by one's own industry or by the weakness of others.

div.p: There are people who will help you to get your 5 basket on your head, because they want to see what's in it. Negro Pr.

p.hi: There are people who would never have been in love if they had never heard love spoken of.
There are proselytes from atheism, but none from superstition.
There are several who would, or at least pretend they would, bear much in their own business who will bear nothing at all.
There are shades in all good pictures, but there are lights too, if we choose to contemplate them.

div.p: There are single thoughts that contain the 10 essence of a whole volume, single sentences that have the beauties of a large work. Joubert.

p.hi: There are soldiers of the ploughshare as well as soldiers of the sword.
There are some cases in which human nature and its deep wrongs will be ever stronger than the world and its philosophy.
There are some faults so nearly allied to excellence that we can scarce weed out the vice without eradicating the virtue.
There are some men who are witty when they are in a bad humour, and others only when they are sad.

div.p: There are some people who give with the air 15 of refusal. Queen Christiana.

p.hi: There are some sorrows cannot be subjected / To man's construction, howsoe'er suspected.
There are some trifles well habited, as there are some fools well clothed.
There are sorrows / Where of necessity the soul must be / Its own support.

There are souls which fall from heaven like flowers; but ere the pure and fresh buds can open, they are trodden in the dust of the earth, and lie soiled and crushed under the foul tread of some brutal hoof.

div.p: There are things in this world to be laughed 20 at, as well as things to be admired; and his is no complete mind that cannot give to each sort his due. Carlyle.

p.hi: There are things that should be done, not spoken; that, till the doing of them is begun, cannot be spoken.
There are those who never reason on what they should do, but what they have done; as if Reason had her eyes behind, and could only see backwards.
There are thousands hacking at the branches of evil to one who is striking at the root.
There are three classes of authors—those who write without thinking, those who think while writing, and those who think before writing.

div.p: There are three difficulties in authorship—to 25 write anything worth the publishing, to find honest men to publish it, and to get sensible men to read it. Colton.

p.hi: There are three material things, not only useful, but essential, to life—pure air, water, and earth; and three immaterial that are equally essential—admiration, hope, and love.
There are three means of believing—by inspiration, by reason, and by custom. Christianity, which is the only rational institution, does yet admit none for its sons who do not believe by inspiration.

There are three religions—the religion which depends on reverence for what is above us, denominated the ethnic; the religion which founds itself on reverence for what is around us, denominated the philosophical; the religion grounded on reverence for what is beneath us, which we name the Christian.
There are three things in this world which deserve no quarter—hypocrisy, pharisaism, and tyranny.

div.p: There are three things which cause perfection 30 in a man—nature, reason, use. Reason I call discipline; use, exercise. If any one of these branches want, certainly the tree of virtue must needs wither. John Lily.

p.hi: There are times when silence, if the preacher did but know, / Shall preach to better purpose than a sermon stale and flat.
There are times when we are diverted out of errors, but could not be preached out of them.
There are truths that shield themselves behind veils, and are best spoken by implication. Even the sun veils himself in his own rays to blind the gaze of the too curious starer.

There are two, and only two, forms of possible gospel or "good message"—one, that men are saved by themselves doing what is right; and the other, that they are saved by believing that somebody also did right instead of them. The first of these gospels is eternally true and holy; the other eternally false, damnable, and damning.

div.p: There are two kinds of genius. The first and 35 highest may be said to speak out of the eternal into the present, and must compel its age to understand it; the second understands its age, and tells it what it wishes to be told. Lowell.

p.hi: There are two levers for moving men—interest and fear.

There are two modes of establishing our reputation—to be praised by honest men, and to be abused by rogues. It is best, however, to secure the former, because it will be invariably accompanied by the latter.
There are two sides to every question.
There are two things that can reach the top of a pyramid, the eagle and the reptile.
There are two ways of attaining an important end—force and perseverance; the silent power of the latter grows irresistible with time.

There are unhappy times in the world's history, when he that is the least educated will chiefly have to say that he is the least perverted; and with the multitude of false eye-glasses, convex, concave, green, even yellow, has not lost the natural use of his eyes.

div.p: There are very few moments in a man's existence 5 when he experiences so much ludicrous distress, or meets with so little charitable commiseration, as when he is in pursuit of his own hat. Dickens.

p.hi: There are very few people in this world who get any good by either writing or reading.
There are, whom heaven has blessed with store of wit, / Yet want as much again to manage it; / For wit and judgment ever are at strife, / Tho' meant each other's aid, like man and wife.
There are words which are worth as much as the best actions, for they contain the germ of them all.
There be some that think their wits have been asleep, except they dart out somewhat that is piquant, and to the quick; that is a vein which would be bridled.

div.p: There can be no excess to love, none to knowledge, 10 none to beauty, when these attributes are considered in the purest sense. Emerson.
There can be no kernel in this light nut; the soul of this man is in his clothes. All's Well, ii. 5.

p.hi: There can be no profanity where there is no fane behind.
There can be no shame in accepting orders from those who have themselves learned to obey.
There can be no true aristocracy but must possess the land.

div.p: There can come no harm of supposing every 15 other man better than yourself; but the supposing any man worse than yourself may be attended with very ill consequences. Thomas à Kempis.

p.hi: There coils a fear beneath the loveliest dream.
There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man.
There have been in all ages children of God and of man; the one born of the Spirit, and obeying it; the other born of the flesh, and obeying it.
There in others' looks discover / What thy own life's course has been, / And thy deeds of years past over, / In thy fellow-men be seen.

div.p: There is a better thing than the great man 20 who is always speaking, and that is the great man who only speaks when he has a great word to say. W. Winter.

p.hi: There is a black speck, say the Arabs, were it no bigger than a bean's eye, in every soul; which, once set a-working, will overcloud the whole man into darkness and quasi-madness, and hurry him balefully into night.

There is a book, who runs may read, / Which heavenly truth imparts, / And all the love its scholars need, / Pure eyes and Christian hearts. / The works of God above, below, / Within us, and around, / Are pages in that book, to show / How God Himself is found.
There is a budding morrow in midnight.

There is a care for trifles which proceeds from love and conscience, and is most holy; and a care for trifles which comes of idleness and frivolity, and is most base. And so, also, there is a gravity proceeding from thought, which is most noble; and a gravity proceeding from dulness and mere incapability of enjoyment, which is most base.

div.p: There is a Cato in every man; a severe censor 25 of his manners. And he that reverences this judge will seldom do anything he need repent of. Burton.

p.hi: There is a certain artificial polish, a commonplace vivacity, acquired by perpetually mingling in the beau monde, which, in the commerce of the world, supplies the place of natural suavity and good-humour; but it is purchased at the expense of all original and sterling traits of character.
There is a certain mien and motion of the body and all its parts, both in acting and speaking, which argues a man well within.
There is a certain noble pride through which merits shine brighter than through modesty.
There is a country accent, not in speech only, but in thought, conduct, character, and manner of existing, which never forsakes a man.

div.p: There is a crack in everything God has made. 30 Emerson.

p.hi: There is a devil dwells in man as well as a divinity.
There is a different kind of knowledge good for every different creature, and the glory of the higher creatures is in ignorance of what is known to the lower.
There is a flush of the body which is full of warmth and life, and another which will pass into putrefaction.
There is a foolish corner even in the brain of the sage.

div.p: There is a frightful interval between the seed 35 and the timber. Johnson.

p.hi: There is a glare about worldly success, which is very apt to dazzle men's eyes.
There is a God within us who breathes that divine fire by which we are animated.
There is a great deal of folly in talking unnecessarily of one's private affairs.
There is a great difference between bearing malice, which is always ungenerous, and a resolute self-defence, which is always prudent and justifiable.

div.p: There is a great discovery still to be made in 40 literature, that of paying literary men by the quantity they do not write. Carlyle.

p.hi: There is a heroic innocence, as well as a heroic courage.
There is a higher law than the constitution.

div.p: There is a history in all men's lives, / Figuring the nature of the times deceased; / The which observed, a man may prophesy, / With a near aim of the main chance of things / As yet not come to life: which, in their seeds / And weak beginnings, lie intreasurèd. 2 Hen. IV., iii. 1.

p.hi: There is a kind of pride in which are included all the commandments of God, and a kind of vanity which contains the seven mortal sins.
There is a life which taketh not its hues / From earth or earthly things; and so grows pure / And higher than the petty cares of men, / And is a blessed life and glorified.
There is a living, literal communion of saints, wide as the world itself, and as the history of the world.

div.p: There is a long and wearisome step between 5 admiration and imitation. Jean Paul.

p.hi: There is a lust in man no charm can tame, / Of loudly publishing his neighbour's shame; / On eagle's wings immortal scandals fly, / While virtuous actions are but born and die.
There is a magic in a great name.
There is a magic in the memory of schoolboy friendships; it softens the heart, and even affects the nervous system of those who have no hearts.

div.p: There is a mean in all things. Even virtue itself hath its stated limits; which not being strictly observed, it ceases to be virtue. (?)
There is a measure of self-regard which is 10 right, wherein the individual self is identified with the universal self. J. C. Sharp.

p.hi: There is a mercy that is weakness, and even treason against the common good.
There is a method in man's wickedness, / It grows by degrees.
There is a nobler ambition than the getting of all California, or the getting of all the suffrages that are on the planet just now.
There is a perennial nobleness, and even sacredness, in work. Were he ever so benighted, forgetful of his high calling, there is always hope in a man that actually and earnestly works.

div.p: There is a period of life when our backward 15 movements are steps in advance. Rousseau.

p.hi: There is a pleasure in poetic pains which only poets know.

There is a pleasure in the pathless woods; / There is a rapture on the lonely shore; / There is society, where none intrudes, / By the deep sea, and music in its roar; / I love not the man the less, / But Nature more.
There is a pleasure, sure, in being mad, which none but mad men know.
There is a power over and behind us, and we are the channels of its communication.

div.p: There is a probity of manners as well as of 20 conscience, and a true Christian will regard in a degree the conventionalities of society. De Boufflers.

p.hi: There is a property in the horizon which no man has but he whose eye can integrate all the parts—that is, the poet.

There is a rabble amongst the gentry as well as the commonalty; a sort of plebeian heads, whose fancy moves in the same wheel with the others,—men in the same level with mechanics, though their fortunes do somewhat gild their infirmities, and their purses compound for their follies.
There is a remedy for everything but death.
There is a remedy for every wrong, and a satisfaction for every soul.

div.p: There is a sacredness in tears. They are not 25 the mark of weakness, but of power. They speak more eloquently than ten thousand tongues. They are the messengers of overwhelming grief, of deep contrition, and of unspeakable love. Washington Irving.

p.hi: There is a skeleton in every house.
Then is a snake in the grass.

There is a Spanish proverb that a lapidary who would grow rich must buy of those who go to be executed, as not caring how cheap they sell; and sell to those who go to be married, as not caring how dear they buy.

div.p: There is a special providence in the fall of a sparrow. Ham., v. 1.
There is a spirit of resistance implanted by 30 the Deity in the breast of man, proportioned to the size of the wrongs he is destined to endure. C. J. Fox.

p.hi: There is a Sunday conscience as well as a Sunday coat; and those who make religion a secondary concern put the coat and conscience carefully by to put on only once a week.
There is a sweet little cherub that sits up aloft, to keep watch for the life of poor Jack.
There is a tendency in things to right themselves.
