There is a third silent party to all our bargains. The nature and soul of things takes on itself the guarantee of the fulfilment of every contract, so that honest service cannot come to loss.

div.p: There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, 35 taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; / Omitted, all the voyage of their life / Is bound in shallows and in miseries; / On such a full sea are we now afloat; / And we must take the current when it serves, / Or lose our ventures. Jul. Cæs., iv. 3.

p.hi: There is a time for all things.
There is a time in every man's education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance.
There is a time of life beyond which we cannot form a tie worth the name of friendship.
There is a time there for every purpose and for every work.

div.p: There is a time wherein one man ruleth over 40 another to his own hurt. Bible.

p.hi: There is a true Church whenever one meets another helpfully, and that is the only holy or Mother Church which ever was or ever shall be.
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
There is a worth in honest ignorance; 'twere almost a pity to exchange for knowledge.
There is always life for a living one.
There is always room for a man of force, and he makes room for many.
There is always some levity in excellent minds; they have wings to rise and also to stray.

div.p: There is always the possibility of beauty 5 where there is an unsealed human eye; of music where there is an unstopped human ear; and of inspiration where there is a receptive human spirit, a spirit standing before. C. H. Parkhurst.
There is an abasement because of glory, and there is that lifteth up his head from a low estate. Ecclus., xx. 11.

p.hi: There is an anger that is majestic as the frown of Jehovah's brow; it is the anger of truth and love.
There is an emanation from the heart in genuine hospitality which cannot be described but is immediately felt, and puts the stranger at once at his ease.

div.p: There is a heroic innocence, as well a heroic courage. (?)
There is an insolence which none but those 10 who deserve some contempt themselves can bestow, and those only who deserve no contempt can bear. Fielding.

p.hi: There is as much difference between the counsel that a friend giveth and that a man giveth himself, as there is between the counsel of a friend and of a flatterer.
There is as much ingenuity in making an felicitous application of an passage as in being the author of it.

There is, at any given moment, a best path for every man; the thing which, here and now, it were wisest for him to do; whatsoever forwards him in that, were it even in the shape of blows and spurnings, is liberty; whatsoever hinders him, were it tremendous cheers and rivers of heavy wet, is slavery.
There is but one case wherein a man may commend himself with good grace, and that is in commending virtue in another, especially if it be such a virtue whereunto himself pretendeth.

div.p: There is but one class of men to be trembled 15 at, and that is the stupid class, the class that cannot see; who, alas! are mainly they that will not see. Carlyle.

p.hi: There is but one misfortune for a man, when some idea lays hold of him which exerts no influence upon his active life, or still more, which withdraws him from it.
There is but one philosophy, and its name is Fortitude; to bear is to conquer our fate.
There is but one solid basis of happiness, and that is the reasonable hope of a happy futurity. This may be had everywhere.

There is but one temple in the world, and that is the body of man. Nothing is holier than this high form. Bending before men is a reverence done to this revelation in the flesh. We touch heaven when we lay our hand on a human body.

div.p: There is but one thing without honour, smitten 20 with eternal barrenness, inability to do or to be—insincerity, unbelief. He who believes nothing, who believes only the shows of things, is not in relation with nature and fact at all. Carlyle.

p.hi: There is certainly something of exquisite kindness and thoughtful benevolence in that rarest of gifts—fine breeding.

div.p: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your butterfly was a grub. Coriolanus, v. 4.

p.hi: There is enjoyment even in sadness, and the same souvenirs which have produced long regrets may also soften them.

There is ever a certain languor attending the fulness of prosperity. When the heart has no more to wish, it yawns over its possessions, and the energy of the soul goes out, like a flame that has no more to devour.

div.p: There is evil in every human heart, which may 25 remain latent, perhaps through the whole of life; but circumstances may rouse it to activity. Hawthorne.

p.hi: There is far less pleasure in doing a thing beautifully than in seeing it beautifully done.
There is for the soul a spontaneous culture, on which depends all its real progress in perfection.
There is forgiveness with God and Christ for the passing sin of the hot heart, but none for the eternal and inherent sin of the cold.
There is genius of a nation, which is not to be found in the citizen, but which characterises the society.

div.p: There is great force hidden in a sweet command. 30 George Herbert.

p.hi: There is in human nature an essential, though somewhat mysterious, connection of love with fear.
There is in human nature generally more of the fool than of the wise, and therefore those faculties by which the foolish part of men's minds is taken are most potent.
There is in man a Higher than love of happiness; he can do without happiness, and instead thereof find blessedness!

There is in nature an accessible and an inaccessible. Be careful to discriminate between the two. Be circumspect, and proceed with reverence.... It is always difficult to see where the one begins and the other leaves off. He who knows it, and is wise, will confine himself to the accessible.

div.p: There is in the heart of woman such a deep 35 well of love that no age can freeze it. Bulwer Lytton.

p.hi: There is in this world infinitely more joy than pain to be shared, if you will only take your share when it is set before you.
There is little hope of equity where rebellion reigns.
There is little wisdom in knowing that every man must be up and doing, and that all mankind are made dependent on one another.

div.p: There is more concern nowadays to interpret interpretations than to interpret things, and more books about books than about any other subject. We do nothing but expound one another. (?)

p.hi: There is more danger in a reserved and silent friend than in a noisy babbling enemy.
There is more pleasure in loving than in being beloved.
There is more serfdom in England now than at any time since the Conquest.

div.p: There is music in all things, if men had ears. 5 Byron.

p.hi: There is need, bitter need, to bring back, if we may, into men's minds, that to live is nothing unless to live be to know Him by whom we live, and that He is not to be known amidst the hurry of crowds and crash of innovation, but in solitary places, and out of the glowing intelligence which He gave to men of old.
There is never a beginning, there is never an end, to the inexplicable continuity of the web of God, but always circular power returning into itself.
There is never but one opportunity of a kind.
There is no better counsellor than time.

div.p: There is no better sign of a brave mind than a 10 hard hand. 2 Hen. VI., iv. 2.

p.hi: There is no better type of a perfectly free creature than the common house-fly.
There is no bridge from one being to another, each is a self, each rests on itself, and wills only itself, knows only itself, understands only itself.
There is no brotherhood possible, at any rate stable, between man and man but a brotherhood of labour.
There is no cause why one man's nose is longer than another's, but because that God pleases to have it so.

div.p: There is no class of men so difficult to be 15 managed in a state, as those whose intentions are honest, but whose consciences are bewitched. Napoleon.

p.hi: There is no communion possible among men who believe only in hearsays.
There is no contingency, and what to us seems only blind chance is an efflux from the depths of being.
There is no courage but in innocence; no constancy but in an honest cause.
There is no creature so lonely as the dweller in the intellect.

div.p: There is no darkness but ignorance. Twelfth 20 Night, iv. 2.

p.hi: There is no darkness unto the conscience, which can see without light.
There is no dearth of charity in the world in giving, but there is comparatively little exercised in thinking and speaking.
There is no defence against reproach but obscurity.
There is no den in the wide world to hide a rogue. Commit a crime, and the earth is made of glass.

div.p: There is no despair so absolute as that which 25 comes with the first moments of our first great sorrow, when we have not yet known what it is to have suffered and be healed, to have despaired and have recovered hope. George Eliot.

p.hi: There is no detraction worse than to overpraise a man.
There is no direr disaster in love than the death of imagination.
There is no dispute managed without passion, and yet there is scarce a dispute worth a passion.
There is no disputing against hobby-horses.

div.p: There is no education like adversity. Disraeli. 30

p.hi: There is no end in nature, but every end is a beginning.
There is no end of settlements; there will never be an end; the best settlement is but a temporary partial one.

div.p: There is no event but sprung somewhere from the soul of man. (?)

p.hi: There is no evil but is mingled with good.

div.p: There is no extremity of distress which of 35 itself ought to reduce a great nation to despair. It is not the disorder, but the physician ... which alone can make a whole people desperate. Junius.

p.hi: There is no fatigue so wearisome as that which comes from want of work.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear.
There is no fiercer hell than failure in a great object.
There is no flock, however watched and tended, / But one dead lamb is there; / There is no fireside, howsoe'er defended, / But has one vacant chair.

div.p: There is no foolishest man but knows one and 40 the other thing more clearly than any the wisest man does. Carlyle.

p.hi: There is no gambling like politics.... Nothing in which the power of circumstance is more evident.
There is no genuine love for art without an ardent love for humanity.
There is no Gethsemane without its angel.
There is no ghost so difficult to lay as the ghost of an injury.

div.p: There is no God but God, the living, the self-subsisting. 45 Koran.

p.hi: There is no going to heaven in a sedan.
There is no good in arguing with the inevitable.
There is no good in emitting smoke till you have made it into fire, which all smoke is capable of becoming.
There is no great and no small / To the soul that maketh all; / And where it cometh, all things are; / And it cometh everywhere.

div.p: There is no great genius free from some tincture 50 of madness. Sen.

p.hi: There is no greater evil among men than a testament framed with injustice; where caprice hath guided the boon, or dishonesty refused what was due.
There is no greater fraud than a promise unfulfilled.
There is no greater proof of human weakness than that which betrays itself in the boast of fortune and ancestry; these cannot ennoble us, but our conduct in life may ennoble or degrade them.
There is no greater punishment than that of being abandoned to one's self.
There is no greater wisdom than well to time the beginnings and onset of things.

div.p: There is no grief like hate! no pains like passions! 5 no deceit like sense! Enter the path! far hath he gone whose foot treads down one fond offence. Sir Edwin Arnold.

p.hi: There is no grief that time will not soften.
There is no harm in anybody thinking that Christ is in bread. The harm is in the expectation of His presence in gunpowder.
There is no heroic poem in the world but is at bottom a biography, the life of a man; and there is no life of a man, faithfully recorded, but is a heroic poem of its sort, rhymed or unrhymed.
There is no jesting with edge tools.

div.p: There is no joy without alloy. Pr. 10

p.hi: There is no hiding of evil but not to do it.
There is no index of character so sure as the voice.
There is no legislation for liars and traitors; they cannot be prevented from the pit; the earth finally swallows them.... There is no law for these but gravitation.
There is no less invention in aptly applying a thought found in a book than in being the first author of the thought.

div.p: There is no lie that many men will not believe; 15 there is no man who does not believe many lies; and there is no man who believes only lies. J. Sterling.

p.hi: There is no loss / In being small; great bulks but swell with dross. / Man is heaven's masterpiece; if it appear / More great, the value's less; if less, more dear.

div.p: There is no lustre (Glanz) without light; that is the first rule to which every author should pay regard. Cötvös.

p.hi: There is no man alone, because every man is a microcosm, and carries the whole world about him.

div.p: There is no man on the streets whose biography I would not like to be acquainted with. (?)
There is no man so friendless but that he can 20 find a friend sincere enough to tell him disagreeable truths. Bulwer Lytton.

p.hi: There is no man so rudely punished as he that is subject to the whip of his own remorse.
There is no man that has not his hour, nor is there anything that has not its place.
There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power in the day of death: and there is no discharge in that war.
There is no man that imparteth his joys to his friend, but he joyeth the more; and no man that imparteth his griefs to his friend, but he grieveth the less.

div.p: There is no man whom fortune does not visit 25 once in his life; but when she does not find him ready to receive her, she walks in at the door, and flies out at the window. Quoted by Montesquieu.

p.hi: There is no merit where there is no trial; and, till experience stamps the mark of strength, cowards may pass for heroes, faith for falsehood.
There is no mistake; there has been no mistake; and there shall be no mistake.
There is no more fatal blunderer than he who consumes the greater part of his life getting his living.
There is no more potent antidote to low sensuality than the adoration of beauty.

div.p: There is no more welcome gift to men than a 30 new symbol. Emerson.

p.hi: There is no mortal extant, out of the depths of Bedlam, but lives all skinned, thatched, covered over with formulas; and is, as it were, held in from delirium and the inane by his formulas. These are the most beneficent and indispensable of human equipments; blessed he who has a skin and tissues, so it be a living one, and the heart-pulse everywhere discernible through it.
There is no mortal truly wise and restless at once; wisdom is the repose of minds.
There is no new thing under the sun.
There is no object of desire the supreme vanity of which we do not recognise and confess when once we have embraced it.

div.p: There is no object so foul that intense light 35 will not make beautiful. And the stimulus it affords to the sense, and a sort of infinitude which it hath like space and time, make all matter gay. Emerson.

p.hi: There is no one the friend of another: there is no one the enemy of another: friends, as well as enemies, are created through our transactions.
There is no one who does not exaggerate.
There is no ordinance obliging us to fight those who are stronger than ourselves. Such fighting, as it were, with an elephant, is the same as men's fighting against rocks.
There is no other ghost save the ghost of our own childhood, the ghost of our own innocence, the ghost of our own airy belief.

div.p: There is no other revelation than the thoughts 40 of the wise. Schopenhauer.

p.hi: There is no outward sign of courtesy that does not rest on a deep moral foundation.
There is no part of the furniture of a man's mind which he has a greater right to exult in than that which he has hewn and fashioned for himself.

There is no part of the world from whence we may not admire these planets, which roll, like ours, in different orbits round the same central sun; ... and whilst my soul is thus raised up to heaven, it imports me little what ground I tread upon.
There is no patriotic art and no patriotic science.

There is no peace in ambition; it is always gloomy, and often unreasonably so. The kindness of the king, the regards of the courtiers, the attachment of my domestics, and the fidelity of a large number of friends, make me happy no longer.
There is no permanence in doubt; it incites the mind to closer inquiry and experiment, from which, if rightly managed, certainty proceeds, and in this alone can man find thorough satisfaction.
There is no permanent love but that which has duty for its eldest brother; so that if one sleeps the other watches, and honour is safe.
There is no place like home.

div.p: There is no place where earth's sorrows / Are 5 more felt than up in heaven; / There is no place where earth's failings / Have such kindly judgment given. F. W. Faber.

p.hi: There is no policy like politeness; and a good manner is the best thing in the world, either to get a good name or to supply the want of it.
There is no pure malignity in nature.
There is no qualification for government but virtue and wisdom.
There is no real life but cheerful life.

div.p: There is no repose for the mind except in the 10 absolute. Amiel.

p.hi: There is no respect for others without humility in one's self.
There is no respect of persons with God.
There is no returning from a
There is no riches above a sound body, and no joy above the joy of the heart.

div.p: There is no right faith in believing what is 15 true, unless we believe it because it is true. Whately.

p.hi: There is no road too long to the man who advances deliberately and without undue haste; there are no honours too distant to the man who prepares himself for them with patience.
There is no royal road to geometry.
There is no sanctuary of virtue like home.
There is no solemnity so deep, to a right thinking creature, as that of dawn.

div.p: There is no solitude in nature. Schiller. 20

p.hi: There is no solitude more dreadful for a stranger, an isolated man, than a great city. So many thousands, and not one friend.
There is no spirit without a body unless it be a ghost, and no body without a spirit unless it be a corpse.
There is no sporting with a fellow-creature's happiness or misery.
There is no sterner moralist than pleasure.

div.p: There is no stronger test of a man's real 25 character than power and authority, exciting, as they do, every passion, and discovering every latent vice. Plutarch.

p.hi: There is no such flatterer as is a man's self, and there is no such remedy against flattery of a man's self as the liberty of a friend.
There is no such thing as a dumb poet or a handless painter. The essence of an artist is that he should be articulate.
There is no such thing as being agreeable without a thorough good-humour, a natural sweetness of temper, enlivened by cheerfulness.
There is no such thing as chance; and what seems to us merest accident springs from the deepest source of destiny.

div.p: There is no such thing as Liberty in the universe: 30 there can never be. The stars have it not; the earth has it not; the sea has it not; and we men have the mockery and semblance of it only for our heaviest punishment. Ruskin.
There is no sure foundation set on blood; / No certain life achieved by others' death. King John, iv. 2.

p.hi: There is no surer argument of a weak mind than irresolution.

div.p: There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats; / For I am armed so strong in honesty / That they pass by me as the idle wind / Which I respect not. Jul. Cæs., iv. 3.

p.hi: There is no thought in any mind, but it quickly tends to convert itself into a power, and organises a huge instrumentality of means.

div.p: There is no time so miserable, but a man may 35 be true. Timon of Athens, iv. 3.

p.hi: There is no traitor like him whose domestic treason plants the poniard within the breast which trusted to his truth.
There is no true action without will.
There is no true love without jealousy.
There is no vague general capability in men.

div.p: There is no vice or folly that requires so much 40 nicety and skill to manage as vanity. Swift.

p.hi: There is no vice or crime that does not originate in self-love; and there is no virtue that does not grow from the love of others out of and beyond self.

div.p: There is no vice so simple but assumes / Some mark of virtue in his outward parts. Mer. of Ven., iii. 2.

p.hi: There is no venom like that of the tongue.
There is no wealth but life—life, including all its powers of love, of joy, and of admiration.

div.p: There is no well-doing, no godlike doing, that 45 is not patient doing. J. G. Holland.

p.hi: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the Lord.
There is no work of genius which has not been the delight of mankind, no word of genius to which the human heart and soul have not, sooner or later, responded.
There is no worse fruit than that which never ripens.
There is no worse joke than a true one.

div.p: There is none so blind as they that won't see. 50 Swift.

p.hi: There is none so poor that he need sit on a pumpkin. That is shiftlessness.
There is not a Red Indian hunting by Lake Winnipeg can quarrel with his squaw but the whole world must smart for it; will not the price of beaver rise?

There is not any benefit so glorious in itself but it may be exceedingly sweetened and improved by the manner of conferring it. The virtue, I know, rests in the intent, but the beauty and ornament of an obligation lies in the manner of it.
There is not in earth a spectacle more worthy than a great man superior to his sufferings.
There is not in national life any real epoch, because there is nothing in reality abrupt. Events, however great or sudden, are consequences of preparations long ago made.

There is not one grain in the universe, either too much or too little, nothing to be added, nothing to be spared; nor so much as any one particle of it, that mankind may not be either the better or the worse for, according as it is applied.

div.p: There is not so agonizing a feeling in the whole 5 catalogue of human suffering as the first conviction that the heart of the being whom we most tenderly love is estranged from us. Bulwer Lytton.

p.hi: There is not so much comfort in having children as there is sorrow in parting with them.
There is not the thickness of a sixpence between good and evil.
There is not yet any inventory of man's faculties.
There is nothing beyond the pleasure which the study of Nature produces. Her secrets are of unfathomable depth, but it is granted to us men to look into them more and more.

div.p: There is nothing born but has to die. Carlyle. 10

p.hi: There is nothing by which I have, through life, more profited than by the just observations, the good opinion, and the sincere and gentle encouragement of amiable and sensible women.
There is nothing capricious in nature.
There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known.
There is nothing divine but what is rational.

div.p: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking 15 makes it so. Ham., ii. 2.

p.hi: There is nothing evil but what is within us; the rest is either natural or accidental.
There is nothing exasperates people more than the display of superior ability or brilliancy in conversation. They seem pleased at the time, but their envy makes them curse him at their hearts.
There is nothing from without a man that entering into him can defile him; but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man.
There is nothing good or evil save in the will.

div.p: There is nothing good or godlike in this world 20 but has in it something of "infinite sadness." Carlyle.

p.hi: There is nothing holier in this life of ours than the first consciousness of love, the first fluttering of its silken wings.
There is nothing in the world more shameful than establishing one's self on lies and fables.
There is nothing in this world that will keep the devil out of one but hard labour.
There is nothing in which the power of circumstance is more evident than in politics.

div.p: There is nothing innocent or good that dies 25 and is forgotten. Dickens.

p.hi: There is nothing lighter than vain praise.
Pr. A cobbler's advice in an emergency.
There is nothing like the cold dead hand of the past to take down our tumid egotism, and lead us into the solemn flow of the life of our race.

div.p: There is nothing little to the truly great in 30 spirit. Dickens.

p.hi: There is nothing more allied to the barbarous and savage character than sullenness, concealment, and reserve.
There is nothing more characteristic than the shakes of the hand.
There is nothing more charming than to see a mother with a child in her arms, and nothing more venerable than a mother among a number of her children.
There is nothing more frightful than for a teacher to know only what his scholars are intended to know.

div.p: There is nothing more frightful than imagination 35 without taste. Goethe.

p.hi: There is nothing more perennial in us than habit and imitation. They are the source of all working and all apprenticeship, of all practice and all learning.
There is nothing more pitiable in the world than an irresolute man, oscillating between two feelings, who would willingly unite the two, and who does not perceive that nothing can unite them.
There is nothing more precious to a man than his will; there is nothing which he relinquishes with so much reluctance.
There is nothing more terrible to a guilty heart than the eye of a respected friend.

div.p: There is nothing new under the sun. Bible. 40

p.hi: There is nothing of which men are so fond and so careless as life.
There is nothing on earth divine beside humanity.
There is nothing on earth which is not in the heavens in a heavenly form, and nothing in the heavens which is not on the earth in an earthly form.

There is nothing on earth without difficulty. Only the inner impulse, the pleasure it gives us, and love we feel, help us to overcome obstruction, to pave our way, and to raise ourselves out of the narrow circle in which others sorrowfully torture themselves.

div.p: There is nothing really more monstrous in any 45 recorded savagery or absurdity of mankind than that governments should be able to get money for any folly they choose to commit, by selling to capitalists the right of taxing future generations to the end of time. Ruskin.

p.hi: There is nothing so agonising to the fine skin of vanity as the application of a rough truth.
There is nothing so great or so goodly in creation, but it is a mean symbol of the gospel of Christ, and of the things that he has prepared for them that love him.
There is nothing so powerful as truth, and nothing so strange.
There is nothing so small but that we may honour God by asking his guidance of it, or insult him by taking it into our own hands.

div.p: There is nothing so secret but it comes to 5 light. Pr.

p.hi: There is nothing so sure of succeeding as not to be over brilliant, as to be entirely wrapped up in one's self, and endowed with a perseverance which, in spite of all the rebuffs it may meet with, never relaxes in the pursuit of its object.
There is nothing so terrible as activity without insight.
There is nothing to be found only once in the world.
There is nothing to which man is not related.

div.p: There is nothing which vanity does not desecrate. 10 Ward Beecher.

p.hi: There is nothing without us that is not also within us.
There is often a complaint of want of parts, when the fault lies in a want of a due improvement of them.
There is often more true spiritual force in a proverb than in a philosophical system.

div.p: There is / One great society alone on earth; / The noble living and the noble dead. (?)
There is one preacher who does preach with 15 effect, and gradually persuade all persons; his name is Destiny, Divine Providence, and his sermon the inflexible course of things. Carlyle.

p.hi: There is only one cure for public distress, and that is public education, directed to make men thoughtful, merciful, and just.
There is only one mendacious being in the world, and that is man.
There is only one thing better than tradition, and that is the original and eternal life out of which all tradition takes its rise.
There is only one true religion, but there may be many forms of belief.

div.p: There is poetry and beauty in the common 20 lives about us, if we look at them with imaginative and sympathetic eye. J. Morley.

p.hi: There is power over and behind us, and we are the channels of its communication.
There is precious instruction to be got by finding that we are wrong.
There is properly but one slavery in the world—the slavery of wisdom to folly.
There is properly no history, only biography.

div.p: There is, properly speaking, no misfortune in 25 the world. Happiness and misfortune stand in continual balance. Every misfortune is, as it were, the obstruction of a stream, which, after overcoming this obstruction, but bursts forth with the greater force. Novalis.

p.hi: There is really something absurd about the Present; all that people think of is the sight, the touch of each other, and there they rest; but it never occurs to them to reflect upon what is to be gained from such moments.

div.p: There is scarce truth enough alive to make societies secure, but security enough to make fellowships accursed. Meas. for Meas., iii. 2.

p.hi: There is scarcely a good critic of books born in our age, and yet every fool thinks himself justified in criticising persons.

div.p: There is sentiment in all women, and sentiment 30 gives delicacy to thought, and tact to manner. But sentiment with men is generally acquired, an offspring of the intellectual quality, not, as with the other sex, of the moral. Bulwer Lytton.

p.hi: There is so much of good among the worst, so much of evil in the best, such seeming partialities in providence, so many things to lessen and expand, yea, and with all man's boast, so little real freedom of his will, that to look a little lower than the surface, garb, or dialect, or fashion, thou shalt feebly pronounce for a saint, and faintly condemn for a sinner.
There is so much trouble in coming into the world, and so much more, as well as meanness, in going out of it, that 'tis hardly worth while to be here at all.

div.p: There is some soul of goodness in things evil, / Would men observingly distil it out. Henry V., iv. 1.

p.hi: There is some use in having two attorneys in one firm. Their movements resemble those of the man and woman in a Dutch babyhouse. When it is fair weather with the client, out comes the gentleman partner to fawn like a spaniel; when it is foul, forth bolts the operative brother to pin like a bull-dog.

div.p: There is something behind the throne greater 35 than the king himself. Chatham.

p.hi: There is something in sorrow more akin to the course of human affairs than joy.
There is something irresistibly pleasing in the conversation of a fine woman; even though her tongue be silent, the eloquence of her eyes teach wisdom.
There is something more awful in happiness than in sorrow.
There is something not solid in the good that is done for us.

div.p: There is something of all men in every man. 40 Lichtenberg.

p.hi: There is something so moving in the very image of weeping beauty.

There is something too dear in the hope of seeing again.... "Dear heart, be quiet;" we say; "you will not be long separated from those people that you love; be quiet, dear heart!" And then we give it in the meanwhile a shadow, so that it has something, and then it is good and quiet, like a little child whose mother gives it a doll instead of the apple which it ought not to eat.

There is still a real magic in the action and reaction of minds on one another. The casual deliration of a few becomes, by this mysterious reverberation, the frenzy of many; men lose the use, not only of their understandings, but of their bodily senses; while the most obdurate unbelieving hearts melt like the rest in the furnace where all are cast as victims and as fuel.
There is still enough to satisfy one in spite of all misfortunes.
There is such a choice of difficulties that I am myself at a loss how to determine.
There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.

div.p: There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth: 5 and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. Bible.

p.hi: There is very great necessity indeed of getting a little more silent than we are.
There is work on God's wide earth for all men that he has made with hands and hearts.
There lives more faith in honest doubt, believe me, than in half the creeds.
There may come a day when there shall be no more curse; in the meantime you must be humble and honest enough to take your share of it.

div.p: There may often be less vanity in following the 10 new modes than in adhering to the old ones. It is true that the foolish invent them, but the wise may conform to, instead of contradicting, them. Joubert.

p.hi: There must always remain something that is antagonistic to good.
There must be a man behind a book.
There must be hearts which know the depths of our being, and swear by us, even when the whole world forsakes us.
There must be work done by the arms, or none of us would live; and work done by the brains, or the life would not be worth having. And the same men cannot do both.

div.p: There must first be seducing men before 15 seduced women. Jean Paul.
There needs no ghost, my lord, come from the grave / To tell us this. Ham., i. 5.

p.hi: There needs not a great soul to make a hero; there needs a god-created soul which will be true to its origin; that will be a great soul.
There never did and never will exist anything permanently noble and excellent in a character which was a stranger to the exercise of resolute self-denial.
There never was a bad man but had ability for good service.

div.p: There never was a great man unless through 20 Divine inspiration. Cicero.

p.hi: There never was a literary age whose dominant taste was not sickly.
There never was a talent, even for real literature, but was primarily a talent for something infinitely better of the silent kind.
There never was any heart truly great and generous that was not also tender and compassionate.
There never was any party, faction, or sect in which the most ignorant was not the most violent.

div.p: There never was so great a thought labouring 25 in the breasts of men as now. Emerson.

p.hi: There occur cases in human life when it is wisdom not to be too wise.
There remaineth a rest to the people of God.
There seems to be no part of knowledge in fewer hands than that of discerning when to have done.
There shall no evil happen to the just.

div.p: There the wicked cease from troubling, and 30 there the weary be at rest. Bible.

p.hi: There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built bulwarks against it. Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city, yet no man remembered that same poor man.

There was a time when meadow, grove, and stream, / The earth and every common sight, / To me did seem / Apparelled in celestial light, / The glory and the freshness of a dream. / It is not now as it has been of yore; / Turn wheresoe'er I may, / By night or day, / The things which I have seen, I now can see no more.
There was a time when the world acted upon books. Now books act upon the world.
There was but one Moses to the thousands of Israel that entered Jordan.

div.p: There was never a nation great until it came 35 to the knowledge that it had nowhere in the world to go for help. C. D. Warner.

p.hi: There was never good or ill but women had to do with it.

div.p: There was never yet philosopher / Who could endure the toothache patiently. Much Ado, v. 1.

p.hi: There was sense in the sentences, but the sum-total was nonsense.
Criticism of a young preacher's discourse.

div.p: There was speech in their dumbness, language in their very gesture. Winter's Tale, v. 2.
There were no ill language if it were not ill 40 taken. Pr.

p.hi: There where thou art, there where thou remainest, accomplish what thou canst.
There will always be a government of force where men are selfish.
There's a brave fellow! There's a man of pluck! / A man who is not afraid to say his say, / Though a whole town's against him.
There's a courage which grows out of fear.

div.p: There's a divinity that shapes our ends, / 45 Rough-hew them as we will. Ham., v. 2.

p.hi: There's a medium in thoughtfulness and gaiety: find it out and keep to it.

div.p: There's a special providence in the fall of a sparrow. Ham., v. 2.

p.hi: There's a sweeter flower than e'er / Blush'd on the rosy spray, / A brighter star, a richer bloom, / Than e'er did western heaven illume / At close of summer day—/ 'Tis Love, the last best gift of Heaven.
There's always life for the living.

div.p: There's beggary in the love that can be reckoned. Ant. and Cleop., i. 1.

p.hi: There's folks as make bad butter, and trusten to the salt t' hide it.
There's folks 'ud stand on their heads and then say the fault was in their boots.

div.p: There's husbandry in heaven; / Their candles are all out. Macb., i. 7.
There's language in her eye, her cheeks, her 5 lip, / Nay, her foot speaks. Troil. and Cress., iv. 5.

p.hi: There's many a good bit o' work done with a sad heart.
There's many a slip / 'Twixt the cup and the lip.
There's mercy in every place, / And mercy, encouraging thought, / Gives even affliction a grace, / And reconciles man to his lot.
There's music in the sighing of a reed; / There's music in the gushing of a rill; / There's music in all things, if men had ears.

div.p: There's nae sorrow there, John, / There's 10 neither cauld nor care, John, / The day is aye fair, / In the land o' the leal. Lady Nairne.
There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face. Macb., i. 4.

p.hi: There's no folk sic idiots as them that looks like geniuses.
There's no glory like his who saves his country.

div.p: There's no grace in a benefit that sticks to the 15 fingers. Sen.

p.hi: There's no great banquet but some fares ill.
There's no pleasure i' living, if you're to be corked up for ever, and only dribble your mind out by the sly, like a leaky barrel.
There's no seeing one's way through tears.
There's no slipping up-hill again, and no standing still when once you've begun to slip down.

div.p: There's no work so tirin' as danglin' about an' 20 starin', an' not rightly knowin' what you're goin' to do next; an' keepin' your face i' smilin' order, like a grocer o' market-day. George Eliot.

p.hi: There's not a joy the world can give like that it takes away.
There's not a place where Rest can say, / I'll not have Labour here; / For Rest itself would pine away / If Labour were not near.
There's not a string attuned to mirth / But has its chord in melancholy.

div.p: There's not one wise man among twenty that will praise himself. Much Ado, v. 2.
There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st, / 25 But in his motion like an angel sings, / Still quiring to the young-eyed cherubims. Mer. of Ven., v. 1.

p.hi: There's nothing but what's bearable as long as a man can work.
There's nothing half so sweet in life / As love's young dream.

div.p: There's nothing situate under heaven's eye, / But hath its bound in earth, in sea, in sky. Comedy of Errors, ii. 1.
There's none that can / Read God aright, unless 30 he first spell man. Quarles.
There's small choice in rotten apples. Tam. of Shrew, i. 1.

p.hi: There's something good in all weathers. If it don't happen to be good for my work to-day, it's good for some other man's to-day, and will come round to me to-morrow.

div.p: There's such divinity doth hedge a king, / That treason can but peep to what it would. Ham., iv. 5.

p.hi: There's things it's best to put off kenning as long as we can.

div.p: Thereby hangs a tale. As You Like It, ii. 7. 35

p.hi: These / Are but the varied God. The rolling year / Is full of thee.
Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, when she presented her five sons to a lady who had paraded her ornaments before her.
These cases, wherein happiness would be sinful, are just as much, but no more, the ordainments of Providence as those more common ones wherein happiness is natural and right.
These fair tales, which we know so beautiful, / Show only finer than our lives to-day / Because their voice was clearer, and they found / A sacred bard to sing them.

div.p: These limbs, whence had we them; this 40 stormy force; this life-blood with its burning passion? They are dust and shadow: a shadow-system gathered round our Me; wherein through some moments or years, the divine essence is to be revealed in flesh. Carlyle.

p.hi: These little things are great to little men.
These moving things, ca'ed wife and weans, / Wad move the very heart o' stanes.

div.p: These violent delights have violent ends. Rom. and Jul., ii. 6.
They are as sick that surfeit with too much, as they that starve with nothing. Mer. of Venice, i. 2.
They are but beggars that can count their 45 worth. Rom. and Jul., ii. 6.

p.hi: They are dead even for this life who hope for no better.
They are never alone that are accompanied with noble thoughts.

div.p: They are not a pipe for fortune's finger, / To sound what stop she please. Ham., iii. 2.

p.hi: They are not all free who scorn their chains.

div.p: They are not kings who sit on thrones, but 50 they who know how to govern. Emerson.

p.hi: They are not sages who do not declare men's duty.
They are slaves who dare not be / In the right with two or three.
They asked Lucman the fabulist, "From whom did you learn manners?" He answered, "From the unmannerly."
They can conquer who believe they can.
They do most by books who could do much without them; and he that chiefly owes himself unto himself is the substantial man.
They ever do pretend / To have received a wrong who wrong intend.

div.p: They fool me to the top of my bent. Ham., iii. 2.

p.hi: They found no end, in wandering mazes lost.

div.p: They grew in beauty side by side, / They fill'd 5 one home with glee; / Their graves are sever'd far and wide, / By mount, and stream, and sea. Mrs. Hemans.

p.hi: They govern the world, these sweet-lipped women, because beauty is the index of a larger fact than wisdom.
They had the divine right of kings to settle, these unfortunate ancestors of ours; ... and they did, on hest of necessity, manage to settle it.

div.p: They have been at a great feast of languages, and stolen the scraps. Love's L. Lost, v. 1.

p.hi: They have destroyed the beaten track to heaven; we are now compelled to make for ourselves ladders.

div.p: They laugh that win. Othello, iv. 2. 10
They lose it (the world) that do buy it with much care. Mer. of Ven., i. 1.
They love least that let men know their love. Two Gent. of Verona, i. 2.

p.hi: They love most who are least valued.

div.p: They love not poison that do poison need. Rich. II., v. 6.
They love us truly who correct us freely. Pr. 15

p.hi: They most assume who know the least.
They must hunger in winter that will not work in summer.
They must often change who would be constant in happiness or wisdom.
They never taste who always drink; / They always talk who never think.

div.p: They only are wise who know that they know 20 nothing. Carlyle.

p.hi: They only babble that practise not reflection.
They only should own who can administer.
They only who build on ideas build for eternity.
They pass best over the world who trip over it quickly; for it is but bog—if we stop, we sink.

div.p: They said that Love would die when Hope was 25 gone, / And Love mourn'd long, and sorrow'd after Hope; / At last she sought out Memory, and they trod / The same old paths where Love had walk'd with Hope, / And Memory fed the soul of Love with tears. Tennyson.
They say best men are moulded out of faults, / And, for the most, become much more the better / For being a little bad. Meas. for Meas., v. 1.

p.hi: They say Doubt is weak, but yet, if life be in the doubt, / The living doubt is more than Faith that life did never know.
"They say so" is half a lie.

They, sweet soul, that most impute a crime / Are pronest to it, and impute themselves, / Wanting the mental range; or low desire / Not to feel lowest makes them level all; / Yea, they would pare the mountain to the plain, / To leave an equal baseness.

div.p: They that are above have ends in everything. 30 Beaumont and Fletcher.

p.hi: They that are against superstition oftentimes run into it of the wrong side. If I wear all colours but black, then I am superstitious in not wearing black.
They that are booted are not always ready.
They that be whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.
They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness, as the stars for ever and ever.

div.p: They that bear a noble mind, / Where they 35 want of riches find. Wither.

p.hi: They that by pleading clothes / Do fortunes seek, when worth and service fail, / Would have their tale believed for their oaths, / And are like empty vessels under sail.
They that deny a God destroy man's nobility. For, certainly, man is of kin to the beasts, by his body; and if he be not of kin to God by his spirit, he is a base and ignoble creature.
They that do change old love for new, / Pray gods, they change for worse.
They that do nothing are in the readiest way to do that which is worse than nothing.

div.p: They that drive away time spur a free horse. 40 Robert Mason.

p.hi: They that govern the most make the least noise.
They that hold by the Divine / Clasp too the Human in their faith.
They that know one another salute afar off.
They that marry ancient people merely in expectation to bury them, hang themselves in hope that one will come and cut the halter.

div.p: They that mean to make no use of friends will 45 be at little trouble to gain them: and to be without friendship is to be without one of the first comforts of our present state. Johnson.

p.hi: They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy.
They that plough iniquity and sow wickedness reap the same.

div.p: They that stand high have many blasts to shake them; and if they fall, they dash themselves to pieces. Richard III., i. 3.

p.hi: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

div.p: They that sow the wind shall reap the whirlwind. 50 Bible.

p.hi: They that will crowd about bonfires may, sometimes very fairly, get their beards singed; it is the price they pay for such illumination; natural twilight is safe and free to all.

div.p: They told me I was everything; 'tis a lie: I am not ague-proof. King Lear, iv. 6.
They well deserve to have / That know the strong'st and surest way to get. Richard II., iii. 3.

p.hi: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us.
They who accuse and blacken thee wrongfully are much the greatest sufferers by their own malice and injustice.
They who but slowly pacèd are / By plodding on may travel far.
They who contract absurd habits are such as have no fear.
They who crouch to those who are above them, always trample on those who are below them.

div.p: They who do not feel the darkness will never 5 look for the light. Buckle.

p.hi: They who embrace the entire universe with love, for the most part love nothing but their narrow selves.
They who gratefully the gods adore, / Still find their joys increasing more and more.
They who have lost an infant are never, as it were, without an infant child.

They who have no other trade but seeking their fortune, need never hope to find her; coquette-like, she flies from her close pursuers, and at last fixes on the plodding mechanic who stays at home and minds his business.

div.p: They who lie soft and warm in a rich estate 10 seldom come to heat themselves at the altar. South.

p.hi: They who oppose a Ministry have always a better field for ridicule and reproof than they who defend it.
They who place their affections on trifles at first for amusement, will find those trifles at last become their serious concern.
They who play with the devil's rattles will be brought by degrees to wield his sword.
They who pretend most to universal benevolence are either deceivers or dupes—men who desire to cover their private ill-nature by a pretended regard for all.

div.p: They who resign life rather than part with 15 liberty do only a prudent action; but those who lay it down for friends and country do a heroic one. Steele.

p.hi: They who resist indiscriminately all improvement as innovation, may find themselves compelled at last to submit to innovations although they are not improvements.
They who seek only for faults see nothing else.
They who sustain their cross shall likewise be sustained by it in return.
They who travel in pursuit of wisdom walk only in a circle, and, after all their labour, at last return to their pristine ignorance.

div.p: They who want a farthing, and have no friend 20 that will lend them it, think farthings very good things. Goldsmith.

p.hi: They who want money when they come to borrow, will always want money when they should come to pay.

div.p: They who will watch Providence will never want a Providence to watch. (?)

p.hi: They whom truth and wisdom lead / Can gather honey from a weed.
Thick as autumnal leaves that strew the brooks / In Vallombrosa.

div.p: Thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, 25 saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left. Bible.

p.hi: Thine is the right, for thine the might.
Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: for better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.
Thine own worm be not: yet such jealousy, As hurts not others, but may make thee better, / Is a good spur.
Things all are big with jest; nothing that's plain / But may be witty, if thou hast the vein ... / Many affecting wit beyond their power, / Have got to be a dear fool for an hour.

div.p: Things are graceful in a friend's mouth which 30 are blushing in a man's own. Bacon.

p.hi: Things are his property alone who knows how to use them.
Things are long-lived, and God above appoints their term; yet when the brains of a thing have been out for three centuries and odd, one does wish it would be kind enough and die.
Things are not so false always as they seem.
Things are sullen, and will be as they are, whatever we think them or wish them to be.

div.p: Things are what they are by nature, not by 35 will. Cudworth.
Things at the worst will cease, or else climb upward / To what they were before. Macb., iv. 2.
Things bad begun make strong themselves by ill. Macb., iii. 2.
Things base and vile, holding no quantity, / Love can transpose to form and dignity. Mid. N.'s Dream, i. 1.

p.hi: Things fasten upon thee only according as the degree of thy own love and inclination for them gives opportunity and advantage.

div.p: Things good, great Jove, asked or unasked, 40 supply: / Things evil, though we ask for them, deny. Anon.

p.hi: Things have their laws as well as men; and things refuse to be trifled with.

div.p: Things ill got had ever bad success.... I'll leave my son my virtuous deeds behind. 3 Hen. VI., ii. 2.
Things may serve long, but not serve ever. All's Well, ii. 2.

p.hi: Things more excellent than every image are expressed through images.

div.p: Things must turn when they can go no farther. 45 Spurgeon.

p.hi: Things refuse to be mismanaged long.
Things seen are mightier than things heard.
Things will always right themselves in time, if only those who know what they want to do, and can do, persevere unremittingly in work and action.
Things will never be bettered by an excess of haste.

div.p: Things without remedy should be without regard; what is done, is done. Macb., iii. 2.
Things won are done; joy's soul lies in the doing. Troil. and Cress., i. 2.

p.hi: Think all you speak, but speak not all you think.

div.p: Think and thank God. Pr. 5

p.hi: Think naught a trifle, though it small appear; / Small sands the mountain, moments make the year, / And trifles life.
Think not, dream not that thou livest, / If thy hand doth idly lie, / If thy soul for ever longing, / Yearn but for the by and bye.
Think not I came to send peace on the earth; I came not to send peace but a sword.
Think not thy fame at every twitch will break; / By great deeds show that thou canst little do; / And do them not; that shall thy wisdom be; / And change thy temperance into bravery.

div.p: Think not thy own shadow longer than that of 10 others. Sir Thomas Browne.

p.hi: Think not your estate your own, while any man can call upon you for money which you cannot pay.
Think of ease, but work on.
Think of "living!" Thy life, wert thou the "pitifullest of all the sons of earth," is no idle dream, but a solemn reality. It is thy own; it is all thou hast to front eternity with.
Think of the hosts of worlds, and of the plagues in this world-mote—death puts an end to the whole.

div.p: Think with awe on the slow, the quiet power 15 of time. Schiller.

p.hi: Think wrongly, if you please, but in all cases think for yourself.

div.p: Think ye that God made the universe, and then let it run round his finger? (am Finger laufen liesse). Goethe.

p.hi: Think you, 'mid all this mighty sum / Of things for ever speaking, / That nothing of itself will come, / But we must still be seeking.
Thinkers are scarce as gold; but he whose thoughts embrace all his subject, pursues it uninterruptedly and fearless of consequences, is a diamond of enormous size.

div.p: Think'st thou existence doth depend on time? / 20 It doth; but actions are our epochs. Byron.

p.hi: Thinking about sin, beyond what is indispensable for the firm effort to get rid of it, is waste of energy and waste of time.
Thinking is but an idle waste of thought; / For nought is everything, and everything is nought.
Thinking is the function; living is the functionary.

Thinking leads man to knowledge. He may see and hear, and read and learn, whatever he pleases, and as much as he pleases; he will never know anything of it, except that which he has thought over, that which by thinking he has made the property of his mind.

div.p: Thinking nurseth thinking. Sir P. Sidney. 25
This above all; to thine own self be true, / And it must follow as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man. Ham., i. 3.
This bodes some strange eruption to our state. Ham., i. 1.

p.hi: This century is not ripe for my ideal; I live a citizen of those that are to come.
"This comes of walking on the earth."
The Spanish swell, as he picked himself up from the ground. Sp. Pr.

div.p: This communicating of a man's self to his 30 friend works two contrary effects, for it redoubleth joys and cutteth griefs in halves. Bacon.
This day / Shall change all griefs and quarrels into love. Henry V., v. 2.

p.hi: This day's propitious to be wise in.

div.p: This even-handed justice / Commends the ingredients of our poison'd chalice / To our own lips. Macb., i. 7.

p.hi: This ever-renewing generation of appearances rests on a reality, and a reality that is alive.

div.p: This fell sergeant, death, / Is strict in his 35 arrest. Ham., v. 2.

p.hi: This hand, to tyrants ever sworn the foe, / For freedom only deals the deadly blow: / Then sheathes in calm repose the vengeful blade / For gentle peace in freedom's hallowed shade.
This I think charity—to love God for himself, and our neighbour for God.
This is a great—properly the greatest—moment in a man's life, when, reconciling himself to necessity, he is able with clearness of purpose to say, "Let the will of the gods be done."
"This is a sharp medicine, but it cures all disorders."
Raleigh of the axe of his executioner.

div.p: This is faith; it is nothing more than obedience. 40 Voltaire.

p.hi: This is how I define talent; it is a gift God has given us in secret, which we reveal without knowing it.
This is not a time for purism of style; and style has little to do with the worth or unworth of a book.

This is not the liberty which we can hope, that no grievance should arise in the commonwealth, but when complaints are freely heard, deeply considered, and speedily reformed, then is the utmost bound of civil liberty attained that wise men look for.
This is the first condition of a living morality as well as of vital religion, that the soul shall find a true centre out from and above itself, round which it shall revolve.

div.p: This is the humour of it. Henry V., ii. 1. 45
This is the monstrosity in love—that the will is infinite, and the execution confined; that the desire is boundless, and the act a slave to limit. Troil. and Cress., iii. 2.

This is the state of man: to-day he puts forth / The tender leaves of hopes; to-morrow blossoms, / And bears his blushing honours thick upon him; / The third day comes a frost, a killing frost; / And when he thinks, good easy man, full surely / His greatness is a-ripening, nips his root, / And then he falls, as I do. Hen. VIII., iii. 2.
This is the very coinage of your brain; / This bodiless creation ecstasy / Is very cunning in. Ham., iii. 4.

p.hi: This is the very curse of an evil deed, that it engenders and must bring forth more evil.
This is true philanthropy, that buries not its gold in ostentatious charity, but builds its hospital in the human heart.
This low man seeks a little thing to do, / Sees it and does it; / This high man, with a great thing to pursue, / Dies ere he knows it.

div.p: This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with 5 them. Said of Jesus by the Jews in way of reproach.

p.hi: This narrow isthmus 'twixt two boundless seas, / The past, the future—two eternities.

div.p: This nothing's more than matter. Ham., iv. 5.

p.hi: This of old is sure, / That change of toil is toil's sufficient cure.
This one fact the world hates—that the soul becomes.

div.p: This present is a ruinous and ruining world. 10 Carlyle.

p.hi: This she knows in joys and woes, / That saints will aid if men will call; / For the blue sky bends over all.

This so solid-seeming world is, after all, but an air-image, our Me the only reality; and Nature, with its thousand-fold production and destruction, but the reflex of our own inward force, the "Phantasy of our Dream," or, what the earth-spirit in "Faust" names it, "the living visible garment of God."
This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but knew what to do with it.

div.p: This was a man. Jul. Cæs., v. 5.
This was the most unkindest cut of all. Jul. 15 Cæs., iii. 2.
This will prove a brave kingdom to me, where I shall have my music for nothing. Tempest, iii. 2.

p.hi: This world belongs to the energetic.
This world is a busy scene, and man a creature destined for a progressive struggle.
This world is all a fleeting show, / For man's illusion given: / The smiles of joy, the tears of woe, / Deceitful shine, deceitful flow, / There's nothing true but heaven.

div.p: This world is full of fools, and he who would 20 not wish to see one must not only shut himself up alone, but must also break his looking-glass. Boileau.
This world surely is wide enough to hold both thee and me! (uncle Toby to the fly). Sterne.

p.hi: This world, where much is to be done and little to be known.
Thistles and thorns prick sore, but evil tongues prick more.
Tho' men may bicker with the things they love, / They would not make them laughable in all eyes, / Not while they loved them.

div.p: Tho' world on world in myriad myriads roll / 25 Round us, each with different powers, / And other form of life than ours, / What know we greater than the soul? Tennyson.
Those are not empty-hearted whose low sound / Reverbs no hollowness. Lear, i. 1.

p.hi: Those are often raised into the greatest transports of mirth who are subject to the greatest depressions of melancholy.
Those deserve to be doubly laughed at that are peevish and angry for nothing to no purpose.
Those faces which have charmed us the most escape us the soonest.

div.p: Those faults conscience has not strength to 30 prevent, it seldom has justice enough to accuse. Goldsmith.
Those friends thou hast, and their adoption tried, / Grapple them to thy soul with hoops of steel. Ham., i. 3.
Those holy fields / Over whose acres walked those blessèd feet / Which, fourteen hundred years ago were nailed, / For our advantage, on the bitter cross. 1 Hen. IV., i. 1.

p.hi: Those of us who are worth anything spend our manhood in unlearning the follies or expiating the mistakes of our youth.
Those only are beautiful which, like the planets, have a steady, lambent light—are luminous, not sparkling.

div.p: Those only are despicable who fear to be 35 despised. La Roche.

p.hi: Those only deserve a monument who do not need one.
Those only obtain love, for the most part, who seek it not.
Those only who know little can be said to know anything. The greater the knowledge the greater the doubt.

Those people who are always improving never become great. Greatness is an eminence, the ascent to which is steep and lofty, and which a man must seize on at once by natural boldness and vigour, and not by patient, wary steps.

div.p: Those persons who do most good are least 40 conscious of it. Ward Beecher.

p.hi: Those tender tears that humanise the soul.
Those that are the loudest in their threats are the weakest in the execution of them.
Those that come unsought for are commonly the most valuable, and should be secured, because they seldom return.
Those that dare lose a day are dangerously prodigal; those that dare misspend it, desperate.

div.p: Those that fly may fight again, / Which he can 45 never do that's slain. Butler.

p.hi: Those that have loved longest love best.
Those that think must govern those that toil.

div.p: Those that with haste will make a mighty fire, / Begin with weak straws. Jul. Cæs., i. 3.

p.hi: Those who are bent to do wickedly will never want tempters to urge them on.

div.p: Those who are elevated enough in life to reason 50 and to reflect, yet low enough to keep clear of the venal contagion of a court—these are a nation's strength! Burns.

p.hi: Those who are quite satisfied sit still and do nothing; those who are not quite satisfied are the sole benefactors of the world.
Those who attempt to level never equalise; they load the edifice of society by setting up in the air what the solidity of the structure requires to be on the ground.
Those who attempt to reason us out of our follies, begin at the wrong end, since the attempt naturally presupposes us capable of reason.
Those who bring sunshine to the lives of others cannot keep it from themselves.
Those who can sit at home and gloat over their thousands in silent satisfaction are generally found to do it in plain clothes.

div.p: Those who carry much upon their clothes 5 are remarked for having but little in their pockets. Goldsmith.

p.hi: Those who do nothing generally take to shouting.
Those who dwell in fear dwell next door to hate; and I think it is the cowardice of women that makes them such intense haters.
Those who educate children well are more to be honoured than they who produce them; for these only gave them life, those the art of living well.
Those who first study fate, and say, Fate is the only cause of fortune and misfortune, terrify themselves.

div.p: Those who give the first shock to a state are 10 naturally the first to be overwhelmed in its ruin. The fruits of public commotion are seldom enjoyed by the man who was the first to set it a-going; he only troubles the waters for another's net. Montaigne.

p.hi: Those who have even studied good books may still be fools.
Those who injure one party to benefit another are quite as unjust as if they converted the property of others to their own benefit.
Those who make the best use of their time have none to spare.
Those who make the worst use of their time most complain of its shortness.

div.p: Those who only run after little things will not 15 go far. J. M. Barrie.

p.hi: Those who profess most are ever the least sincere.
Those who regularly undertake to cultivate friendship find ingratitude generally repays their endeavours.
Those who seek for something more than happiness in this world must not complain if happiness be not their portion.
Those who seem to doubt or deny us what is justly ours, let us either pity their prejudice or despise their judgment.

div.p: Those who set their minds to deny things, and 20 are fond of pulling things to pieces, must be treated like deniers-of-motion; one need only keep incessantly walking up and down before them in as composed a manner as possible. Goethe.

p.hi: Those who trust us educate us.
Those who will not be ruled by the rudder must be ruled by the rock.
Those who would make us feel must feel themselves.
Thou art Heaven's tasker; and thy God requires / The purest of thy flour, as well as of thy fires.

div.p: Thou art ignorant of what thou art, and much 25 more ignorant of what is fit for thee. Thomas à Kempis.

p.hi: Thou art in the end what thou art.
Thou art not alone if thou have faith. There is a communion of saints, unseen, yet not unreal, accompanying and brotherlike embracing thee, so thou be worthy.

div.p: Thou art the ruin of the noblest man / That ever lived in the tide of times. Jul. Cæs., iii. 1.

p.hi: Thou art thyself to all eternity.

div.p: Thou awakest us to delight in thy praise; for 30 thou madest us for thyself, and our heart is restless until it repose in thee. St. Augustine.
Thou bear'st thy heavy riches but a journey, / And death unloads thee. Meas. for Meas., iii. 1.

p.hi: Thou canst not be entirely free till thou hast attained to such a mastery as entirely to subdue and deny thyself.
Thou dost not strive, O Sun, but, meek and still, / Thou dost the type of Jesus best fulfil, / A noiseless revelation in the sky.

div.p: Thou hast given me / A world of earthly blessings to my soul, / If sympathy of love unite our thoughts. 2 Hen. VI., i. 1.
Thou hast not what others have, and others 35 have not the gift thou hast. From this imperfection springs sociability. Gellert.

p.hi: Thou little thinkest what a little foolery governs the world.
Thou mayest as well expect to grow stronger by always eating, as wiser by always reading.
Thou mayest be more prodigal of praise when thou writest a letter than when thou speakest in presence.
Thou must learn to break thine own will in many things if thou wilt have peace and concord with others.

div.p: Thou must live unto another if thou wilt live 40 unto thyself. Sen.

p.hi: Thou must renounce; thou must abstain! is the eternal song which sounds in the ears of every one, which every hour is singing to us all our life long.

div.p: Thou, Nature, art my goddess; to thy law / My services are bound. King Lear, i. 2.

Thou of an independent mind, / With soul resolved, with soul resigned; / Prepared Power's proudest frown to brave, / Who wilt not be, nor have a slave; / Virtue alone who dost revere, / Thy own reproach alone dost fear, / Approach this shrine (Independence), and worship here. Burns.

p.hi: Thou shall hear no more complaints from me; thou shalt hear only what happens to the wanderer.

div.p: "Thou shalt" is written upon life in characters 45 as legible as "Thou shalt not." Carlyle.

p.hi: Thou shalt look outward, not inward.
Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn.
Thou, too curious ear, that fain / Wouldst thread the maze of Harmony, / Content thee with one simple strain, / ... Till thou art duly trained, and taught / The concord sweet of Love divine.
Thou who didst the stars and sunbeams know, / Self-schooled, self-scanned, self-honoured, self-secure, / Didst walk on earth unguessed at.

div.p: Thou! why, thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a hair more or a hair less in his beard than thou hast. Thou wilt quarrel with a man for cracking nuts, having no other reason but because thou hast hazel eyes.... Thy head is full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat. Rom. and Jul., iii. 1.

p.hi: Thou wilt never sell thy life, or any part of thy life, in a satisfactory manner. Give it like a royal heart; let the price of it be nothing; then hast thou in a certain sense got all for it.

div.p: Thou would'st as soon go kindle fire with snow, / As seek to quench the fire of love with words. Two Gent. of Verona, ii. 7.
Thou wouldst do little for God if the devil 5 were dead. Sc. Pr.
Though a man may become learned by another's learning, he never can be wise but by his own wisdom. (?)

p.hi: Though a sinner do evil an hundred times, and his days be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him.
Though all his works abroad, / The heart benevolent and kind / The most resembles God.
Though ambition in itself is a vice, yet it is often the parent of virtues.

div.p: Though an honourable title may be conveyed 10 to posterity, yet the ennobling qualities which are the soul of greatness are a sort of incommunicable perfections, and cannot be transferred. (?)

p.hi: Though gentle, yet not dull, / Strong without rage, without o'erflowing, full.
Though great the force of little words, / Sped in an evil hour, / As great the might, and great the good, / Of one in Wisdom's power.
Though He comes in many shapes, / His love is throbbing in them all, / And from His love no soul escapes, / And from His mercy none can fall.
Though he says nothing, he pays it with thinking, like the Welshman's jackdaw.

div.p: Though He slay me, I shall yet trust in Him. 15 Bible.

p.hi: Though I am always in haste, I am never in a hurry.

div.p: Though justice be thy plea, consider this—/ That in the course of justice none of us / Should see salvation. Mer. of Venice, iv. 1.
Though last, not least. Jul. Cæs., iii. 1.
Though little fire grows great with little wind, / Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all. Tam. of Shrew, ii. 1.
Though losses and crosses / Be lessons right 20 severe, / There's wit there ye'll get there, / Ye'll find nae ither where. Burns.

p.hi: Though lost to sight, to memory dear.
Though love cannot plant morals in the human breast, it cultivates them when there.
Though much is taken, much abides.
Though old the thought and oft repress'd, / 'Tis his at last who says it best.

div.p: Though peace be in every man's wishes, yet 25 the qualifications and predispositions necessary for procuring and preserving it are the care of very few. Thomas à Kempis.

p.hi: Though scorn's malignant glances / Prove him poorest of his clan, / He's the noble—who advances / Freedom, and the cause of Man!
Though stars in skies may disappear, / And angry tempests gather, / The happy hour may soon be near / That brings us pleasant weather.
Though the cat winks a while, yet sure she is not blind.
Though the heavens fall, the orbs of truth and justice fall not.

div.p: Though the world exists for thought, thought 30 is daunted in presence of the world. Emerson.
Though this be madness, yet there is method in't. Ham., ii. 2.

p.hi: Though thousands hate physic, because of the cost, / Yet thousands it helpeth, that else should be lost.
Though we lose our fortune, yet we should not lose our patience.
Though wisdom wake, suspicion sleeps / At wisdom's gate; and to simplicity / Resigns her charge, while goodness thinks no ill where no ill seems.

div.p: Though you can fret me, you cannot play upon 35 me. Ham., iii. 2.

p.hi: Though you had the wisdom of Newton or the wit of Swift, garrulousness would lower you in the eyes of your fellow-creatures.
Though you stroke the nettle ever so kindly, yet it will sting you.

Thought and science follow their own law of development; they are slowly elaborated in the growth and forward pressure of humanity, in what Shakespeare calls ... The prophetic soul / Of the wide world dreaming on things to come.
Thought discovered is the more possessed.

div.p: Thought disturbs the world, and thought of 40 God / Unsettles most of all; for it is life, / And only life can comprehend its force, / Or guide it. Dr. W. Smith.

p.hi: Thought expands, but lames; action animates, but narrows.
Thought is deeper than all speech; / Feeling deeper than all thought; / Souls to souls can never teach / What unto themselves was taught.

div.p: Thought is free. As You Like It, i. 3.

p.hi: Thought is like opium: it can intoxicate us while it leaves us broad awake.

div.p: Thought is silence. Sheridan. 45

p.hi: Thought is the property of him who can entertain it, and of him who can adequately place it.

Thought is the seed of action; but action is as much its second form as thought is its first. It rises in thought, to the end that it may be uttered and acted. The more profound the thought, the more burdensome. Always in proportion to the depth of its sense does it knock importunately at the gates of the soul, to be spoken, to be done.
Thought is the wind, knowledge the sail, and mankind the vessel.
Thought means life, since those who do not think do not live in any high or real sense. Thinking makes the man.
Thought once awakened does not again slumber.
Thought takes man out of servitude into freedom.

div.p: Thought, true labour of any kind, highest 5 virtue itself, is it not the daughter of pain? Born as out of the black whirlwind; true effort in fact, as of a captive struggling to free itself—that is thought. Carlyle.

p.hi: Thought without reverence is barren, perhaps poisonous; at best dies, like cookery, with the day that called it forth.
Thought works in silence, so does virtue.
Thoughtlessness is precisely the chief public calamity of our day.
Thoughts are but dreams till their effects be tried.

div.p: Thoughts are not always at our beck; we 10 must wait till they come. Schopenhauer.
Thoughts (are) the slaves of life, and life time's fool; / And time, that takes survey of all the world, / Must have a stop. 1 Hen. IV., v. 4.

p.hi: Thoughts are your own; your words are so no more.
Thoughts come into our minds by avenues which we never left open, and thoughts go out of our minds through avenues which we never voluntary opened.
Thoughts shut up want air, and spoil, like bales unopened to the sun.

div.p: Thoughts take up no room. Jeremy Collier. 15

p.hi: Thoughts that breathe and words that burn.
Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears.
Thoughts that voluntary move / Harmonious numbers.
Thoughts we have had and pictures we have seen can be recalled by the mind; but the heart is not so obliging; it does not reproduce our pleasing emotions.

div.p: Threaten the threatener, and outface the 20 brow / Of bragging horror; so shall inferior eyes, / That borrow their behaviours from the great, / Grow great by your example, and put on / The dauntless spirit of resolution. King John, v. 1.

p.hi: Three may keep a secret—if two of them are dead.

Three poets in three distant ages born, / Greece, Italy, and England did adorn. / The first in loftiness of thought surpass'd; / The next, in majesty; in both, the last. / The force of Nature could no further go; / To make a third, she join'd the former two.
Three removes are as bad as a fire.

div.p: Three things drive a man out of doors—smoke, 25 a leaking roof, and a scolding wife. Pr.

p.hi: Three things that enrich genius are contentment of mind, the cherishing of good thoughts, and the exercise of memory.
Three thousand miles of ocean space are less impressive than three miles bounded by rugged mountain walls.
Three women and a goose make a market.
Thrice happy he who without rigour saves.

div.p: Thrice happy life that's from ambition free. 30 Allan Ramsay.
Thrice is he arm'd that hath his quarrel just; / And he but naked, though locked up in steel, / Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted. 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.

p.hi: Thrift must begin with little savings.
Through certain humours or passions, and from temper merely, a man may be completely miserable, let his outward circumstances be ever so fortunate.

div.p: Through every star, through every grass 35 blade, and most through every living soul, the glory of a present God still beams. Carlyle.

p.hi: Through steep ascents, through strait and rugged ways, / Ourselves to glory's lofty seats we raise: / In vain he hopes to reach the bless'd abode / Who leaves the narrow path for the more easy road.

div.p: Through tatter'd clothes small vices do appear; / Robes and furr'd gowns hide all. King Lear, iv. 6.

p.hi: Through "the ruins of a falling era," not once missing his footing.
Through want of enterprise and faith men are where they are, buying and selling, and spending their lives like serfs.

div.p: Through wisdom is an house builded; and by 40 understanding it is established; and by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches. Bible.

p.hi: Throw no gift again at the giver's head; / Better is half a loaf than no bread.

div.p: Throw physic to the dogs; I'll none of it. Macb., v. 3.
Thu' nur das Rechte in deinen Sachen, / Das Andre wird sich von selber machen—In thy affairs do thou only what is right, the rest will follow of itself. Goethe.

p.hi: Thursday come, and the week's gone.

div.p: Thus grief still treads upon the heels of pleasure; 45 / Married in haste, we may repent at leisure. Congreve.
Thus the native hue of resolution / Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought. Ham., iii. 1.
Thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges. Twelfth Night, iv. 2.
Thus we play the fools with the time; and the spirits of the wise sit in the clouds, and mock us. 2 Hen. IV., ii. 2.
Thus when I shun Scylla, your father, I fall into Charybdis, your mother. Mer. of Venice, iii. 5.

Thus with the year / Seasons return; but not 50 to me returns / Day, or the sweet approach of even or morn, / Or sight of vernal bloom or summer's rose, / Or flocks, or herds, or human face divine; / But cloud instead, and ever-during dark / Surrounds me. Milton.

p.hi: Thy actions, and thy actions alone, determine thy worth.
Thy friend put in thy bosom; wear his eyes / Still in thy heart, that he may see what's there. / If cause require, thou art his sacrifice.... / But love is lost; the way of friendship's gone.
Thy hand is never the worse for doing thy own work.
Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.

div.p: Thy nature / It is too full of the milk of human 5 kindness / To catch the nearest way. Macb., i. 5.

p.hi: Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power.
Thy praise or dispraise is to me alike, / One doth not stroke me, nor the other strike.
Thy soul was like a star and dwelt apart.

div.p: Thy spirit, Independence, let me share; / Lord 10 of the lion-heart and eagle-eye! / Thy steps I follow with my bosom bare, / Nor heed the storm that howls along the sky! Smollett.

p.hi: Thy sum of duty let two words contain; / Be humble and be just.
Thy true beginning and Father is in heaven, whom with the bodily eye thou shalt never behold, but only with the spiritual.

div.p: Thy wish was father, Harry, to that thought. 2 Hen. IV., iv. 4.
