div.p: Worte sind der Seele Bild—Words are the soul's magic. Goethe.
Worte sind gut, wenn Werke folgen—Words are good if works follow. Ger. Pr.

p.hi: Worth makes the man, and want of it the fellow; / The rest is all but leather or prunello.

div.p: Worth many thousand is the first salute; / 20 Him that salutes thee, therefore, friendly greet. Goethe.

p.hi: Worthless people live only to eat and drink; people of worth eat and drink only to live.
Would they could sell us experience, though at diamond prices, but then no one would use the article second-hand!
Would we but pledge ourselves to truth as heartily as we do to a real or imaginary mistress, and think life too short only because it abridges our time of service, what a new world we should have!
Would we but quit ourselves like men, and resolutely stand our ground, we should not fail of succours from above.

div.p: Would Wisdom for herself be wooed, / And 25 wake the foolish from his dream, / She must be glad as well as good, / And must not only be, but seem. Coventry Patmore.

p.hi: Would you have men think well of you, then do not speak well of yourself.
Wouldst thou a maiden make thy prize, / Thyself alone the bribe must be.
Wouldst thou both eat thy cake and have it?
Wouldst thou know thyself, then see how others act; wouldst thou understand others, look thou into thine own heart.

div.p: Wouldst thou plant for eternity? then plant 30 into the deep infinite faculties of man, his fantasy and heart. Wouldst thou plant for year and day? then plant into his shallow superficial faculties, his self-love and arithmetical understanding, what will grow there. Carlyle.

p.hi: "Wouldst thou," so the helmsman answered, / "Learn the secret of the sea? / Only those who brave its dangers / Comprehend its mystery!"
Wouldst thou subject all things to thyself? Subject thyself to reason.
Wouldst thou the life of souls discern? / Nor human wisdom nor divine / Helps thee by aught beside to learn; / Love is life's only sign.
Wouldst thou travel the path of truth and goodness? Never deceive either thyself or others.

div.p: Wounds and hardships provoke our courage, 35 and when our fortunes are at the lowest, our wits and minds are commonly at the best. Charron.

p.hi: Wounds cannot be cured without searching.
Wrap thyself up like a woodlouse, and dream revenge.
Write down the advice of him who loves you, though you like it not at present.
Write how you will, the critic shall show the world you could have written better.

div.p: Write, so much given to God; thou shalt be 40 heard. George Herbert.

p.hi: Writers of novels and romances in general bring a double loss on their readers—they rob them both of their time and money; representing men, manners, and things, that never have been, nor are likely to be; either confounding or perverting history and truth, inflating the mind, or committing violence upon the understanding.

Writing is not literature unless it gives to the reader a pleasure which arises not only from the things said, but from the way in which they are said; and that pleasure is only given when the words are carefully or curiously or beautifully put together into sentences.

div.p: Written all of it (Christianity) in us already in sympathetic ink. Bible awakens it, and you can read. Dr. Chalmers to Carlyle in conversation.

p.hi: Wrong is not only different from right, but it is in strict scientific terms infinitely different.

Wrongs are often forgiven, but contempt never is. Our pride remembers it for ever. It implies a discovery of weaknesses, which we are much more careful to conceal than crimes. Many a man will confess his crimes to a common friend, but I never knew a man who would tell his silly weaknesses to his most intimate one.

div.p: Würf er einen Groschen auf's Dach, fiel ihm 5 ein Thaler herunter—If he threw a penny up, a dollar came down. Ger. Pr.

div.head: Y.

p.hi: Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you.
Ye are the light of the world.
Ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you.
Ye are the salt of the earth.

div.p: Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat and 10 swallow a camel. Jesus.

p.hi: Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Ye fearful saints, fresh courage take; / The clouds ye so much dread / Are big with mercy, and shall break / In blessings on your head.
Ye gentlemen of England / That live at home at ease, / Ah! little do you think upon / The dangers of the seas.

div.p: Ye gods, it doth amaze me / A man of such a feeble temper should / So get the start of the majestic world / And bear the palm alone. Jul. Cæs., i. 2.
Ye good yeomen, whose limbs were made in 15 England. Hen. V., iii. 1.

p.hi: Ye hae a stalk o' carl-hemp in you.
Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you.
Ye mariners of England, / That guard our native seas, / Whose flag has braved a thousand years / The battle and the breeze.

Ye may darken over the blue heavens, ye vapoury masses in the sky. It matters not! Beyond the howling of that wrath, beyond the blackness of those clouds, there shines, unaltered and serene, the moon that shone in Paradise.... The moon that promises a paradise restored.

div.p: Ye men of gloom and austerity, who paint the 20 face of Infinite Benevolence with an eternal frown, read in the everlasting book, wide open to your view, the lesson it would teach. Its pictures are not in black and sombre hues, but bright and glowing tints; its music—save when ye drown it—is not in sighs and groans, but songs and cheerful sounds. Listen to the million voices in the summer air, and find one dismal as your own. Dickens.

p.hi: Ye shall know them by their fruits.

Ye stars! which are the poetry of heaven!... In our aspirations to be great, / Our destinies o'erleap their mortal state, / And claim a kindred with you; for ye are / A beauty and a mystery, and create / In us such love and reverence from afar, / That fortune, fame, power, life, have named themselves a star.
Ye think the rustic cackle of your bourg / The murmur of the world.
Ye'll find mankind an unco squad, / And muckle they may grieve ye.

div.p: Yea, let all good things await / Him who cares 25 not to be great, / But as he saves or serves the state. Tennyson.

p.hi: Yea, surely the sea like a harper laid hand on the shore as a lyre.
Year chases year, decay pursues decay, / Still drops some joy from withering life away.
Years do not make sages; they only make old men.
Years following years steal something every day; / At last they steal us from ourselves away.

div.p: Years steal / Fire from the mind as vigour 30 from the limb, / And life's enchanted cup but sparkles near the brim. Byron.

p.hi: Yes, there are things we must dream and dare, / And execute ere thought be half aware.
Yes, you find people ready enough to do the good Samaritan without the oil and twopence.

Yet a little while, and we shall all meet there, and our Mother's bosom will screen us all; and Oppression's harness, and Sorrow's fire-whip, and all the Gehenna bailiffs that patrol and inhabit ever-vexed Time, cannot harm us any more.
Yet all that poets sing, and grief hath known, / Of hopes laid waste, knells in that word—Alone.

div.p: Yet better thus, and known to be contemn'd, / 35 Than still contemn'd and flatter'd. King Lear, iv. 1.
Yet do I fear thy nature; / It is too full o' the milk o' human kindness. Macb., i. 5.

p.hi: Yet I doubt not through the ages one increasing purpose runs, / And the thoughts of men are widen'd by the process of the suns.
Yet I've heard say, by wise men in my day, / That none are outwitted so easy as they / Who reckon with all men as if they suspect them, / And traffic in caution, and watch to detect them.
Yet one thing secures us, whatever betide, / The Scripture assures us the Lord will provide.
Yet taught by Time, my heart has learned to glow / For other's good and melt at other's woe.
Yet there are surely times when there is nought / So needed as unsettling, just to get / Out of old ruts, and seek a nobler life.
Yet this grief / Is added to the griefs the great must bear, / That howsoever much they may desire / Silence, they cannot weep behind a cloud.

div.p: Yield not thy neck / To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind / Still ride in triumph over all mischance. 3 Hen. VI., iii. 3.
Yield not to temptation, for yielding is sin; / 5 Each victory will help you some other to win. H. M. Palmer.

p.hi: Yield to God's word and will, and you will escape many a calamity.
Yielding is sometimes the best way of succeeding.
Yielding, timid weakness is always abused and insulted by the unjust and unfeeling; but meekness, when sustained by the "fortiter in re," is always respected, commonly successful.
You accuse woman of wavering affection. Blame her not; she is but seeking a constant man.

div.p: You always aspire to very little at first, but 10 as you mount the ladder, you are sure to look down upon what you formerly looked up to as the height of happiness. Brothers Mayhew.
You always end ere you begin. Two Gent. of Verona, ii. 4.

p.hi: You are always willing enough to read lives, but never willing to lead them.

div.p: You are my true and honourable wife, / As dear to me as are the ruddy drops / That visit my sad heart. Jul. Cæs., ii. 1.

p.hi: You are not very good if you are not better than your best friends imagine you to be.

div.p: You are obliged to your imagination for three-fourths 15 of your importance. Garrick.

p.hi: You are prosperous, you are great, you are "beyond the world," as I have heard people say, meaning the power or the caprice thereof; but you are not beyond the power of events.
You are to come to your study as to the table, with a sharp appetite, whereby that which you read may the better digest. He that has no stomach to his book will very hardly thrive upon it.

div.p: You are transported by calamity / Thither where more attends you. Coriolanus, i. 1.

p.hi: You arrive at truth through poetry, and I arrive at poetry through truth.

div.p: You beat your pate, and fancy wit will come; / 20 Knock as you please, there's nobody at home. Pope.

p.hi: You begin in error when you suggest that we should regard the opinion of the many about just and unjust, good and evil, honourable and dishonourable.

div.p: You can easily ascertain (verstehen) what comes from the heart, for what comes from it in another's must go to your own. Körner.

p.hi: You can imagine thistle-down so light that when you run after it your running motion would drive it away from you, and that the more you tried to catch it the faster it would fly from your grasp. And it should be with every man, that, when he is chased by troubles, they, chasing, shall raise him higher and higher.
You can never be wise unless you love reading.

div.p: You can never by persistency make wrong 25 right. Johnson.

p.hi: You can speak well, if your tongue deliver the message of your heart.
You canna expect to be baith grand and comfortable.
You cannot abolish slavery by Act of Parliament, but can only abolish the name of it, which is very little.
You cannot climb a ladder by pushing others down.

div.p: You cannot fathom your mind. There is a well 30 of thought there which has no bottom; the more you draw from it, the more clear and fruitful it will be. G. A. Sala.

p.hi: You cannot get anything out of Nature or from God by gambling;—only out of your neighbour.

You cannot have the ware and the money both at once; and he who always hankers for the ware without having heart to give the money for it, is no better off than he who repents him of the purchase when the ware is in his hands.
You cannot have your work well done if the work be not of a right kind.

div.p: You cannot lead a fighting world without 35 having it regimented, chivalried; nor can you any more continue to lead a working world unregimented, anarchic. Carlyle.

p.hi: You cannot love the real sun, that is to say, physical light and colour, rightly, unless you love the spiritual sun, that is to say, justice and truth, rightly.
You cannot make a silk purse out of a sow's ear.
You cannot push a man far up a tree.
You cannot put a quartern loaf into a child's head; you must break it up, and give him the crumb in warm milk.

div.p: You cannot rear a temple like a hut of sticks 40 and turf. Dr. W. Smith.

p.hi: You cannot save men from death but by facing it for them, nor from sin but by resisting it for them.
You cannot secure even enjoyment in stagnation.
You can't be lost on a straight road.
You can't "have" your pudding unless you can "eat" it.

div.p: You can't order remembrance out of a man's 45 mind. Thackeray.

p.hi: You can't see the wood for the trees.
You can't tell a nut till you crack it.
You complain of the difficulty of finding work for your men; the real difficulty rather is to find men for your work.
You do not believe, you only believe that you believe.
You do not educate a man by telling him what he knew not, but by making him what he was not, and what he will remain for ever.
You don't value your peas for their roots or your carrots for their flowers. Now that's the way you should choose women.

div.p: You draw me, you hard-hearted adamant; / But yet you draw not iron, for my heart / Is true as steel; leave you your power to draw, / And I shall have no power to follow you. Mid. N.'s Dream, ii. 2.

p.hi: You feel yourself an exile in the East; but in the West too it is exile; I know not where under the sun it is not exile.

div.p: You find faut wi' your meat, and the faut's 5 all i' your own stomach. George Eliot.

p.hi: You find yourself refreshed by the presence of cheerful people. Why not make earnest effort to confer that pleasure on others? You will find half the battle is gained if you never allow yourself to say anything gloomy.
You frighten me out of my seven senses.
You gazed at the moon and fell in the gutter.
You give me nothing during your life, but you promise to provide for me at your death. If you are not a fool, you know what I wish for.

div.p: You have deserved / High commendation, true 10 applause and love. As You Like It, i. 2.
You have many enemies that know not / Why they are so, but, like to village curs, / Bark when their fellows do. Hen. VIII., iv. 2.

p.hi: You have no business with consequences; you are to tell the truth.
You have no hold on a human being whose affections are without a tap-root!
You have not outgrown, you cannot outgrow, the need of a great and authoritative teacher.

div.p: You have scotched the snake, not killed him. 15 Macb., iii. 2.
You have too much respect upon the world; / They lose it that do buy it with much care. Mer. of Ven., i. 1.

p.hi: You knock a man into the ditch, and then you tell him to remain content in the "position in which Providence has placed him."
You know how slight a line will tow a boat when afloat on the billows, though a cable would hardly move her when pulled up on the beach.
You know it is not my interest to pay the principal, nor is it my principle to pay the interest.
Sheridan to a creditor of his.

div.p: You know no rules of charity, / Which renders 20 good for bad, blessings for curses. Rich. III., i. 2.

p.hi: You know not where a blessing may light.
You know that in everything women write there are always a thousand faults of grammar, but, with your permission, a harmony which is rare in the writings of men.
You lie nearest to the river of life when you bend to it. You cannot drink but as you stoop.
You live one half year with deception and art; / With art and deception you live t'other part.

div.p: You make but a poor trap to catch luck if you 25 go and bait it with wickedness. George Eliot.

p.hi: You may as soon separate weight from lead, heat from fire, moistness from water, and brightness from the sun, as misery, discontent, calamity, and danger from man.
You may as well ask a loom which weaves huckaback why it does not make cashmere, as expect poetry from this engineer, or a chemical discovery from that jobber.

You may depend upon it, religion is, in its essence, the most gentlemanly thing in the world. It will alone gentilise, if unmixed with cant; and I know nothing else that will, alone; certainly not the army, which is thought to be the grand embellisher of manners.
You may depend upon it that he is a good man whose intimate friends are all good.

div.p: (You may) dig the deep foundations of a long-abiding 30 fame, / And wist not that they undermine (your) home of love and peace. Dr. W. C. Smith.

p.hi: You may do anything with bayonets except sit on them.
You may fail to shine, in the opinion of others, both in your conversation and actions, from being superior as well as inferior to them.
You may grow good corn in a little field.
You may have to wait a bit—some of you a shorter, some a longer time; but do wait, and everything will fit in and be perfect at last.

div.p: You may imitate, but never counterfeit. Balzac. 35

p.hi: You may know a wise man by his election of an aim, and a sagacious by his election of the means.
You may overthrow a government in the twinkling of an eye, as you can blow up a ship or upset and sink one; but you can no more create a government with a word than an iron-clad.
You may paint with a very big brush, and yet not be a great painter.

You may rest upon this as an unfailing truth, that there neither is, nor ever was, any person remarkably ungrateful who was not also insufferably proud; nor any one proud who was not equally ungrateful.

div.p: You may ride 's / With one soft kiss a thousand 40 furlongs ere / With spur we heat an acre. Winter's Tale, i. 2.

p.hi: You may say, "I wish to send this ball so as to kill the lion crouching yonder ready to spring upon me. My wishes are all right, and I hope Providence will direct the ball." Providence won't. You must do it; and if you do not, you are a dead man.
You might as well ask an oyster to make progress, as the people of any country in which grumbling could by any possibility be prohibited.
You must be content sometimes with rough roads.
"You must be in the fashion," is the utterance of weak-headed mortals.
You must begin at a low round of the ladder if you mean to get on.

div.p: You must confine yourself within the modest limits of order. Twelfth Night, i. 3.

p.hi: You must educate for education's sake only.

div.p: You must empty out the bathing-tub, but not 5 the baby along with it. Ger. Pr.
You must either be directed by some that take upon them to know, or take upon yourself that which I am sure you do not know, or jump the after-inquiry on your own peril. Cymbeline, v. 4.

p.hi: You must get your living by loving, else your life is at least half a failure.
You must live for another if you wish to live for yourself.

div.p: You must lose a fly to catch a trout. Pr. 10

p.hi: You must not equivocate, nor speak anything positively for which you have no authority but report, or conjecture, or opinion.
You must not fear death, my lads; defy him, and you drive him into the enemy's ranks.
You must not fight too often with one enemy, or you will teach him all your art of war.
You must not measure every man's corn by your own bushel.

div.p: You must not suppose that everything goes 15 right at first even with the best of us. Mrs. Gatty.
You must not think / That we are made of stuff so flat and dull, / That we can let our beard be shook with danger, / And think it pastime. Ham., iv. 7.

p.hi: You must rouse in men a consciousness of their own prudence and strength, if you would raise their character.
You must seek and find God in the heart.
You need not tell all the truth, unless to those who have a right to know it all. But let all you tell be truth.

div.p: You never can elude the gods when you even 20 devise wrong. Thales.

p.hi: You never long the greatest man to be; / No! all you say is; "I'm as good as he." / He's the most envious man beneath the sun / Who thinks that he's as good as every one.
You never will love art well till you love what she mirrors better.
You often understand the true connection of important events in your life not while they are going on, nor soon after they are past, but only a considerable time afterwards.
You ought to read books, as you take medicine, by advice, and not advertisement.

div.p: You rub the sore, when you should bring the 25 plaster. Tempest, ii. 1.

p.hi: You said your say; / Mine answer was my deed.
You see when they row in a barge, they that do drudgery work, slash, and puff, and sweat; but he that governs sits quietly at the stern, and scarce is seen to stir.

div.p: You shall never take a woman without her answer, unless you take her without her tongue. As You Like It, iv. 1.
You shall not shirk the hobbling Times to catch a ride on the sure-footed Eternities. "The times (as Carlyle says) are bad; very well, you are there to make them better." John Burroughs.
You take my house, when you do take the 30 prop / That doth sustain my house; you take my life / When you do take the means whereby I live. Mer. of Ven., iv. 1.
You that choose not by the view, / Choose as fair, and choose as true. Mer. of Ven., iii. 2.

p.hi: You traverse the world in search of happiness, which is within the reach of every man; a contented mind confers it on all.

You watch figures in the fields, digging and delving with spade or pick. You see one of them from time to time straightening his loins, and wiping his face with the back of his hand.... It is there that for me you must seek true humanity and great poetry.

div.p: You were used / To say, extremity was the trier of spirits; / That common chances common men could bear; / That when the sea was calm, all boats alike / Showed mastership in floating. Coriolanus, iv. 1.
You who are ashamed of your poverty, and 35 blush for your calling, are a snob; as are you who boast of your pedigree, or are proud of your wealth. Thackeray.

p.hi: You who follow wealth and power with unremitting ardour, / The more in this you look for bliss, you leave your view the farther.
You who forget your friends, meanly to follow after those of a higher degree, are a snob.
You will as often find a great man above, as below, his reputation, when once you come to know him.
You will catch more flies with a spoonful of honey than with a cask of vinegar.

div.p: You will find angling to be like the virtue of 40 humility, which has a calmness of spirit and a world of other blessings attending upon it. Izaac Walton.

p.hi: You will find rest unto your souls when first you take on you the yoke of Christ, but joy only when you have borne it as long as He wills.
You will find that most books worth reading once are worth reading twice.
You will find that silence, or very gentle words, are the most exquisite revenge for reproaches.

You will get more profit from trying to find where beauty is, than in anxiously inquiring what it is. Once for all, it remains undemonstrable; it appears to us, as in a dream, when we behold the works of the great poets and painters; and in short, of all feeling artists; it is a hovering, shining, shadowy form, the outline of which no definition holds.
You will never live to my age, without you keep yourselves in breath with exercise, and in heart with joyfulness.
You will never miss the right way if you only act according to your feelings and conscience.
You will never see anything worse than yourselves.
You wise, / To call him shamed, who is but overthrown?

div.p: You wish, O woman, to be ardently loved, and 5 for ever, even until death, be thou the mother of your children. Jean Paul.

p.hi: You write with ease to show your breeding, / But easy writing's cursed hard reading.
You'll repent if you marry, and you'll repent if you don't.
Young authors give their brains much exercise and little food.
Young Christians think themselves little; growing Christians think themselves nothing; full-grown Christians think themselves less than nothing.

div.p: Young folk, silly folk; old folk, cold folk. 10 Dut. Pr.
Young hot colts, being raged, do rage the more. Rich. II., ii. 1.

p.hi: Young men are apt to think themselves wise enough, as drunken men are to think themselves sober enough.
Young men are fitter to invent than to judge; fitter for execution than for counsel; and fitter for new projects than for settled business.
Young men soon give, and soon forget affronts; old age is slow in both.

div.p: Young men think that old men are fools; but 15 old men know young men are fools. Chapman.
Young people are quick enough to observe and imitate. (?)

p.hi: Your acts are detectives, keener and more unerring than ever the hand of sensational novelist depicted; they will dog you from the day you sinned till the hour your trial comes off.
Your born angler is like a hound that scents no game but that which he is in pursuit of.
Your cause belongs / To him who can avenge your wrongs.

div.p: Your goodness must have some edge to it, 20 else it is none. Emerson.

p.hi: Your hands in your own pockets in the morning, is the beginning of the last day; your hands in other people's pockets at noon, is the height of the last day.

div.p: Your "if" is the only peacemaker; much virtue in "if." As You Like It, v. 4.

p.hi: Your labour only may be sold; your soul must not.
Your learning, like the lunar beam, affords light but not heat.

div.p: Your levellers wish to level down as far as 25 themselves; but they cannot bear levelling up to themselves. J. Boswell.

p.hi: Your noblest natures are most credulous.
Your own soul is the thing you ought to look after.
Your own words and actions are the only things you will be called to account for.
Your prime one need is to do right, under whatever compulsion, till you can do it without compulsion. And then you are a Man.

div.p: Your tongue runs before your wit. Swift. 30

p.hi: Your rusty kettle will continue to boil your water for you if you don't try to mend it. Begin tinkering and there is an end of your kettle.
Your voiceless lips, O flowers, are living preachers,—each cup a pulpit, and each leaf a book.
Your words are like notes of dying swans—/ Too sweet to last.
You're always sure to detect / A sham in the things folks most affect.

div.p: Yours is a pauper's soul, a rich man's pelf: / 35 Rich to your heirs, a pauper to yourself. Lucillius.

p.hi: Youth, abundant wealth, high birth, and inexperience, are, each of them, the source of ruin. What then must be the fate of him in whom all four are combined?
Youth beholds happiness gleaming in the prospect. Age looks back on the happiness of youth, and, instead of hopes, seeks its enjoyment in the recollection of hope.
Youth, enthusiasm, and tenderness are like the days of spring. Instead of complaining, O my heart, of their brief duration, try to enjoy them.
Youth ever thinks that good whose goodness or evil he sees not.

div.p: Youth fades; love droops; the leaves of friendship 40 fall; a mother's secret hope outlives them all! Holmes.

p.hi: Youth holds no society with grief.
Youth is a blunder; manhood, a struggle; old age, a regret.
Youth is ever apt to judge in haste, and lose the medium in the wild extreme.
Youth is ever confiding; and we can almost forgive its disinclination to follow the counsels of age, for the sake of the generous disdain with which it rejects suspicion.

div.p: Youth is full of sport, age's breath is short; / 45 Youth is nimble, age is lame: / Youth is hot and bold, age is weak and cold; / Youth is wild, and age is tame. Shakespeare.

p.hi: Youth is not rich in time; it may be, poor; part with it, as with money, sparing; pay no moment but in purchase of its worth; and what its worth ask death-beds, they can tell.

Youth is not the age of pleasure; we then expect too much, and we are therefore exposed to daily disappointments and mortifications. When we are a little older, and have brought down our wishes to our experience, then we become calm and begin to enjoy ourselves.
Youth is the season of credulity.

Youth is too tumultuous for felicity; old age too insecure for happiness. The period most favourable to enjoyment, in a vigorous, fortunate, and generous life, is that between forty and sixty. Life culminates at sixty.
Youth may make / Even with the year; but age, if it will hit, / Shoots a bow short, and lessens still his stake, / As the day lessens, and his life with it.
Youth never yet lost its modesty where age had not lost its honour; nor did childhood ever refuse its reverence, except where age had forgotten correction.

div.p: Youth no less becomes / The light and careless livery that it wears, / Than settled age his sables and his weeds, / Importing health and graveness. Ham., iv. 7.
Youth to itself rebels, though none else near. 5 Ham., i. 3.

p.hi: Youth would rather be stimulated than instructed.
Youth, when thought is speech and speech is truth.

Youth will never live to age, without they keep themselves in breath with exercise, and in heart with joyfulness. Too much thinking doth consume the spirits; and oft it falls out, that while one thinks too much of doing, he leaves to do the effect of his thinking.
Youthful failing is not to be admired except in so far as one may hope that it will not be the failing of old age.

div.head: Z.
div.p: Zahltag kommt alle Tag—Pay-day comes every 10 day. Ger. Pr.
Zankt, wenn ihr sitzt beim Weine, / Nicht um Kaisers Bart—Wrangle not over your winecups about trifles (lit. about the Emperor's beard). Geibel.

p.hi: Zeal ever follows an appearance of truth, and the assured are too apt to be warm; but it is their weak side in argument, zeal being better shown against sin than persons, or their mistakes.

Zeal for uniformity attests the latent distrusts, not the firm convictions, of the zealot. In proportion to the strength of our self-reliance is our indifference to the multiplication of suffrages in favour of our own judgment.
Zeal is fit for wise men, but flourishes chiefly among fools.

div.p: Zeal is like fire; it needs both feeding and 15 watching. Pr.

p.hi: Zeal is no further commendable than as it is attended with knowledge.
Zeal is very blind or badly regulated when it encroaches upon the rights of others.
Zeal without knowledge is a runaway horse.
Zeal without knowledge is like expedition to a man in the dark.

div.p: Zeit ist's, die Unfälle zu beweinen, / Wenn sie 20 nahen und wirklich erscheinen—It is time enough to bewail misfortunes when they come and actually happen. Schiller.
Zeit verdeckt und entdeckt—Time covers and uncovers everything. Ger. Pr.
Zeitungsschreiber: ein Mensch, der seinen Beruf verfehlt hat—A journalist, a man who has mistaken his calling. Bismarck.

Zerstreuung ist wie eine goldene Wolke, die den Menschen, / Wär es auch nur auf kurze Zeit, seinem Elend entrückt—Amusement is as a golden cloud, which, though but for a little, diverts man from his misery. Goethe.
Zerstörend ist des Lebens Lauf, / Stets frisst ein Thier das andre auf—Destructive is the course of life; ever one animal eats up another. Bodenstedt.
Zerstreutes Wesen führt uns nicht zum Ziel—A 25 distracted existence leads us to no goal. Goethe.

p.hi: Zeus hates busybodies and those who do too much.

div.p: Zielen ist nicht genug; es gilt Treffen—To aim is not enough; you must hit. Ger. Pr.
Zonam perdidit—He has lost his purse (lit. his girdle). Hor.
Zu leben weiss ich, mich zu kennen weiss ich nicht—How to live I know, how to know myself I know not. Goethe.
Zu Rom bestehen die 10 Gebote aus den 10 30 Buchstaben; / Da pecuniam—gieb Gelder—At Rome the Ten Commandments consist of ten letters—Da pecuniam—Give money. C. J. Weber.
Zu schwer bezahlt man oft ein leicht Versehn—One often smarts pretty sharply for a slight mistake. Goethe.
Zu viel Demuth ist Hochmuth—Too much humility is pride. Ger. Pr.
Zu viel Glück ist Unglück—Too much good luck is ill luck. Ger. Pr.
Zu viel Weisheit ist Narrheit—Too much wisdom is folly. Ger. Pr.

Zu viel Wissbegierde ist ein Fehler, und aus 35 einem Fehler können alle Laster entspringen, wenn man ihm zu sehr nachhängt—Too much curiosity is a fault; and out of one fault all vices may spring, when one indulges in it too much. Lessing.
Zufrieden sein, das ist mein Spruch—Contentment is my motto. M. Claudius.
Zum Kriegführen sind dreierlei Dinge nötig—Geld! Geld! Geld!—To carry on war three kinds of things are necessary—Money! money! money! The German Imperial commandant, Lazarus von Schwendi, in 1584.
Zum Leiden bin ich auserkoren—To suffer am I elected. Schikaneder-Mozart.
Zur Tugend der Ahnen / Ermannt sich der Held—The hero draws inspiration from the virtue of his ancestors. Goethe.
Zwar eine schöne Tugend ist die Treue, / Doch 40 schöner ist Gerechtigkeit—Fidelity indeed is a noble virtue, yet justice is nobler still. Platen.
Zwar nicht wissen—aber glauben / Heisst ganz richtig—Aberglauben—Not to know, but to believe, what else is it, strictly speaking, but superstition? Franz v. Schönthan.

Zwar sind sie an das Beste nicht gewöhnt, / Allein sie haben schrecklich viel gelesen—It is true they (the public) are not accustomed to the best, but they have read a frightful deal (and are so knowing therefore). Goethe, the theatre manager in "Faust."
Zwar weiss ich viel, doch möcht' ich alles wissen—True, I know much, but I would like to know everything. Goethe, "Faust."
Zwei Fliegen mit einer Klappe schlagen—To kill two flies with one flapper; to kill two birds with one stone. Ger. Pr.
Zwei gute Tage hat der Mensch auf Erden; / Den Hochzeitstag und das Begrabenwerden—Man has two gala-days on earth—his marriage-day and his funeral-day. Ger. Pr.
Zwei Seelen und ein Gedanke, / Zwei Herzen und ein Schlag—Two souls and one thought, two hearts and one pulse. Halen.
Zwei Seelen wohnen, ach! in meiner Brust, / 5 Die eine will sich von der andern trennen—Two souls, alas! dwell in my breast; the one struggles to separate itself from the other. Goethe, "Faust."

Zwei sind der Wege, auf welchen der Mensch zur Tugend emporstrebt, / Schliesst sich der eine dir zu, thut sich der andre dir auf, / Handelnd erreicht der Glückliche sie, der Leidende duldend; / Wohl ihm, den sein Geschick liebend auf beiden geführt—There are two roads on which man strives to virtue; one closes against thee, the other opens to thee; the favoured man wins his way by acting, the unfortunate by endurance; happy he whom his destiny guides him lovingly on both. Schiller.

Zweierlei Arten giebt es, die treffende Wahrheit zu sagen; / Oeffentlich immer dem Volk, immer dem Fürsten geheim—There are two ways of telling the pertinent truth—publicly always to the people, always to the prince in private. Goethe.
Zwischen Amboss und Hammer—Between the anvil and the hammer. Ger. Pr.
Zwischen heut' und morgen sind Grüfte, zwischen Versprechen und Erfüllen Klüfte—Between to-day and to-morrow are graves, and between promising and fulfilling are chasms. Rückert.
Zwischen Lipp' und Kelchesrand / Schwebt 10 der dunkeln Mächte Hand—Between cup and lip hovers the hand of the dark powers. F. Kind.
Zwischen uns sei Wahrheit—Let there be truth between us. Goethe.
